**Yes, but only with approval.** Friday isn't banned. A Friday prod deploy needs sign-off from the on-call engineering manager first [6]. The October 2026 pipeline update repeats this, so it is still current [8].

## The rule
- The standard deploy window is Monday–Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific [6][8].
- Friday deploys need approval from the on-call engineering manager [6][8].
- The sources don't say whether the 09:00–16:00 hours also apply on Fridays, or who the on-call engineering manager is in a given week. Ask in `#eng-leads` if you're unsure.
- Rollbacks are allowed at any time, with no approval, including during freezes [6][7][8].

## Extra requirements on any deploy
- **Canary bake:** since October 12, every deploy sits in canary (5% of traffic) for 45 minutes, not 20. It must pass the error-rate and p95 latency checks. It must also show no sustained TLS handshake errors and no runner consumer lag growth above 2 minutes [8].
- **Friday timing:** a typical non-data-plane change takes about 50 minutes from merge to all cells. Data-plane changes (`ingest/` or `runner/`) roll out in waves and take about 2.5 hours [8]. A Friday afternoon deploy can therefore still be mid-rollout late in the day.
- **Two approvals:** changes to billing, authentication and the data plane need two approvals [8].
- **Normal changes:** schema migrations, infrastructure config, retention settings, and auth or billing logic need sign-off from your team's change approver. Add the `change:normal` label and fill in the risk and rollback sections [7]. Approvals last 7 days [7].
- **Restricted-data services:** these also need Security sign-off [7].
- **Holding a deploy:** anyone can stop a promotion with `/deploy hold <deploy-id>` [8].

## Other freezes to check
- **Month-end billing freeze:** no normal changes to Ledger from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually the 2nd [7]. This month's freeze started Friday, October 30, and is expected to end around November 2 [9]. Today is Saturday, October 31, so Ledger is frozen right now.
- **Holiday freeze:** December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027. Only standard and emergency changes ship [7].

## Emergencies
During a declared incident, the incident commander can approve emergency changes. The owning team's change approver reviews them within two business days [7]. The IC can also skip the canary bake with `/deploy expedite`, which is logged in `#eng-changes` [8]. Exceptions are also logged in `#eng-changes` [7].

## Not found
I found no vendor agreement or support policy that restricts when production changes can be made. The on-call runbook covers severity levels and response times, but nothing specific to Friday deploys [1].

**Short answer:** A patient whose household income is under 250% of the federal poverty level (FPL) qualifies for the sliding-fee program. The program reduces visit costs by 40–100% [1].

**What the knowledge base doesn't say**
- **Tier breakdown.** I found no schedule showing which income band gets which discount within the 40–100% range. For example, I can't tell you what percentage a patient at 150% FPL gets compared with one at 240%. Check the sliding-fee program contact or Revenue Cycle/billing for the actual schedule.
- **Documents and household size.** I found no documentation requirements and no household-size rules. The FAQ says only that front desk staff can start the application at check-in [1].
- **Minimum fees.** I found no stated minimum fee or other exclusions.

**What you can tell the patient**
- No patient is ever denied care because of inability to pay [1].
- Self-pay visit prices before any discount are [1]:
  - New patient: $165
  - Established patient: $120
  - Telehealth: $79
  - Annual physical: $195
- Self-pay patients also get a 20% prompt-pay discount if they pay in full that day [1]. This is a separate benefit from the sliding-fee program. The vaccine and injectable formulary says the prompt-pay discount doesn't apply to vaccines or injectables, and that sliding-fee patients get the program discount on those instead [4].
- Other benefits for sliding-fee patients:
  - Records and forms fees are waived [3].
  - The 2025 policy didn't bill the $25 no-show fee to sliding-fee patients [7]. That fee has since been eliminated for everyone, effective October 5, 2026 [5].
- If a patient has a balance over $200, interest-free payment plans of up to 12 months are available [1].
- Statements go out 7 days after the insurance claim is processed, and balances are due within 30 days [1].
- Accounts are never sent to collections without a final notice and a call from the billing team [1].
- A patient with an outstanding balance over $250 is referred to the billing team but never turned away [6].

A critical lab result has to reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes. If you can't reach them within 30 minutes, the result goes to the on-call medical director. This comes from Halcyon's clinical escalation protocol [1].

## Time limits and escalation
- **60 minutes:** Critical results must reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes [1].
- **30 minutes:** If the ordering clinician can't be reached in 30 minutes, the result goes to the medical director on call [1].
- **Separate 30-minute rule:** The same protocol says to notify the supervising physician within 30 minutes for "a critical lab value called in by the reference lab" [1]. The documents don't explain how this fits with the 60-minute rule for the ordering clinician. The safe reading is to start trying the ordering clinician and the supervising physician right away. Don't use the full 60 minutes.

## How to reach the on-call medical director
- Call the Halcyon answering service at **555-0144** and choose **option 2** [3].
- The service pages the on-call medical director. If there is no callback within 10 minutes, it pages the backup [3].
- On-call medical directors must answer pages within 10 minutes, day or night [3].
- Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers. Answering-service pages are logged and timed, and the chart documentation needs that record [3].
- This week (week 44, October 26 to November 2, with handover Monday at 08:00 Eastern) the on-call director is Dr. Priya Natarajan. The backup is Dr. Samuel Achterberg [3].
- The next rota starts November 2 with Dr. Helen Mwangi, and Dr. Luis Carvalho as backup [3].

## Documentation
Chart every critical result notification with the **time** and the **person notified** [1]. If you escalate to the on-call medical director, the logged page gives you that timestamp [3]. The on-call director's Monday handover also covers pending critical results [3].

## What I couldn't find
- **Read-back:** I found no read-back or verification requirement in the documents I searched.
- **Who takes the lab's call:** I found nothing on who at the clinic receives the lab's call or is responsible for passing it on.
- **Contract terms:** I found no contractual turnaround time for Bayline Reference Laboratories to phone critical values. The Bayline items I found cover only the results feed:
  - a P1 response of 30 minutes from a 24/7 interface desk [4];
  - an agreement amendment in progress that would require 30 days' notice of feed changes [2].

  Check the lab services agreement itself, or ask Lab contracts in Clinical Operations.
- **Covering provider:** I found no covering-provider step between the ordering clinician and the medical director.

A customer who prepays for Growth annually saves **15%, or $2,160 in the first year**.

- Growth lists at $1,200 per month, which is $14,400 over 12 months [1].
- The annual prepay price is $12,240 per year, a 15% discount [1].
- The difference is $14,400 − $12,240 = $2,160, or about $180 per month. That is the same as getting 1.8 months free (my calculation).

**Is the discount still current?** Yes. The September 24, 2026 sales desk memo, effective for quotes issued on or after October 1, 2026, says the 15% annual prepay discount on Growth is unchanged [2].

**Conditions and related rules**
- Discounts are measured against the first-year contract value at list price [1][2].
- Multi-year deals can add 5% per committed year, capped at 10%. That extra doesn't count toward the approval thresholds [1][2].
- Under the new matrix, a Growth discount of up to 15% can be approved by an account executive with no deal desk review. Anything above 15% goes to the deal desk [2].
- Registered non-profits and accredited educational institutions get 50% off Growth automatically, with no approval needed [1][2].
- Annual contracts are refundable within the first 30 days, minus usage at list price. Monthly plans can be cancelled at any time, effective at the end of the billing period, and are not prorated [1].

**Gaps in the sources**
- The sources don't say whether the 15% prepay discount stacks with the non-profit 50% discount.
- They don't mention seat minimums or regional price differences for Growth.
- The $12,240 figure assumes the base plan with 100 million events per month. Overage is $8 per additional million [1]. The sources don't say whether overage is discounted.

**A visit link keeps working for 2 hours after the appointment's scheduled end time, then it expires.** The telehealth platform requirements say this directly [1]. The October 21, 2026 Juniper steering committee notes repeat it: "Visit links will expire 2 hours after the scheduled end time, as in the requirements" [2].

- **The clock runs from the scheduled end, not the actual end.** If a 30-minute visit scheduled for 10:00–10:30 ends early, the link still works until 12:30. The sources don't say what happens to a visit that runs past its scheduled end.
- **The rule is for the new platform.** It comes from the requirements for the new telehealth platform, which is still in development, and from the Juniper steering committee notes [1][2]. The new platform is built on Coriander Media's video SDK [2][3].
- **Larkspur's current behavior isn't documented.** Larkspur Telehealth is the current platform. Pilot clinics move off it in January 2027 and all clinics by early March 2027 [4]. I found nothing on how long Larkspur links stay active.
- **Guest links:** interpreters join through a guest link [6]. The requirements describe caregivers joining with a single link [1]. The sources don't say whether those links expire on a different schedule.

I found no vendor-side setting for link expiry or session timeout, and no exceptions for follow-ups, late joins or extended sessions. The Coriander record lists only connection logs, which are kept for 30 days, and says recordings are disabled [3]. That log retention doesn't affect how long a link works.

Patients are sent the join link by SMS 2 hours before a telehealth visit [7].

Emergency access to a customer workspace lasts **2 hours**. A **second engineer** has to approve it.

## Duration
- Access expires after 2 hours. That is deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport production session [3].
- If you need more time, request access again and add an update to the case [3].

## Approval
- You request access with `nwctl access request --workspace <id> --reason <case-or-incident-id>`. You need an open support case or a declared incident, and the request must cite its ID [3].
- A second engineer from the support or on-call rotation approves the request in Teleport [3].
- You can't approve your own request, and the approver can't be on the same case [3].
- **Write access needs more.** Access is read-only by default. To edit a pipeline for the customer, you first need their written consent in the case [3].

## Recording and review
- All sessions are recorded and kept for one year [3].
- The workspace's audit log shows "Northwind support accessed this workspace", with the time and case ID. Enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours [3].
- Security reviews a sample of sessions every week. It also reviews every session that used write access [3].

## Rules while you have access
- Don't export or download event payloads, and don't paste them into tickets, Slack, or support replies. Use field names and counts instead [3].
- Don't share your session or screen-share it with a customer [3].
- Don't use emergency access on a workspace belonging to someone you know personally [3].
- If you see data you didn't expect, such as another customer's data, end the session and report it in `#security-help` immediately [3].

The documents don't describe a different approver for different severities. They also don't describe a way to extend a session without a new request.

The Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Kenji Watanabe, chairs the Patient Safety Committee.

- The Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy (updated March 1, 2026) says completed root cause analyses go to the Patient Safety Committee. It names the Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Kenji Watanabe, as chair. The committee meets monthly and tracks every action item to closure [3].
- The Clinical systems change control policy says the same thing. It adds that Dr. Watanabe reviews sentinel events and is not part of software change approval [2].

**No. Taking the name out doesn't make it allowed.** Halcyon's policy says not to paste a patient's history into a public chatbot, even without the name.

**Policy on AI tools**
- PHI may only be stored in the EHR, the practice management system, and approved Halcyon systems. The HIPAA policy says never to put PHI into "AI tools that are not on the approved list" [1].
- The approved AI tools page says "De-identified" is not a loophole. Removing a name isn't enough to make a case non-identifiable, so you should treat any patient details as PHI [2].
- Public chatbots and general-purpose AI assistants are on the not-approved list. That covers any device, including personal phones. Browser extensions that summarize pages are also on it [2].

**Approved tools**

| Tool | PHI allowed? | What it's for |
|---|---|---|
| Quillon Ambient | Yes | Drafts visit notes from the conversation. It's limited to the Riverside and Elm Park pilot clinics. The patient must give verbal consent at the start of every visit, and the clinician reviews and signs every note [2]. |
| Meridian draft replies | Yes | Drafts replies to patient portal messages inside the EHR. A clinician must edit or approve each one before it's sent [2]. |
| Halcyon Assist | **No** | Answers policy questions only. Don't paste patient details into it, even without names [2][3]. |

None of the approved tools summarizes a patient's history for you. The Quillon vendor record also says other AI scribes are not approved, even for trials [4]. I found no approved chatbot for history summaries.

**If you want an AI summarization tool**
Email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) at privacy@halcyon.example. A tool that will handle PHI needs four things [2]:
1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed business associate agreement with the vendor.
3. An entry in the systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO.

This usually takes 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [2]. The October 28 CSCAB minutes repeat that a new place where PHI is stored needs a risk assessment and an inventory entry before go-live, not after [5].

**If you've already pasted patient information into an unapproved tool**
- Report it as a suspected privacy incident to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours. Email privacy@halcyon.example or call the compliance hotline [1]. Breaches affecting 500 or more people must be reported to HHS within 60 days, and the Privacy Officer handles that [1].
- I couldn't find a policy that sets specific sanctions for putting PHI into an AI tool. Related policies do say that looking up records of family, coworkers or yourself is a terminable offense [1], and that inappropriate break-the-glass use is a privacy incident that "may lead to sanctions up to termination" [7]. Ask the Privacy Officer if you need to know how an AI-tool incident would be handled.

**What to do instead**
Write the summary yourself in the EHR. If the goal is faster documentation, ask whether your clinic can use Quillon Ambient or Meridian draft replies.

**287 workspaces** got duplicate invoices in the October billing incident (INC-2340). We refunded **$184,300** in total, across 201 card charges.

**Workspaces and invoices**
- The month-end invoicing job produced duplicate September invoices. Arjun Mehta counted 312 duplicate invoices across 287 workspaces on October 6 [1].
- Of those 312 invoices, 201 were auto-charged to card customers on auto-pay. The other 111 were invoiced but not charged [1].

**Refunds**
- Harriet Vance decided to refund all 201 charges the same day, without waiting for customers to ask. She also decided to void the other 111 invoices [1].
- At 12:30 UTC she confirmed that "refunds issued for all 201 charges, $184,300 total. voids done" [1].
- The incident log's one-line summary matches, listing "201 card charges refunded" [2]. It gives no dollar figure.

**Cause and resolution**
- The payment provider's webhook for the first batch timed out. Our retry logic re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [1].
- The fix was an idempotency key per workspace and billing period. It was deployed on October 6 [1], and the weekly status lists it as shipped October 8 [3].
- INC-2340 was resolved after 3h 19m, and the postmortem was published October 13 [2].

**Revisions**
- Nothing I found revises the 287, 312, 201 or $184,300 figures. The October 26 status update and the incident log both leave them unchanged [2][3].
- I couldn't find the published postmortem itself. The incident log describes it as the Slack export plus a postmortem, but only the Slack export is in the knowledge base. The figures above come from the live incident channel, so check them against the postmortem if you need them for an external audience.
- The Vendors collection has no payment-processor record for this incident, so I have no provider-side confirmation of the refund total.

**17 lab results** from Bayline Reference Laboratories were filed into the wrong patient's chart over three days at the Riverside and Northgate clinics [1]. This is incident RCA-26-07.

**Why it happened**

- **Trigger:** On July 20, Bayline changed its results feed and moved the medical record number (MRN) into a different HL7 segment. It gave no notice [1].
- **Fallback matching:** On July 21, Halcyon's interface engine (Switchyard) could no longer find the MRN. It fell back to a secondary rule that matched results on last name and birth year only [1]. That rule had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume [1].
- **Why it went unnoticed:** Nobody was alerted that 100% of Bayline results were being matched by the fallback rule, because unmatched and fallback-matched messages weren't monitored [1].
- **Missing contract term:** The Bayline agreement did not require advance notice of feed format changes [1].

**Detection and impact**

- A medical assistant at Riverside noticed on July 23 that a potassium result didn't fit the patient's history. The charge nurse filed a SafeReport and stopped the Bayline feed [1].
- Two patients whose abnormal results went to another chart had follow-up delayed by four and six days. Neither suffered lasting harm [1].
- All 17 results were moved to the correct charts by July 24. The affected patients and the patients whose charts were wrongly updated were contacted [1].
- The feed was restored on July 24 with the MRN mapping corrected [1].

**Corrective actions** [1]

| Action | Status |
|---|---|
| Remove the name-and-birth-year fallback. Unmatched results go to a manual work queue. | Done (due Sept 15) |
| Alert when more than 1% of a lab's results use a fallback match in an hour. | Done (due Sept 30) |
| Amend the lab services agreement to require 30 days' notice of feed changes. | In progress (due Dec 31) |
| Add a positive patient identification check before results are released to the patient portal. | In progress (due Nov 30) |

The documents I found don't include Bayline's own account of the change. The cause above comes from Halcyon's RCA.

rows.answer:
**Halcyon's equivalent deadline is 45 calendar days, not five business days.** After a serious patient safety event, the root cause analysis (RCA) must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].

## Northwind's rule, for comparison
- Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 gets a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution [10].
- The incident commander picks the author, and the postmortem is reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [10].

## Halcyon's rule
The rule is in Halcyon's Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy, owned by Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) [1].

**Which events it covers:**
- A "really serious" event is a **Level 1 sentinel event**. Examples are patient death or permanent harm not related to the natural course of illness, severe temporary harm, a wrong-patient or wrong-site procedure, or patient suicide within 72 hours of a visit [1].
- Level 2 events (adverse events with harm) also get an RCA on the same 45-day clock [1].
- If you're unsure how to classify an event, report it at the higher level. QPS reclassifies if needed [1].

**Deadlines for a sentinel event:**

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Immediately | Make the patient safe and tell the charge nurse. In clinics without a charge nurse on shift, tell the clinic manager [1]. |
| Within 1 hour | The charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director [1]. |
| Within 24 hours | Everyone involved or who witnessed the event files a report in SafeReport. The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1]. |
| Within 72 hours | QPS charters the RCA team [1]. |
| Within 45 calendar days | The RCA is completed [1]. |
| After completion | The Patient Safety Committee reviews the RCA and its action plan. The Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Kenji Watanabe, chairs it. It meets monthly and tracks every action item to closure [1]. |

**External reporting:** QPS decides whether the event must go to a state health department or accrediting body, and QPS makes those reports. The policy gives no deadline for this. Privacy breaches are separate and go to the Privacy Officer under the HIPAA privacy policy [1].

**Differences in approach:**
- Halcyon's RCA is a just-culture review that looks for system causes, not someone to blame [1]. That is similar in spirit to Northwind's blameless postmortem.
- Halcyon's clock starts when the event becomes *known*. Northwind's starts at *resolution* [1][10].
- The Halcyon RCA is led by QPS, which charters an RCA team. Northwind's postmortem is written by one responder [1][10]. In the example RCA-26-07, a QPS staff member was the RCA lead [3].

## Example
RCA-26-07 was a Level 2 event. The mismatch was spotted on July 23, 2026, and the RCA was completed on August 28, 2026 [3]. That is about 36 days, inside the 45-day limit. The Patient Safety Committee reviewed it on September 10 [3].

## Gaps in the documents
- I found nothing on extensions to the 45-day deadline.
- I found nothing on who is accountable if the deadline is missed.
- Apart from QPS chartering the team, the policy doesn't name who owns the RCA. The People And Policy documents I found don't cover post-event reviews.
- Events caused by software or patient-facing automation follow the same policy. Any fixes then go through clinical systems change control [1].

rows.answer:
Halcyon's documents never use the term "incident commander". The role that does the same job is the **charge nurse** on shift. The sentinel and adverse event reporting policy describes that job, and the staffing standard confirms who fills it.

## Who fills the role
- **Charge nurse:** After staff make the patient safe, they tell the charge nurse on shift. The charge nurse "coordinates the immediate response" [1].
- **Large clinics:** These clinics (over 80 visits per day) must have at least 2 RNs on site, one of them a designated charge nurse. That person coordinates the immediate response to any patient safety event [2].
- **Medium and small clinics:** A charge nurse is designated whenever two or more RNs are on shift. Otherwise the **clinic manager** fills the role [2].
- **No charge nurse on shift:** Staff tell the clinic manager instead [1].

The clinic manager is therefore the fallback. The documents don't name any further backup beyond that.

## What the charge nurse does
1. **Assigns the immediate tasks.** The charge nurse decides who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications or records involved [1].
2. **Notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour** if the event is a sentinel event (Level 1) [1].
3. **Is present at disclosure.** The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].

Before any of this, staff first make the patient safe. They follow the clinical escalation protocol and call 911 if needed [1]. The protocol lists red flags that need a 911 call and immediate notice to the on-site clinician, such as chest pain, stroke signs and SpO2 below 90% [3].

## What happens afterward
- Anyone involved in or witnessing the event files a report in SafeReport. Reporting is never optional and never punished [1].
- Level 1 and Level 2 events get a root cause analysis. QPS charters the team within 72 hours, and the analysis must be finished within 45 calendar days [1].
- The Patient Safety Committee reviews completed analyses. The Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Kenji Watanabe, chairs it [1].

## Gaps
I found no document covering training, eligibility or on-call requirements for the charge nurse or "incident commander" role. The staffing standard sets only the designation rules above [2].

Halcyon Health gives a fixed, fairly generous leave entitlement, while Northwind Labs gives "flexible PTO" with a stated minimum of 15 days. For most Halcyon staff, the entitlement is guaranteed and larger. The knowledge base says very little about Northwind's time off beyond that one line.

## Annual leave / PTO

| | Halcyon Health (from Oct 1, 2026) | Northwind Labs |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Accrued every pay period [2] | Flexible PTO [3] |
| Amount | 20 days a year in years 1–3, then 25 days a year from year 4 [2] | Minimum of 15 days a year, "that we actually expect you to take" [3] |
| Accrual rate (full-time) | 6.15 hours per pay period in years 1–3, then 7.7 hours from year 4 [2] | No accrual described |
| Part-time | Accrue pro rata based on scheduled hours [2] | Not documented |
| Carry-over | Up to 56 hours into the next year, with the first carry-over under the new limit on January 1, 2027 [2] | Not documented |
| Excess balance | Anything above 56 hours is paid out in January at your current rate [2] | Not applicable or not documented |
| Request process | Request in RotaLeaf [2] | Not documented |

Halcyon's carry-over limit went up on October 1, 2026. It was 40 hours under the old PTO policy [1][2]. The accrual amounts did not change [2].

At the minimum, Northwind's 15 days is 5 days fewer than Halcyon's years 1–3 entitlement and 10 fewer than Halcyon's year 4+ entitlement. Because Northwind's PTO is flexible, actual use could be higher. The documents I found don't give a typical figure.

## Other time off

**Halcyon Health**
- **Paid holidays:** 9, with Juneteenth added in the new policy (it was 8) [2]. Staff who work a holiday get 1.5× pay plus a floating holiday [2].
- **Sick time:** 48 hours a year, separate from PTO and available from day one. You don't need a doctor's note for absences shorter than three consecutive shifts [1]. Sick leave rules are unchanged by the new annual leave policy [2].
- **CME:** Clinical staff get 5 days of paid continuing medical education time [10].

**Northwind Labs**
- **Time off in lieu:** If you are paged for more than three hours between 22:00 and 07:00 local time while on call, you take the next morning off. This needs no approval. You tell your manager and post in your team channel [4].
- **Holiday change freeze:** The week of December 22 is a holiday change freeze. Only standard and emergency changes ship [8]. This is an engineering release rule, not a company shutdown.
- **Parental leave:** Leadership reviewed parental leave benchmarking. The decision is deferred to the December meeting, and there is no change to the current policy yet [6]. The current policy itself isn't in the knowledge base.
- **Sick leave and public holidays:** I found no documented policy.

## Does tenure or role matter?

- **Halcyon:** Tenure matters. Year 4 moves you from 20 to 25 days [2]. Part-time staff accrue pro rata [2]. Role affects how you request leave rather than how much you get:
  - Clinicians must give at least 60 days' notice, because patient schedules are booked up to 8 weeks out.
  - Non-clinical staff must give at least 2 weeks' notice [2].
  - Approvals for Thanksgiving week and December 20 to January 2 rotate year to year [2].
  - Clinical staff also get the 5 CME days [10].
- **Northwind:** I found nothing that varies leave by tenure, role or employment type.

## Gaps

I couldn't find a full Northwind time-off policy. Northwind's sick leave, public holidays, carry-over, parental leave terms and any tenure effects are missing. Halcyon's parental leave and bereavement policies are also absent. The People team (Joanne Pryce, VP People, at Northwind) would be the source for the full Northwind policy.

Halcyon needs a signed business associate agreement (BAA) and a completed security risk assessment before it shares patient data with a vendor. Halcyon's documents don't mention a "DPA". The HIPAA equivalent is the BAA. I found no separate data sharing agreement requirement.

## What must be in place

Any tool or vendor that will handle protected health information (PHI) needs the following [7]:

1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed BAA with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO.

The systems inventory says the same thing: a new system that will hold PHI needs a risk assessment, a BAA if a vendor is involved, and an inventory entry before go-live [4]. The Clinical Safety and Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) minutes of October 28, 2026 repeat that this applies "before go-live, not after" [8].

## The BAA rule

- **When a vendor counts as a business associate:** Under the HIPAA privacy policy, this is any vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on Halcyon's behalf [5].
- **Timing:** A signed BAA must exist before any PHI is disclosed. That includes test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [5].
- **De-identification is not a workaround:** Removing a name isn't enough, so any patient details are treated as PHI [7].
- **Tallgrass Survey Co. (an example):**
  - Its security risk assessment passed with conditions in September 2026.
  - Its BAA is not executed. Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable responses for 5 years, and Halcyon will accept 18 months.
  - The signed order form is on hold and no PHI can be shared [5].
  - The Privacy Officer is to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026.
  - If the BAA isn't signed by January 31, 2027, Quality & Patient Safety will look at other vendors [5].

## Who is involved and how to start

- **Request:** Email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) at privacy@halcyon.example [7]. The systems inventory page says to email the HIPAA Security Officer for new systems [4].
- **Inventory:** The HIPAA Security Officer maintains it and reviews it quarterly. It is the "approved Halcyon systems" list in the HIPAA privacy policy [4].
- **Clinical use:** The CMIO (Dr. Anjali Rao) does the clinical safety review [7][11].
- **Business owner:** Each business associate record names an internal owner, such as Clinical Informatics for Quillon or Revenue Cycle Management for Brightwater [11][9].
- **Timeline:** Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [7].
- **Expansion:** Widening a pilot may need further sign-off. Quillon's expansion beyond its pilot clinics needs a CSCAB decision and a clinical safety review [11].

I found no document that sets out a formal sequence of approvals, such as budget or executive sign-off, beyond the steps above.

## Obligations once a vendor is live

- **Breach notification:** Each vendor's term is set in its own BAA. Coriander must notify the Privacy Officer within 72 hours of discovery [2]. Polyglen has 5 business days [3]. The 72-hour and 5-business-day figures are contract terms. The sources don't present them as a Halcyon standard for all vendors.
- **Halcyon's own reporting:**
  - Staff report suspected privacy incidents to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours.
  - Breaches affecting 500 or more people go to HHS within 60 days [1].
- **Data terms in the BAA:** These can include retention limits and bans on secondary use. Quillon's BAA prohibits model training on Halcyon data and requires audio to be deleted within 7 days after the note is signed [11]. Coriander's account has recording disabled, and it can't enable it [2].
- **Reassessment:** Risk assessments are refreshed over time. Larkspur's was refreshed in March 2026, Brightwater's in June 2026, and Polyglen's in September 2026 for a new use case [12][9][3]. I found no stated refresh interval.
- **Vendor performance:** Two missed P1 support responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in the vendor's annual review [6].
- **Contract end:** Larkspur's BAA stays in force until all data is returned or destroyed [12].
- **PHI handling rules:**
  - Staff can access only the minimum PHI they need.
  - PHI may live only in approved systems.
  - PHI never goes into AI tools that aren't on the approved list [1][7].

Yes. Northwind's closest equivalent is its **Emergency access to customer workspaces** procedure. It also has a break-glass pattern, but it works differently. Halcyon's version is fast and self-service, with review afterward. Northwind's requires a second person to approve before access starts.

## How Halcyon's break-the-glass works
- **Purpose:** Meridian EHR normally limits users to patients they have a treatment, payment or operations relationship with. Break-the-glass lets you open a chart outside those limits when care genuinely requires it [2].
- **Justification:** You click **Emergency access**, pick a reason (*Emergency care*, *Coverage* or *Other*), and type a short justification [2].
- **Approval:** No one approves it in the moment, because patient care comes first [2].
- **Duration:** Access lasts until the end of your shift, up to 12 hours [2].
- **Audit:** Every event is logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days. If the reason is unclear, your manager is asked to confirm it [2]. Inappropriate use is a privacy incident and can lead to sanctions up to termination [2].
- **Off-limits uses:** Checking on a family member, coworker, public figure or yourself [2].

## How Northwind's emergency access works
- **Purpose:** It lets support, solutions and on-call engineers look inside a customer's workspace to fix something urgent, such as a pipeline dropping data, a misconfigured connector, or a locked-out customer [1].
- **Trigger:** There must be an open support case or a declared incident, and the request must cite its ID. "Curiosity" and "it would be faster" are not valid reasons [1].
- **Request:** You run `nwctl access request --workspace <id> --reason <case-or-incident-id>` [1].
- **Approval:** A second engineer from the support or on-call rotation must approve it in Teleport. You can't approve your own request, and the approver can't be on the same case [1].
- **Permissions:** Access is read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent in the case [1].
- **Duration:** Access expires after 2 hours. That is deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport production session. For more time, you request again with a case update [1][3].
- **Audit:**
  - All sessions are recorded and kept for one year [1].
  - The customer's workspace audit log shows "Northwind support accessed this workspace" with the time and case ID, and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours [1].
  - Security reviews a weekly sample of sessions, plus every session that used write access [1].
- **Prohibited:**
  - Exporting or downloading event payloads.
  - Sharing or screen-sharing your session.
  - Accessing a workspace belonging to someone you know personally [1].
  - If you see unexpected data, such as another customer's, you must end the session and report it in `#security-help` immediately [1].

## Key differences

| | Halcyon break-the-glass | Northwind emergency access |
|---|---|---|
| Protects | Patient charts (PHI) in Meridian EHR | Customer workspaces and event data (Restricted class) |
| Pre-approval | None | Second engineer must approve |
| Justification | Free-text reason chosen at access time | Must reference a case or incident ID |
| Duration | Rest of shift, up to 12 hours | 2 hours, then re-request |
| Write access | Not distinguished in the policy | Read-only unless the customer consents in writing |
| Review timing | Every event, within 2 business days | Weekly sample, plus all write sessions |
| Session recording | Not mentioned (events are logged) | All sessions recorded, kept 1 year |
| Notification | None described | Customer audit log entry, and enterprise admins emailed within 24 hours |
| Penalties | Sanctions up to termination | Not stated in this procedure |

## Why they differ
- **Halcyon's priority is speed.** Delay could harm a patient, so Halcyon trusts the clinician and checks afterward.
- **Northwind's priority is control.** Access is meant to be exceptional, so it adds a second approver, a case link and a short expiry. The customer is also told about the access.
- **Halcyon reviews every event; Northwind samples.** Halcyon also runs monthly automated anomaly detection on EHR access logs [4]. Northwind has no equivalent full-review step in the sources I found.
- **Northwind's general policy backs this up.** Customer data access needs a ticket linked to a case or incident, all sessions are recorded, and exceptions need the Head of Security's written approval and expire after 90 days [3].

I found nothing in Northwind's documents about EHR or health-data access exceptions. Its policies cover customer event data and production access only.

# Can sensitive data go into Slack at Northwind or Halcyon?

**Short answer:** For the most sensitive data, no. At Halcyon the answer is never for PHI. At Northwind it is never for Restricted data, though Confidential data is treated differently. I found no document describing an exception at either company.

## Northwind Labs

Northwind sorts data into four classes in its information security policy [2]:

| Class | Examples | Slack? |
|---|---|---|
| **Restricted** | Customer event payloads, credentials, encryption keys | **No.** "Never leaves production; never in tickets or Slack" [2] |
| **Confidential** | Financials, contracts, employee data | Not banned outright. Shared on a need-to-know basis [2] |
| **Internal** | Roadmaps, handbooks, the policy itself | Shared freely inside Northwind [2] |
| **Public** | Marketing site, public docs | No restrictions [2] |

- **Restricted data:** The emergency-access procedure repeats the rule. Don't paste payloads into tickets, Slack, or a support reply. Use field names and counts instead [4]. Support has the same instruction for tickets and customers [23][18].
- **Credentials:** Work credentials must live in 1Password, which is mandatory [2]. Because credentials are Restricted, they don't belong in Slack.
- **Confidential data:** This is the only gray area. The policy sets "need-to-know" as the standard and doesn't name Slack as allowed or forbidden for it [2]. In practice, keep it to the people who need it and ask in `#security-help` if you're unsure. That advice is my inference, not written policy.
- **Slack Connect:** Slack Connect messages with customers don't start an SLA clock [23]. This is a support-process point, not a data-handling rule.

## Halcyon Health

Halcyon's rule is absolute.

- The HIPAA policy says: "Never put PHI in email subject lines, Slack, personal notes apps, or AI tools that are not on the approved list" [3].
- The systems inventory lists Slack under systems that must not hold PHI: **"Never, including DMs"** [1].
- Removing a name doesn't make patient details safe. The approved-AI-tools document says to treat any patient details as PHI [7]. The same logic applies to Slack, though that document is about AI tools.
- PHI may only be stored in the EHR, the practice management system, and approved systems on the inventory [3]. Slack isn't on that list [1].
- I found nothing on non-PHI employee information in Slack. The knowledge base has no Halcyon HR messaging policy.

**Could Slack ever become approved?** Only through the formal route. Any tool that will handle PHI needs a security risk assessment, a signed business associate agreement (BAA), an inventory entry, and, for clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO. This typically takes 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [7]. No document shows Slack going through this process.

## Slack's own configuration

The knowledge base has no vendor record for Slack at either company. That means I found no BAA status, retention settings, or DLP configuration. Northwind's vendor register covers Cobaltline, Saltmarsh, Hollowpine, and Parcelwise, but not Slack [14][17][18][20]. The Slack rules above come from data-handling policies, not from a review of Slack as a vendor.

## What to do instead

**Northwind**
- Keep credentials in 1Password [2].
- Describe payloads with field names and counts [4].
- Work with customer data through Teleport sessions tied to a support case or incident ticket. These sessions are recorded and expire after 8 hours [2].

**Halcyon**
- Use the EHR's secure messaging for patient communication [3].
- Send PHI to outside providers by encrypted email, typing `[secure]` in the subject line, or use a referral fax with the cover sheet [3].
- Keep PHI out of the email subject line itself [1].

## If it happens by mistake

- **Northwind:** Report it immediately in `#security-help` or at security@northwind.example. Good-faith reporting is never penalized, even if it turns out to be nothing [2]. The policy doesn't spell out cleanup steps, such as deleting the message or rotating an exposed credential.
- **Halcyon:** Report a suspected privacy incident to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours. Email privacy@halcyon.example or call the compliance hotline [3]. Breaches affecting 500 or more people must be reported to HHS within 60 days, and the Privacy Officer handles that [3]. The policy's examples don't include Slack, but PHI in Slack is itself a violation [3][1], so report it.

rows.answer:
## Short answer

Northwind's equivalent is a **$1,500 annual learning budget** for courses, books and conferences [8]. Halcyon gives clinical staff **$2,000 per year for CME, plus 5 days of paid CME time** [1]. Halcyon's allowance is $500 (about 33%) larger. It also comes with dedicated paid time, and I found no matching time-off provision at Northwind.

## Side by side

| | Halcyon Health (clinical staff) | Northwind Labs |
|---|---|---|
| Annual amount | $2,000 [1] | $1,500 [8] |
| Scope | Continuing medical education [1] | Courses, books and conferences [8] |
| Dedicated paid time | 5 days of paid CME time [1] | None specified in the sources I found |
| Who gets it | Clinical staff [1] | Listed under benefits for all employees in the welcome guide [8]. No eligibility conditions are stated. |

## Things that aren't documented

I couldn't find the following for either program:

- **Approval process, carry-over, or rollover of unused funds.** Neither the Halcyon onboarding guide nor the Northwind welcome guide covers these. The carry-over rules I found at Halcyon apply only to annual leave (up to 56 hours from January 1, 2027) [3].
- **Reimbursement mechanics for the learning budget.** Northwind's general expense policy says to submit expenses in Ramp within 30 days, with an itemized receipt for anything over $25 [9]. It doesn't say the learning budget uses this process. Travel rules (Navan booking, hotel and meal caps) are in the same policy [9]. They would presumably apply to conference travel, but the policy doesn't say so.
- **Detailed CME rules at Halcyon.** I found nothing on which expenses qualify, how to claim them, or whether the 5 days count separately from annual leave.

## Context

The two aren't a like-for-like comparison. Halcyon's CME benefit is for licensed clinicians, who need CME to keep their credentials current. Northwind's budget is a general benefit for all staff. Northwind also lists other perks, such as a $500 one-time home office stipend [8], but none of them replace paid learning time.

To get exact claim rules, ask Halcyon's People team for the CME policy. At Northwind, `#ask-anything` is the channel for benefits questions [8].

**Halcyon's deadline is 24 hours.** Report a suspected privacy incident to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours. Email privacy@halcyon.example or call the compliance hotline. The HIPAA privacy policy names a misdirected fax as an example of a reportable incident. It also names a lost device and a patient's chart left open on an unattended screen [2].

**Related points at Halcyon**
- A breach affecting 500 or more people must be reported to HHS within 60 days. The Privacy Officer handles that report, not the person who found the incident [2].
- The sentinel and adverse event policy is a separate track. It covers patient-safety events, with the charge nurse, SafeReport and a root cause analysis. It says privacy breaches are separate and go to the Privacy Officer under the HIPAA policy [3]. A misdirected fax therefore goes through the Privacy Officer route, not the SafeReport/charge-nurse route.
- I found no other timeframe for misdirected faxes in the Clinical Operations documents.

**Comparison with Northwind**
Northwind's rule is "immediately," with no number of hours. Report suspected incidents, phishing or lost devices in `#security-help` or by emailing security@northwind.example. Good-faith reports are never penalized [1]. Lost badges are reported the same way as lost laptops [4].

| | Northwind Labs | Halcyon Health |
|---|---|---|
| Deadline | Immediately | Within 24 hours |
| Where to report | `#security-help` or security@northwind.example [1] | privacy@halcyon.example or the compliance hotline [2] |
| Who receives it | Security team | Privacy Officer |

Halcyon's policy tells you to report without delay. Treat 24 hours as the outer limit, not a target.

rows.answer:
You need two sign-offs, plus an ADR. A third step applies if you shorten retention.

## Required sign-offs

1. **PLAT's change approver: Oluwaseun Adeyemi, or his delegate Kofi Mensah.**
   - Archived customer events live in Driftwood, which the service catalog lists as owned by PLAT [13].
   - The retention standard says the Driftwood lifecycle rules delete objects once they pass the retention period for their workspace. It also says changing those rules is a normal change under the production change approval policy [8].
   - Normal changes need sign-off from the change approver of the team that owns the affected service. The policy names "data retention settings, lifecycle rules, or anything that deletes customer data on a schedule" as normal changes [1].
   - PLAT's approver and delegate are in the team directory [3].

2. **Head of Security, Tomasz Wierzbicki, or the security on-call delegate.**
   - Driftwood is classed as Restricted in the service catalog [13].
   - Normal changes to a service that stores Restricted data also need Head of Security or security on-call delegate sign-off [1].
   - In the PR, request `@northwind/security` [1].

## Other requirements

- **ADR:** Any change to how long customer data is kept needs an ADR. Link it from the PR [1].
- **Customer notice if you shorten retention:** The account team must give 30 days' notice to Enterprise customers whose contracts reference a retention period [1].
- **Longer retention for an Enterprise customer:** The retention standard v2 lets Enterprise customers contract for up to 730 days, with security team approval [8]. The security team (Tomasz Wierzbicki) owns that standard [8]. Per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags [8].

## How to submit

- Add the `change:normal` label to the PR and fill in the risk and rollback sections [1].
- Request review from the approver or delegate as a CODEOWNERS reviewer, and add `@northwind/security` [1].
- Approvals expire after 7 days, so re-request if the change hasn't shipped by then [1].
- Holiday freeze: from December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, only standard and emergency changes are allowed. Ship before then or wait [1].

## Caveats

- The current default archive retention is **365 days**. Standard v2 reduced it from 400 days, and v1 no longer applies [8]. Check which baseline your change starts from.
- The RFC-031 Tributary snapshots will sit in a separate Driftwood bucket, not the event archive buckets. PLAT owns that bucket and its lifecycle rules [14]. If your change touches that bucket, the same PLAT approver applies.
- I didn't find a separate legal or DPA requirement for Driftwood retention. Only the Cobaltline DPA turned up, and it covers application logs, not event archives [12]. Check the actual contracts for any customer that has a retention clause.

**Short answer:** The Identity & Billing (IDB) team owns the service, which is Ledger. If Harriet Vance is out, her delegate, **Arjun Mehta**, can approve changes to it.

## The service and its owner
- The October duplicate invoices came from **Ledger**. This was incident INC-2340 on October 6. Duplicate September invoices went out and 201 card charges were refunded [3].
- The month-end invoicing job ran twice for some workspaces. The payment provider's webhook timed out, the retry logic re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [1].
- The service catalog lists Ledger (plans, invoicing and payment collection) as owned by **IDB** [6].
- Harriet Vance is IDB's engineering manager [5].

## Who approves changes
- Normal production changes need sign-off from the change approver of the team that owns the affected service. Changes to billing logic count as normal changes [7].
- Each team has one named change approver and one delegate who can approve when the approver is out [5].
- For IDB, the approver is **Harriet Vance** and the delegate is **Arjun Mehta** [5].
- On a normal PR, add the `change:normal` label and request review from the approver or their delegate as a CODEOWNERS reviewer [7].
- Ledger is classed Confidential, not Restricted, so the extra Head of Security sign-off doesn't apply [6][7].

## Edge cases
- **Both out:** If the approver and delegate are both unavailable, the VP Engineering (Dmitri Sokolov) may approve. These exceptions are logged in `#eng-changes` [7][5].
- **Harriet and Arjun both out November 24–27:** The IDB status notes say to plan normal Ledger changes around that week or use the exceptions route [4]. In that case the VP Engineering is the fallback.
- **Declared incident:** The incident commander can approve emergency changes. The owning team's approver must then review them retroactively within two business days [7]. During INC-2340, Harriet said Kofi Mensah could approve as IC [1].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** No normal Ledger changes are allowed from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent. The current freeze started October 30 and is expected to end around November 2 [7][4]. Rollbacks are always allowed [7].

**Start with Workspace Experience (WX), and in particular Theo Lindqvist.** If Theo can't help, ask the team's manager, Camille Ortega.

**Why WX**
- Our transactional email provider is Parcelwise (VEN-022). It sends password resets, invites, billing emails and alert notifications [1].
- Atlas is the source system. It sends the recipient name, email address and template variables through the Parcelwise API [1].
- The vendor register says questions about what we send to Parcelwise should go to the team that owns the source system [1].
- The service catalog lists WX as the owner of Atlas, which stores workspace settings and customer user names, email addresses and roles [6].

**Who to contact**
- **Theo Lindqvist** is WX's delegate change approver and the tech lead for workspace settings and notifications [7]. That makes him the most likely person to know what goes into the email templates.
- **Camille Ortega** is WX's engineering manager and change approver [7].
- The team's Slack channel is `#team-wx` [7].

**What the register says about the data**
- Parcelwise receives names and email addresses of customer users, plus the content of billing and alert emails [1].
- It does not receive event payloads. Alert emails contain only pipeline names and error counts [1].
- Billing emails gained a usage-breakdown link in October 2026. The link points at the Northwind app and contains no customer data itself [1].
- Bounce and complaint webhooks come back to Atlas, which suppresses addresses that hard-bounce [1].

**Security and privacy questions**
- Parcelwise's DPA is signed (November 20, 2023, amended September 2025 for EU standard contractual clauses). Its security review passed under ticket VR-41 in `#vendor-review` [1].
- For a security angle, the Security team is led by Tomasz Wierzbicki, Head of Security, at `#security-help` [7]. I found no document naming him as the owner of the Parcelwise review. I'm suggesting him because he heads Security.
- Parcelwise renews on December 15, 2026, with a 30-day notice period [1]. If you're asking because of the renewal, that deadline is close.

**Gaps in the documents**
- The Parcelwise entry has no business owner listed, unlike the Hollowpine and Saltmarsh entries [1][2][3]. I couldn't find a non-engineering owner for the vendor.
- Billing emails may involve Ledger, which is owned by Identity & Billing (IDB). The register names only Atlas as the sender [1][6]. If your question is specifically about billing email content, also check with Harriet Vance, IDB's manager, or Arjun Mehta, IDB's delegate [7].

**The Head of Security approved it. Under policy the approval lasts at most 90 days, so it should lapse around November 22, 2026.**

**Who signed off**
- The helpdesk is Hollowpine Helpdesk, run by Hollowpine Software Co. (register ID VEN-031). Support Operations (Gwen Talbot) is the business owner [1].
- The DPA is not signed. Hollowpine's draft arrived in July 2026, and the redlines have been with legal since August. The main open point is Hollowpine's right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model [1].
- Interim cover is security exception SEC-EX-117, approved by the Head of Security on August 24, 2026 [1].
- The engineering directory names the Head of Security as Tomasz Wierzbicki [10]. The vendor register gives only the title, not his name [1].

**How long it lasts**
- The information security policy says exceptions need written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [6].
- Counting 90 days from August 24, 2026 gives **November 22, 2026**. That is about three weeks from today (October 31).
- That date is my calculation. The register doesn't state an expiry date for SEC-EX-117 [1]. Check the exception record itself to confirm.
- The contract is separate. It renews on January 31, 2027 [1], so the exception will lapse well before then.

**What happens at expiry**
- If the DPA is still unsigned when the exception lapses, Support Operations must either get the exception renewed or move ticket intake back to email [1].
- The sources don't say whether an exception can be renewed more than once, or what a renewal requires beyond the Head of Security's written approval [6].

**Conditions while the exception runs**
- The security review (VR-102) was only a conditional pass. AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until the DPA is signed [1].
- Restricted data must never be pasted into tickets. Support must not attach event payloads, credentials or encryption keys, and should ask customers for field names and counts instead [1].

The exception will probably need renewing in the next few weeks unless legal and Hollowpine settle the model-training clause first.

rows.answer:
**A change to when medication reminder texts go out is a "significant change," so it needs three approvals.** I found no policy that treats send-time changes differently from other reminder changes. I also found nothing on quiet hours or consent rules.

**The three approvals**

Under the clinical systems change control policy, anything affecting patient-facing automation, including reminders, is a significant change [1]. It needs all three of these:

1. **System steward approval.** Medication reminders run on Pillbox, an in-house SMS and app-push reminder scheduler owned by Digital Health Engineering – Patient Engagement (DHE-PE) [10]. That team's steward is **Felix Brandt** [1].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao.** Her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei, can sign instead [1].
3. **Review at the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB).** It meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1].

**How to start**
- The project lead brings the change to CSCAB as a change request with a CHG number [3]. Felix Brandt's team would normally do this for Pillbox.
- CSCAB sets the go-live date [3].
- The next CSCAB meetings are on Wednesdays, so November 4 and November 11, 2026. The last meeting was October 28 [5].
- At the October 28 meeting, a patient-facing message was deferred because the CMIO's delegate withheld sign-off over its wording [5]. The safety sign-off is a real review, not a formality.

**Why it's this strict**
- After incident IR-0412, Halcyon decided that patient-facing automation is a clinical system. Its changes get the same safety review as clinical protocols [2].
- IR-0412 was a reminder scheduler change that caused duplicate medication reminders [2]. Reminders now carry an idempotency key made up of patient, medication and scheduled time, so a reminder with an existing key is never sent again [2]. A change to send times should be tested against that key.

**Other points**
- **Vendor:** Pillbox has no outside vendor [10][11]. No vendor approval is needed, and the Service Desk pages the owning team directly [11].
- **Emergency route:** The on-call medical director can approve a change only to stop ongoing patient harm. CSCAB then reviews it at its next meeting [1]. A routine time change doesn't qualify.
- **Not a separate change class:** Only cosmetic changes, report tweaks and adding a user count as minor changes, which need steward approval alone [1]. I found no rule that puts a send-time change in that class. If you think yours qualifies, confirm that with the Office of the CMIO.
- **Compliance review:** I found no TCPA or quiet-hours policy, and no patient-consent requirement tied to send times. If a compliance check applies, the Privacy Officer is Margaret Holloway [15], though I can't confirm she is the right contact for this.
- **Appointment reminders:** Appointment reminders are separate from medication reminders. They go out 3 days and 1 day before each visit, and 2 hours before telehealth visits [6]. Changing those would also count as patient-facing automation.

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** Any fix that changes how lab results are routed is a significant change. It needs three approvals [4]:

1. The system steward for the team that owns the system.
2. Clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei.
3. Review at the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB), which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern.

The RCA says the same thing: "Changes to result routing are significant changes under clinical systems change control" [1].

**Which fix, and which steward**

The RCA (RCA-26-07) found that 17 Bayline results went into the wrong charts. Bayline changed its feed without notice and moved the MRN. Switchyard, the interface engine, then fell back to matching on last name and birth year [1]. There are several fixes, so the approver depends on which one you mean:

| Fix | Owner | Steward who approves | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Remove the name/birth-year fallback, and add an alert on fallback matching | Interface team (Integration Services, INT), which owns Switchyard [1][6] | Owen Mbeki [4] | Both done [1] |
| Heron: positive patient ID check before results go to the patient portal | Clinical Informatics (CI), project lead Grace Oyelaran [3] | Grace Oyelaran [4] | CSCAB approved it on Oct 28 [5] |
| Amend the Bayline agreement to require 30 days' notice of feed changes | Lab contracts, Clinical Operations [1] | Not specified | In progress, due Dec 31 [1] |

- **Switchyard fixes:** I found no CSCAB record of these two changes. The sources don't say whether they went through CSCAB.
- **Heron (CHG-2026-121):** Its steward approval is recorded as "GO", which matches Grace Oyelaran's initials. "AR" (Dr. Rao) gave clinical safety sign-off after 400 test releases held every mismatched identifier for manual review [5]. CSCAB approved release on November 18, 2026 [5]. Heron is the last open clinical informatics action from RCA-26-07 [3].
- **Contract amendment:** It is a contract change, not a system change. The change control policy doesn't cover it, so the sources name no approver.

**Who does not approve**

- The CMO, Dr. Kenji Watanabe, chairs the Patient Safety Committee and reviews sentinel events. He is not part of software change approval [4].
- Clinical protocol changes go to the Medical Executive Committee, not CSCAB [4].

**Exception for emergencies**

A change made to stop ongoing patient harm can be approved by the on-call medical director. CSCAB then reviews it at its next meeting [4]. Changes made without the required approvals are reported to QPS as safety events [4].

**Related requirement**

At CSCAB, Lorraine Pike (QPS) asked that every result held by the Heron check in its first two weeks be reported to QPS [5].

**Yes. The video vendor behind the new platform is Coriander Media, Inc., and it has a signed BAA. Its contract renews on August 31, 2028.**

**Which vendor**
- Juniper is the new telehealth platform (v3). It replaces Larkspur and is built in-house on the Coriander Media SDK [8].
- The steering committee confirmed Coriander as the video SDK provider, and the contract was completed in August 2026 [4].

**BAA status**
- Coriander's BAA (record BA-020) was executed on August 18, 2026 [2].
- The BAA record lists the PHI involved as live encrypted audio and video streams, participant display names, and room metadata [2].
- Recording is disabled at the account level, and Coriander cannot enable it [2].
- A security risk assessment was completed in August 2026 [2].
- Coriander must report a breach to the Privacy Officer within 72 hours of discovery [2].
- Interpreter and caregiver guests join through the same SDK, so three-way calls need no second vendor [2].
- Polyglen Interpreting, the interpreter vendor, has its own executed BAA, dated March 3, 2025 [3].

**Contract term and renewal**
- The contract term is 2 years, and the renewal date is **August 31, 2028** [2].
- Spend is about $140,000 a year at projected volume, billed per participant-minute [2].
- I found no notice period or auto-renewal terms for Coriander. The record doesn't list them, so check the contract itself.

**Dates for the old vendor, Larkspur**
- Larkspur's BAA was executed on February 14, 2022. Its contract renewal date is December 31, 2026, and Halcyon is not renewing it on a full term [1].
- A month-to-month extension runs through March 31, 2027. The BAA stays in force during the extension and until all data is returned or destroyed [1].
- The pilot starts January 12, 2027, and the network-wide launch is March 2, 2027. Larkspur shuts down on March 31, 2027 [4].
- Both vendors are covered by a BAA during the transition.

## Short answer

Five business associates have an executed BAA on file, according to the Vendors records. One more, Tallgrass Survey Co., does not have one yet.

## Executed BAAs

| Business associate (ID) | What they do | BAA executed | Contract renewal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Larkspur Telehealth Corp. (BA-005) | Current telehealth video platform | Feb 14, 2022 [2] | Dec 31, 2026, with a month-to-month extension through Mar 31, 2027 [2] |
| Brightwater Billing Services, Inc. (BA-003) | Claims scrubbing, patient statements, payment plans | Apr 1, 2023, updated Oct 2024 [1] | Nov 30, 2026, auto-renews for 1 year unless 60 days' notice is given [1] |
| Polyglen Interpreting, LLC (BA-007) | Medical interpreting | Mar 3, 2025 [4] | Feb 28, 2027, 90-day notice period [4] |
| Quillon Ambient, Inc. (BA-019) | AI scribe pilot | Jul 30, 2026 [6] | Jul 31, 2027 [6] |
| Coriander Media, Inc. (BA-020) | Video and audio SDK and media servers | Aug 18, 2026 [5] | Aug 31, 2028 [5] |

Notes on these five:
- **Larkspur:** The BAA stays in force during the extension and until all data is returned or destroyed [2]. The Juniper notes show Larkspur shutting down on March 31, 2027 [16].
- **Brightwater:** The renewal is 30 days away. Pricing renegotiation is in progress and no notice has been given [1]. The 60-day notice window has therefore already passed, so the contract will auto-renew. This is my inference from the dates.
- **Polyglen:** Renewal discussions start in November 2026 [4].
- **Quillon:** The BAA prohibits model training on Halcyon data [6].
- **Coriander:** The agreement includes a 72-hour breach notification term [5].

## Not executed

**Tallgrass Survey Co. (BA-021, proposed)** handles post-visit satisfaction surveys.
- The BAA is not executed. Halcyon received a draft in August 2026 [3].
- The open issue is data retention. Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable responses for 5 years, and Halcyon will accept 18 months [3].
- The signed order form is on hold until the BAA is executed [3].
- No PHI may be shared with Tallgrass until then, including test files [3]. The in-app survey is used in the meantime [3].
- The Privacy Officer, Margaret Holloway, is due to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026 [3].
- If the BAA is not signed by January 31, 2027, Quality & Patient Safety will look at other survey vendors [3].

## Gaps in the records

- **No BAA records for some external vendors.** The systems inventory names Meridian Clinical Systems (Meridian EHR) and ClearPath Software (ClearPath PM) as vendors of systems that hold PHI [12]. I found no business associate records or BAA status for either. They may well have BAAs, but they are not documented in the Vendors collection I can see.
- **Missing record IDs.** The IDs run up to BA-021, but only six records exist here (BA-003, 005, 007, 019, 020, 021). The other numbers may be vendors I can't see or retired entries.
- **No expired or lapsed BAAs.** None of the records shows one.
- **Brightway Medical Supply is not a business associate.** It delivers clinic supplies and is easy to confuse with Brightwater [1].

## What policy requires

- A vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI is a business associate. A signed BAA must be in place before any PHI is disclosed [3].
- Any tool that handles PHI needs a security risk assessment, a signed BAA, an inventory entry, and, for clinical use, a CMIO clinical safety review [8]. Turnaround is typically 6–10 weeks, mostly spent waiting on the BAA [8].
- New systems that will hold PHI need a BAA (if a vendor is involved) and an inventory entry before go-live [12].

I found no written policy on BAA renewal or a periodic review schedule. The only review cadence I found is the quarterly review of the systems inventory [12].

**Suggested follow-up:** confirm BAA status for Meridian Clinical Systems and ClearPath Software.

The cycle 5 pitch review picked three big bets: Tributary, Lantern and Hydrant. It was held on Tuesday, September 8, 2026. That was a Tuesday rather than the usual Monday because of Labor Day. Seven pitches came in, and the handbook caps big bets at three [1][3].

## Who and when
- Attendees were DS, MA, LZ, PR, OA, HV, NH, CO and RS. Noor took the notes [1].
- Cycle 5 ran September 14 to October 23, with cool-down from October 26 to November 6 [1].
- The notes don't record individual votes or the reasons behind each choice. They only list what was picked and what wasn't.

## The three big bets

| Bet | What it is | Pitched by | Scope and targets at the review |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tributary** | Streaming joins (the Enrich step) | Mateo and LZ | CDC-backed snapshots, editor preview, dead-letter routing for unmatched events, and a private beta with design partners in October. GA target January 2027 [1]. |
| **Lantern** | Self-serve billing portal | NH and HV | Customers see invoices, change plans, update payment methods and download usage reports without emailing support. Beta in December and GA in January 2027. It depends on the payment-provider migration finishing first [1]. |
| **Hydrant** | Automatic scaling of ingest gateways per cell | OA | Replaces hand-run `nwctl scale ingest` at 3am. It includes the gateway TLS session ticket change from INC-2291 as a small batch item [1]. |

## Where each stands now
- **Tributary:** Private beta has run since October 1. GA is still January 2027. The owning team is DP, led by Lin Zhou [2].
  - At the review, LZ flagged that snapshot rebuilds after a runner restart are too slow at 50M rows. She wrote RFC-031 on persisting snapshots. It is "accepted with conditions" [1][7].
  - Security (TW) has not yet signed off, and nothing ships to the private beta until TW does [7].
- **Lantern:** The October 28 codename register shows the schedule has slipped. Beta is now February 2027 and GA is March 2027. The owning team is IDB, led by Noor Haddad [2]. The payment-provider migration it depends on is Undertow, which is in progress [2].
- **Hydrant:** Shipped to all production cells on October 22, 2026. The owner is Oluwaseun Adeyemi on PLAT [2][4].

## Small batch items (not big bets)
- Reduce the gateway TLS session ticket lifetime to 30 minutes (INC-2291 action item 3). The owner is the ingest folks on DP.
- Snowflake key-pair auth in Conduit.
- Flag cleanup: 23 flags over 90 days old [1].

## Considered but not picked
- **Postgres CDC v2** (codename Tidepool): re-pitch next cycle with a smaller scope [1][2].
- **Stream-to-stream joins:** explicitly out of scope until Tributary is GA [1].
- **Usage alerts by SMS:** WX to re-pitch with email only [1]. This became Bellbuoy, which is slated for a cycle 6 re-pitch [2].
- **Dark mode for the pipeline editor:** not picked [1].

Under the handbook, anything not picked is dropped rather than carried over. If it still matters, it has to be re-pitched [3].

## Other follow-ups from the review
- RS is to make sure Beacon's hourly counts are exposed to Lantern, so the portal can show usage without querying Ledger.
- DS reminded everyone that cool-down is protected. That means no customer commitments in it, including beta onboarding calls [1].
- The next pitch review is Monday, November 9 [1].

- **Item 3 is the only one the postmortem doesn't mark done.** It was later scheduled as a small-batch item in the Cycle 5 pitch review, owned by the ingest team [3]. The September 12 changelog records it as an internal change, "shipped ahead of the September 15 due date" [4].
- **Items 1, 2 and 4 rest on the postmortem alone.** I found no changelog entry, deploy record or ticket for them. The postmortem's own timestamp is August 14, the incident date, though the incident log says it was published August 21 [1][2]. Treat "done" as the owners' report, not independent confirmation.
- **The changelog's panel doesn't match item 4.** It mentions new ingest dashboard panels for p99 gateway latency by cell [4]. That is not the TLS handshake errors panel.

**Related change outside the action list:** the October deploy-pipeline update cites INC-2291 as its reason [7]. It does three things:
- It raises canary bake time from 20 to 45 minutes.
- It adds a promotion check for zero sustained TLS handshake errors in canary.
- It rolls out data-plane changes in waves.

The postmortem's action items don't include any of this [1], so it's extra hardening. I didn't find a rollout date for it beyond the note's "October 2026" title.

**Vendors, support and leadership:**
- None of the four items depends on a vendor or a support process change [1].
- The Q3 board update says "all action items are on track." That is consistent with the evidence, and it doesn't mention any overdue or descoped items [5].

**The default is 365 days.** Archived event payloads are kept in Driftwood, our object-storage archive, for 365 days [1]. Older runbooks call Driftwood the "cold store" [4].

**What changed.** Retention standard v2 took effect on September 15, 2026. It cut the default from 400 days to 365 days, and it supersedes v1 from February 2026 [1][2]. If you see 400 days in an older document, that is the v1 figure [2].

**Variation and overrides**
- **Per workspace:** Overrides are stored as bucket tags on the Driftwood buckets, so retention can differ by workspace [1].
- **Enterprise customers:** Under v2 they can contract for longer archive retention, up to 730 days, with security team approval [1]. In v1 enterprise customers could only contract for a shorter period, and longer periods weren't offered [2].
- **Changing the rules:** Changing the lifecycle rules is a normal change under the production change approval policy [1].
- **Not found:** I found nothing that varies the default by region or by plan other than Enterprise.

**How it's enforced.** Lifecycle rules on the Driftwood buckets delete objects once they pass their workspace's retention period [1].

**Related timelines in v2** [1]
- **Verified deletion requests, such as GDPR erasure:** These are completed in all live systems within 14 days. Backups still age out on the 35-day schedule.
- **Hot buffer (Kafka):** 7 days.
- **Reference-table snapshots:** 7 days after the snapshot is replaced.

**Vendors.** The vendor register entries I found (Cobaltline and Hollowpine) don't set retention for archived event data. Driftwood retention is governed by the internal standard and lifecycle rules above.

rows.answer:
**You have 14 days.** The current Customer data retention standard (v2, updated 2026-09-15) says verified deletion requests, such as GDPR erasure, must be completed in all live systems within 14 days [2].

**Which version applies:** The older v1 standard (2026-02-02) gave 30 days [1]. v2 is newer and replaces it, so use 14 days. Some people may still be working from the 30-day figure.

**What the standard says about the process**
- **Logging:** Support logs every request in the `data-requests` queue. The queue alerts at day 10, which leaves about four days to finish [2].
- **Who deletes:** The v1 standard says the owning team of each system implements deletion, and the cold store is cleared by lifecycle rules [1]. I found no v2 text that changes this.
- **Archive:** Driftwood (the former "cold store") is cleared by object-storage lifecycle rules, and per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags [2][8]. Retention is 365 days by default, so a deletion request needs the archive data removed explicitly rather than waiting for it to age out [2].
- **Backups:** Backups are outside the 14-day deadline. They age out on the normal 35-day schedule [2]. v1 also says backups are never restored to read deleted data [1].

**What I couldn't find**
- No documented extension, complex-request exception or legal-hold carve-out for the 14-day deadline.
- No rule on who tells the customer deletion is complete, or by when.
- No vendor-specific deletion timelines.

**Third-party vendors**
Two vendors hold customer personal data. The register entries don't give any deletion timelines, so check them separately:
- **Parcelwise** (transactional email) receives customer user names and email addresses. It has a signed DPA [6].
- **Hollowpine** (support ticketing) holds ticket content, customer names and emails. Its DPA is **not signed**, and it operates under security exception SEC-EX-117 [3]. Any customer data in tickets is therefore a gap to raise with Support Operations (Gwen Talbot) and legal.
- **Saltmarsh Analytics** holds only pseudonymous app-usage data, with 14-month retention, and no customer event payloads [4].

If the request involves vendor-held data, or you want to know whether an extension is possible, ask in `#security-help`. That is the channel the retention standard names [1].

For on-call shifts starting in mid-November 2026, primary on-call pays **$500 per week** and **$150 per page outside business hours**. A cap of **$1,500 per week** applies to out-of-hours page pay.

A memo from October 19, 2026 raised the rates for shifts starting on or after Tuesday, November 3, 2026. It replaces the older figures in the on-call runbook, which were $400 per week and $100 per page [1][2]. Shifts starting November 10 and November 17 both fall under the new rates. The published November–December rota also says pay follows the October 2026 update [4].

| Item | Rate for mid-November shifts |
|---|---|
| Primary on-call stipend | $500 per week [1] |
| Page outside business hours | $150 per page [1] |
| Cap on out-of-hours page pay | $1,500 per week [1] |

- **Cap:** $1,500 is 10 pages at $150. Pages beyond that in the same week earn no extra pay. This is my arithmetic from the memo's figures, not something the memo states.
- **Duplicate pages:** Pages acknowledged and resolved as duplicates of an earlier page in the same incident count once [1].
- **Payment:** Stipends and page pay are added to the next payroll after the shift ends. PagerDuty is the record, so a swapped shift must be reflected there or the pay goes to whoever PagerDuty shows [1].
- **Time off in lieu:** If you are paged for more than three hours between 22:00 and 07:00 local time, you can take the next morning off without approval [1].
- **Shift timing:** Shifts run one week, starting Tuesday at 10:00 local time [2].
- **Holiday multipliers:** I found no multipliers or role- or region-based differences. Thanksgiving week (starting November 24) is outside mid-November. For that week, the rota only allows US-based engineers to hand overnight hours to London cover, and it doesn't mention any pay change [4].

I found no precise definition of "business hours" in the memo or the runbook.
