**You can roll over up to 56 hours of unused leave into next year.** The new annual leave policy set that limit, and it took effect October 1, 2026. It replaced the old 40-hour PTO limit [2]. The first carry-over under the 56-hour limit happens on January 1, 2027 [2].

**Excess hours:** Anything above 56 hours is paid out in January at your current rate. It isn't forfeited [2].

**Old policy:** The older "PTO and clinic scheduling policy" still says 40 hours [1]. The annual leave policy states that it replaces that section, and it is the newer document, so 56 hours applies [2].

**Employee types:** The policy gives one carry-over limit and doesn't vary it by role, tenure or clinical status. Part-time staff accrue leave pro rata based on scheduled hours [2]. The documents don't say whether their 56-hour cap is also prorated. I found no exceptions process for exceeding the cap and no state-specific rules.

**Timing:** Clinicians must request leave at least 60 days ahead. Non-clinical staff must give at least 2 weeks' notice. Requests go through RotaLeaf and are approved in the order submitted. Approvals for Thanksgiving week and December 20 to January 2 rotate year to year [2]. If you want to use hours before year-end, request them soon, because the 60-day lead time for clinicians has largely passed for this year.

For part-time questions or edge cases, contact your clinic manager or people@halcyon.example [2].

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** The design target for Enterprise is reference tables of up to 500 million rows per workspace [1]. That is a goal in an internal spec. I found nothing confirming it as a shipped or contractual limit. For comparison, the Growth target is 50 million rows [1].

**What the sources say**
- The Streaming joins product spec lists "reference tables up to 50 million rows per workspace on the Growth plan and 500 million on Enterprise" as a goal. The limit is per workspace and is measured in rows. I found no limit in bytes or columns [1].
- "Tributary" is the internal codename for streaming joins, the Enrich step in the pipeline editor [9]. It has been in private beta with design partners since October 1 and is targeted for GA in January 2027 [8][9].
- Streaming joins are included on Growth and Enterprise. Each enriched event counts as 1.2 events against the monthly quota [1].
- Codenames must never appear in customer-facing material [9]. Customers should hear "Enrich step" or "streaming joins", not "Tributary".

**Can Enterprise customers get higher limits?**
- I found no documented process for raising the reference-table size limit.
- The only documented Enterprise raise is for API ingest limits. `/v2/events` and `/v2/events/batch` can be raised up to 3x by contract, and the DP team checks gateway headroom first [2]. This doesn't cover reference-table size.
- Enterprise pricing is custom, with a minimum of $60,000 a year [7]. I found no reference-table terms in the pricing policy.

**Technical caveats for large tables**
- Sources can be Postgres, MySQL or Snowflake. Tables are snapshotted into the runner's local RocksDB state and kept current with change data capture (CDC). Each partition holds only the keys it needs [1].
- Tables that change more than 1,000 times per second are out of scope [1].
- A runner rebuilds its snapshot from scratch if CDC lag exceeds 10 minutes. Per RFC-031, a runner also rebuilds on restart. For a 50M-row table that takes about 25 minutes, and Enrich steps on that partition stall meanwhile [1][3].
- RFC-031 proposes persisted snapshots to fix this, with a target restore time under 90 seconds for 50M rows. It is not fully approved: one reviewer (TW) is still pending, and nothing ships to the private beta until that sign-off [3].
- Reference-state memory is budgeted at 2 GiB per partition. Partitions that would exceed it spill to disk instead of failing [3].
- The forced-refresh endpoint (`POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh`) is limited to 1 per 2 minutes on Enterprise and 1 per 10 minutes on Growth. A forced refresh discards the snapshot and does a full table scan, which is expensive for large tables [2].
- The 25-minute rebuild and the restore target are quoted only for 50M rows. I found no performance numbers for tables near 500M rows, so I can't say how well the Enterprise maximum will perform.

**Gaps**
- I found no customer-facing documentation or support article that states the limit.
- The 500M figure comes from a pre-GA spec. Check with the DP team (Tributary lead: Lin Zhou) before quoting it to a customer [9].

# Juniper telehealth platform go-live

Patients get the new telehealth platform, codenamed **Juniper**, in two phases. The pilot starts **January 12, 2027**. Every clinic is on it by **March 2, 2027**. The Juniper steering committee set these dates on October 21, 2026 [1].

## Phased schedule

| Phase | Date | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Pilot | January 12, 2027 | Riverside, Elm Park and Northgate clinics [1] |
| Network-wide | March 2, 2027 | All clinics and the telehealth front desk [1] |
| Larkspur shutdown | March 31, 2027 | The current platform ends after its month-to-month extension [1] |

The Larkspur vendor record gives the same timeline: pilot clinics move off Larkspur in January 2027 and all clinics by early March 2027 [9].

## The pilot date is not yet final

The pilot is subject to a go/no-go decision at the **December 16, 2026** steering meeting. The criteria are [1]:
- Join success above 98% for two consecutive weeks.
- Zero open Level 1–2 safety findings.
- Approval from the clinical systems change board (CSCAB) as a significant change.

So far, internal testing shows 98.7% join success across 1,900 test visits [1]. Android join success is now level with iOS [1]. The notes don't say whether this counts toward the two-consecutive-week requirement.

## Vendor status

- **Coriander Media** supplies the video SDK. Its contract was completed in August 2026 [1]. Its business associate agreement was signed August 18, 2026, and its security risk assessment was completed in August 2026 [12].
- **Juniper itself** is built in-house by Virtual Care on the Coriander SDK, so it has no outside vendor [11][15].
- **Larkspur** is not renewing on a full term after December 31, 2026. A month-to-month extension runs through March 31, 2027 [9]. Larkspur must return visit metadata exports by April 15, 2027 and certify data destruction by April 30, 2027 [9].
- I found no reported schedule slips from any vendor. The only dated vendor commitments I found are the ones above.

## Readiness items still open

- **CSCAB review:** Booked for **December 9, 2026**. The clinical safety case is due to circulate by December 2 [2].
- **Licensing block:** Patients in states where the clinician isn't licensed must be blocked at scheduling, not at join. CSCAB approved this rule (the Kestrel project), and it ships in the ClearPath November release on **November 14, 2026** [2].
- **Clinician training:** 410 clinicians need a 30-minute module before the network-wide date, and Clinical Operations is to schedule it [1]. Clinic managers asked that pilot training not fall in the week of December 21 [1].
- **Post-visit survey:** Tallgrass would send it, but its business associate agreement isn't signed. Until it is, Juniper uses the in-app survey [1][10].
- **Security and inventory:** CSCAB reminded the board that any project adding a new place to store PHI needs a security risk assessment and a systems inventory entry before go-live [2]. Juniper is already listed in the inventory as "in development" [15].

## Already done

- Three-way calls with Polyglen interpreters work end to end [1].
- Caregiver links were tested with 40 volunteer families [1].
- Screen sharing for lab results is finished [1].

**No, not as far as the knowledge base shows.** Tomasz Wierzbicki (TW), the Head of Security, hasn't signed off on RFC-031, "Persisting Tributary snapshots," which Lin Zhou (LZ) wrote. [3]

**Who is involved**
- Tomasz Wierzbicki is listed as Head of Security. "TW" is the initials convention used in RFCs and reviews. [3]
- RFC-031 was created September 18, 2026. Its author is L. Zhou, the DP staff engineer and tech lead for streaming joins. [1][3]
- LZ said at the Cycle 5 pitch review that she would write an RFC on persisting snapshots. The reason was that snapshot rebuilds after a runner restart are too slow at 50M rows. [2]

**Review status in the RFC [1]**

| Reviewer | Decision | Date |
|---|---|---|
| PR (Data Plane) | Approve | Sep 22 |
| OA (Platform) | Approve with conditions | Sep 24 |
| TW (Security) | Pending | — |

- OA's conditions are that snapshots go in a separate Driftwood bucket, not the event archive buckets, and that PLAT owns the bucket and its lifecycle rules. [1]
- TW wants a threat model for copying Restricted data across tiers before approving. [1]
- The RFC's overall status is "Accepted with conditions." Implementation can start behind a flag, but nothing ships to the private beta until TW signs off. [1]

**Other evidence that it's still open**
- The Leadership offsite notes (updated October 1) say security sign-off on persisted snapshots is "still outstanding and is the main risk" for Tributary. [5]
- The Tributary private beta started October 1 with eight design partners. [5]
- One action item is for Dmitri Sokolov (VP Engineering) to unblock the RFC-031 security review with Tomasz by the end of October. [5]

**Caveats**
- The RFC page shows no update date, and I found no later threat-model document, ticket or thread. The knowledge base doesn't show whether TW signed off after the offsite notes.
- The project codename register (October 28) says only that the private beta has been running since October 1. It doesn't mention security sign-off. [4]
- Today is October 31, the deadline for Dmitri's action item. I'd confirm with Tomasz, Lin or Dmitri before relying on this.

The self-serve billing portal (codename Lantern) is now expected to reach **general availability in March 2027**, with the **beta in February 2027** [2].

**Original plan:** The cycle 5 pitch targeted a December beta and a January 2027 GA [1].

**Why it slipped** (leadership offsite, October 2026) [4]:
- The payment-provider migration, codenamed Undertow, won't finish until mid-January.
- INC-2340 showed the invoice-history view needed to handle voided invoices properly.

Together, these moved GA from January to March 2027 and the beta from December to February [4]. The cycle 5 pitch had already listed the portal as dependent on the payment-provider migration finishing first [1].

**Where things stand** (Identity & Billing weekly status, week of October 26) [3]:
- **Undertow cutover:** Full cutover to the new provider is scheduled for January 19, 2027. Dual-running has been on since October 19, covering 5% of Growth workspaces, and reconciliation has shown no mismatches so far [3].
- **Token migration rehearsal #2:** It moved from October 30 to November 12 because of the month-end billing freeze [3].
- **Open risk:** The new provider's webhook retries are faster than the old one's. The team is making sure the handler is idempotent before cutover [3].
- **Plan changes:** They are blocked on Undertow. The team won't build them against the old provider's API [3].
- **Beta waitlist:** 23 workspaces have signed up, against a target of 40 by the February beta [3].
- **Invoice history:** The view now hides voided duplicate invoices [3].
- **Usage view:** It reads hourly counts from Beacon, so the portal doesn't have to query Ledger [3].

**Vendors and support:** The only dependency affecting the timeline is the payment-provider migration. I found no vendor or support dependency on the launch date. The Hollowpine Helpdesk vendor record doesn't mention the portal [6]. Support tickets from INC-2340 did lead to the voided-invoice requirement [7].

The Undertow date is the one to watch. The cutover is set for January 19, 2027, and plan changes can't be built until it happens. Any slip there would put pressure on the March GA.

All of their access should be revoked within **one hour of their final working time** [1]. Northwind's Information Security Policy sets that limit. It says: "When someone leaves Northwind, all access is revoked within one hour of their final working time." [1]

- **Applies to everyone:** The policy covers every employee, contractor and system [1].
- **The clock starts at their final working time:** It does not start at midnight. If they finish at 5:00 pm Friday, access should be gone by about 6:00 pm Friday. Check what "final working time" means for your teammate, for example whether they are leaving at end of day or earlier.
- **Exceptions:** Any exception needs written approval from the Head of Security, and it expires after 90 days [1]. So don't promise anyone extended access without that approval.
- **Standing production access:** Production access through Teleport expires after 8 hours, and standing access to production databases isn't allowed for anyone [1]. Production access therefore ends by itself, in addition to the one-hour rule.

I didn't find these in the knowledge base:
- An offboarding checklist.
- Per-system timelines (email, SSO, repositories, VPN).
- Who runs the revocation.
- How much notice a manager must give IT or HR.
- Separate rules for involuntary departures.

Tell IT and HR well before Friday so the one-hour deadline can be met. Ask the Security team how revocation is triggered in practice.

**Emergency workspace access session recordings are kept for one year.** The "Emergency access to customer workspaces" page says: "All sessions are recorded and kept for one year" [1].

**What the knowledge base doesn't say**
- **Governing policy:** The one-year figure appears only on the emergency access page, which the Security team owns [1]. The information security policy says all sessions are recorded but gives no retention period [6]. The customer data retention standard (v2) doesn't list session recordings. It covers event payloads, run logs, backups and metadata [2].
- **Exceptions:** I found no documented legal hold, investigation or audit extension for these recordings. The information security policy allows exceptions only with written approval from the Head of Security, and they expire after 90 days [6]. That policy doesn't mention recordings specifically.
- **Storage and deletion:** I found nothing on where the recordings are stored or how they are deleted. Teleport handles production access sessions and is owned by Security [7], but no document ties the recordings to it or describes their deletion. Don't assume the Driftwood lifecycle rules apply to them. Those rules cover archived event payloads [2].

**Don't confuse this with other numbers**
- Archived customer event payloads in Driftwood are kept 365 days by default under the v2 standard [2]. The v1 standard said 400 days [5]. This is a separate data set from session recordings, even though the periods look alike.
- The emergency access itself expires after 2 hours. That is the length of a session, not how long it's retained [1].

For the storage location or any hold process, ask the Security team in `#security-help` [1][5].

**Timing:** The Google Workspace account is created three days before the start date [1]. For someone starting Monday, November 2, that's Friday, October 30. I'm assuming "three days" means calendar days, because the guide doesn't say. If so, the account should already exist. Because the date has already passed, I'd confirm with IT that it was created.

**Password:** The new hire gets a temporary password by text message [1].

**Day one:**
- There is an IT setup call at 09:30 in the new hire's local time. A welcome session with the People team follows it [1].
- They must set up 1Password, Slack and two-factor authentication on every account. This is mandatory before they can access any production system [1].

- SMS two-factor authentication isn't allowed for any work account [2]. That rule covers 2FA, not delivery of the temporary password. The text message is only how the first password arrives. The new hire still has to enrol a hardware key for Google.
- The laptop is shipped to their home address. It's a MacBook Pro for engineering roles and a MacBook Air for everyone else [1].

**Gaps in the knowledge base:**
- It doesn't say who creates the account (IT, People or the manager).
- It doesn't say who to contact if the password text doesn't arrive or the login fails.
- It doesn't say how the YubiKey reaches the new hire.

The only related details are that IT runs the day-one setup call and handles badge access during onboarding [1][3]. The new hire's manager and onboarding buddy walk them through the first two weeks [1]. The most practical route is to raise it with the manager or buddy, or on the IT setup call. If the password text hasn't arrived by then, I'd tell IT before Monday morning rather than waiting for the call. That's my suggestion, not a documented process.

A hold on the ingest gateway count can last **at most 4 hours**. After that, Hydrant takes over scaling again [1]. Hydrant is the automatic gateway scaler that went live on October 22, 2026.

**How to pin the count**
- Run `nwctl hydrant hold --cell <cell> --replicas <n> --ttl 2h` [1].
- The example in the launch notes uses a 2-hour TTL. That is only the example value. The 4-hour cap is the actual limit [1].
- Holds are standard changes and need no approval [1].
- To release a hold early, run `nwctl hydrant release --cell <cell>` [1].

**Don't use `nwctl scale ingest`**
- Hydrant treats the replica count as its own and reverts a manual change within 2 minutes [1].
- The on-call runbook's "Ingest 5xx rate above 1%" entry still tells you to run `nwctl scale ingest --cell <cell> --replicas +4` [2]. The Hydrant launch notes say they replace that scaling step [1]. Use a hold instead.

**What to know during a long debug**
- The notes don't say whether you can extend a hold or place a new one right after it expires. They only say Hydrant takes over once the hold ends [1]. If your debugging may run past 4 hours, plan for Hydrant resuming control, or check with PLAT, who own Hydrant [1].
- Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call if a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes. The notes say this usually points to a gateway problem rather than real traffic [1].
- Hydrant never scales in the first 10 minutes after a gateway deploy [1].
- If the Hydrant controller goes down, gateways keep their last replica count, and the Platform primary is paged [1].
- Changing a cell's floor or ceiling is a different thing from a hold. It is a normal change that needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver [1].

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** The API rejects the request with HTTP 429 and a `Retry-After` header. The header gives the number of seconds to wait before retrying [1]. The knowledge base doesn't document the 429 response body or any other rate-limit headers.

## What triggers throttling
- Limits are per workspace, not per API key. Ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- Bursts of up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds. Throttling starts after that [1].
- Limits differ by endpoint and plan. For example, `POST /v2/events` allows 100 req/s on Starter, 2,000 on Growth and 10,000 on Enterprise by default [1].
- Some endpoints are limited by time window rather than per second. Enrich snapshot refresh is 1 per 10 minutes on Growth and 1 per 2 minutes on Enterprise. Audit-log export is 1 per hour on Growth and 6 per hour on Enterprise [1].

## What the customer gets back
- **Over the limit:** HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header [1].
- **Endpoint not on the plan:** HTTP 403, not 429. For example, `/v2/events/batch` on Starter returns 403 [1].
- **Quota impact:** Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].

## How they know when to retry
- `Retry-After` gives the seconds to wait [1].
- Northwind's SDKs honour it automatically and back off exponentially [1].
- A customer on a raw HTTP integration has to implement that behaviour themselves. I found no customer-facing retry guide in the knowledge base. The only guidance is the internal description of what the SDKs do.

## Raising limits
There is no documented temporary-block or penalty process for customers who repeatedly exceed limits. The documented routes are all ways to get more headroom [1]:
- **Enterprise:** Ingest limits on `/v2/events` and `/v2/events/batch` can be raised up to 3x the default by contract. The account team files a request in the Data Plane (DP) queue. DP first checks that the customer's cell has gateway headroom.
- **Growth:** Limits are fixed by contract. Customers who need more should talk to sales about Enterprise.
- **One-off backfills:** The DP on-call primary can grant a temporary raise of up to 72 hours on any plan that has the endpoint.
- **Legacy `/v1/track`:** Limits won't be raised for anyone. Customers should move to `/v2/events`, which every SDK released after March 2025 already uses. `/v1/track` stops accepting events on April 30, 2027.

## Gaps
The sources don't cover the 429 JSON body or any `X-RateLimit-*` headers. The rate-limits page is internal and says the public docs copy it on each release [1]. Check the public docs before telling a customer what the response contains.

**Where to ask:** Post your request in `#eng-leads` [1]. The codename register is maintained by Mateo Alvarez (Group PM) [1]. The documents don't describe a formal approval step or say who picks the name. The only stated process is to ask in that channel.

**Naming rules:**
- A new codename must not collide with any of these [1]:
  - a production service name, such as Keystone, Ledger, Atlas, Beacon, Lookout, Conduit or Driftwood [13]
  - a vendor name, such as Cobaltline, Saltmarsh, Hollowpine or Parcelwise [6][7][8][9]
  - an existing codename, either active or retired [1]
- Codenames are for internal use only. They must never appear in customer-facing material, release notes or the status page [1].
- Anything meant to outlive the conversation, such as runbooks, postmortems and tickets, should use the real service name instead of a nickname [1]. The register says this about informal service nicknames like "the firehose". It's reasonable to apply the same habit to codenames, but the register doesn't say so explicitly.

**Names already taken:**
- Active or recent: Tributary, Lantern, Hydrant, Undertow, Sandbar, Tidepool, Bellbuoy, Wayfinder [1].
- Retired: Keel and Gannet [1].
- Retired names still appear in the register. Whether they can be reused isn't stated, so ask in `#eng-leads`.

**Style:** The documents set no required format or theme. The existing names lean towards water and nautical words, such as Tidepool, Sandbar, Undertow and Bellbuoy [1]. That looks like a habit rather than a rule. The register also warns about near-duplicates like Sandbar and Saltmarsh, and Tidepool and Tributary [1]. Pick something clearly distinct.

**Not found:** I found no documented rules on character limits, prohibited words, how long a name stays reserved, or whether codenames can be shared with vendors. rows.answer:
**Only the VP Engineering, Dmitri Sokolov, can approve a normal change to Ledger on November 25.** Ledger's usual approver and delegate are both out that day.

## Who normally approves
- A normal change needs sign-off from the change approver of the team that owns the affected service [5].
- The service catalog lists Ledger as owned by IDB (Identity & Billing) [1].
- IDB's change approver is Harriet Vance, and its delegate is Arjun Mehta [4].

## Why that doesn't work on November 25
- Harriet and Arjun are both out November 24–27 (Thanksgiving week) [3].
- The IDB status update says to plan normal changes to Ledger around that, or use the policy's exceptions route [3].
- Under that route, if the approver and delegate are both unavailable, the VP Engineering may approve. The exception is logged in `#eng-changes` [5].
- The team directory names Dmitri Sokolov as VP Engineering [4].

## Other requirements
- **No security sign-off needed.** Ledger is classed Confidential, not Restricted [1]. The extra Head of Security sign-off applies only to Restricted services [5].
- **No freeze applies.**
  - The month-end billing freeze runs from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually the 2nd [5]. The current one is October 30 to about November 2 [3]. The next starts at the end of November, after the 25th.
  - The holiday freeze doesn't start until December 18 [5].
- **Deploy window.** November 25 is a Wednesday, so it falls in the Monday–Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific deploy window [8].
- **Two code approvals.** Billing changes need two PR approvals, one from a code owner [11].

## How to request it
1. Add the `change:normal` label to the PR and fill in the risk and rollback sections [5].
2. Request review from the approver or delegate as a CODEOWNERS reviewer [5]. For this change, that means asking Dmitri as the exception approver.
3. Make sure the exception is logged in `#eng-changes` [5].

## An option to avoid the exception
Approvals are valid for 7 days [5]. Harriet or Arjun could approve on or after November 18, and the approval would still cover a ship on November 25. They are both out from November 24 [3].

The knowledge base doesn't say whether Dmitri is available on November 25. Confirm that with him before you rely on this route.

rows.answer:
**You need one sign-off: PLAT's change approver, Oluwaseun "Seun" Adeyemi. If he's out, his delegate Kofi Mensah can approve.** [5][6]

## Why PLAT's approver
- Raising or lowering a Hydrant floor or ceiling is a **normal change**, classed as infrastructure configuration. It needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver [5]. The cell inventory says the same [2].
- PLAT owns Hydrant, and its configuration, including each cell's floor and ceiling, lives in the PLAT infrastructure repo [5]. The gateways themselves are owned by DP [5].
- Today us-east is set to 16 floor / 64 ceiling replicas [2].

## No security sign-off
Normal changes to a service that stores Restricted data also need the Head of Security or the security on-call [1]. `ingest-gateway` is classed Restricted [12]. But the change here is to Hydrant's configuration, and Hydrant stores no customer data and isn't Restricted. The launch notes say no security sign-off is needed for these changes [5].

## How to get it
1. Open a PR against the PLAT infrastructure repo with the new us-east ceiling [5].
2. Add the `change:normal` label and fill in the risk and rollback sections of the template [1].
3. Request review from Seun (or Kofi) as a CODEOWNERS reviewer [1].
4. Ship within 7 days of approval, or re-request [1].

## Check with DP first
- Hydrant pages the **Data Plane primary on-call** when a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes. The launch notes say this usually means a gateway problem rather than real traffic [5].
- Talk to DP before raising the ceiling, to rule out a bad gateway build or similar. DP's approver is Priya Raman, with Lin Zhou as delegate [6]. Nothing I found makes DP sign-off a requirement for this change.
- Scale-up happens when gateway CPU stays above 65%, or Kafka produce p95 stays above 250 ms, for 3 minutes [5]. If you're pinned because Kafka is the bottleneck, more gateway replicas may not help. Broker counts change only through capacity planning with PLAT [2]. us-east has 12 brokers [2].
- us-east passed 6,000 workspaces and now has 6,240. New US workspaces go to us-central or us-west by default [2].

## Short-term option
To pin the replica count while you debug, use `nwctl hydrant hold --cell us-east --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. A hold lasts at most 4 hours and is a standard change that needs no approval [5]. Don't use `nwctl scale ingest`, because Hydrant reverts manual changes within 2 minutes [5].

## Not found
The knowledge base has no budget or vendor-contract approval step for this. Hydrant is an internal Northwind service, not a vendor product. It also has no separate region-specific review for us-east capacity beyond the normal change process.

If you meant a *customer's* API rate limit rather than Hydrant's replica ceiling, that's a different process. The account team files a request in the DP queue, and DP checks the cell has gateway headroom [3].

**Priya Raman can approve it. She is the incident commander (IC) for Thanksgiving week, and she normally manages the Data Plane (DP) team.**

## Who can approve
- The policy says emergency changes "may be approved by the incident commander during a declared incident" [1].
- The IC can approve even changes that would normally need the owning team's change approver [2].
- The owning team's change approver reviews the change afterwards, within two business days [1].
- For Thanksgiving week, the rota lists Priya Raman as IC for the week starting Tuesday, November 24 [6]. Thanksgiving is Thursday, November 26.
- The later swaps listed in the rota affect Nov 10 and Dec 8/15 only. They don't touch Nov 24 [6].

## Her team
- Priya Raman is the engineering manager and change approver for Data Plane (code DP). Lin Zhou is her delegate [3].
- The on-call runbook describes Data Plane as covering ingest gateways, pipeline runners and connectors [7].
- Priya is on the IC rotation separately from team on-call [3]. She doesn't have to be an owner of the affected service to approve as IC.

## Things to check
- **Shift timing:** IC shifts start Tuesday at 10:00 local time [7]. For an incident on Monday, Nov 23, or early Tuesday before 10:00, the IC is probably the previous week's IC, Oluwaseun Adeyemi. He manages Platform (PLAT) [3][6]. I inferred this from the shift rules and didn't find it stated outright.
- **No freeze:** The holiday freeze runs December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027 [1]. I found no Thanksgiving freeze, so normal rules apply that week.
- **Retroactive review:** The affected service's own change approver does the review, and that may not be Priya. Examples are Oluwaseun for Platform and Harriet Vance for Identity & Billing [3]. If both the approver and the delegate are unavailable, the VP Engineering (Dmitri Sokolov) may approve [1][3].
- **Deploys:** The IC can also approve skipping the canary bake with `/deploy expedite`, which is logged in `#eng-changes` [5]. Rollbacks never need approval, even during freezes [1][5].
- **Backup if Priya is unavailable:** The knowledge base doesn't name a backup IC. The IC rotation also includes Kofi Mensah (Platform), Harriet Vance (Identity & Billing), Oluwaseun Adeyemi (Platform) and Ravi Subramanian (Observability) [3].

The $1,200/month plan is Growth [8]. On Growth, the bulk endpoint is `POST /v2/events/batch`. A customer can send up to **50 requests per second**, with up to **10,000 events or 10 MB per request** [1].

## Limits for Growth on `POST /v2/events/batch`

- **Request rate:** 50 req/s [1]. The limit applies per workspace, not per API key, so ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- **Bursts:** Short bursts of up to 2x the limit (about 100 req/s) are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- **Request size:** Up to 10,000 events or 10 MB per request [1].
- **Over the limit:** The API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header giving the seconds to wait. Northwind's SDKs honor it automatically and back off exponentially [1]. Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].
- **Don't use `/v2/events` for the backfill:** It allows 2,000 req/s but only 500 events or 1 MB per request. It is meant for SDK and HTTP API ingest, not bulk loads [1].

## Higher rates for the backfill

- **Contract limits:** On Growth they are fixed. Apart from the one-off backfill raise below, customers who need more should talk to sales about Enterprise [1].
- **Temporary raise:** The data-platform (DP) on-call primary can grant a raise of up to 72 hours for a one-off backfill, on any plan that has the endpoint [1]. A year-long backfill is a good candidate. The sources don't say what the raise can be or how to ask for it, so I'd ask DP on-call.
- **Enterprise:** The default is 200 req/s. It can be raised up to 3x by contract, and DP must confirm the customer's cell has gateway headroom [1].

## Monthly event quota

Growth includes 100 million events per month, with overage at $8 per additional million [8]. A year of history could use up the quota or add overage charges. The sources don't say whether backfilled events count toward the quota. Check this with the customer before they start.

I found no backfill-specific guidance, such as off-peak windows or approval steps, beyond the temporary raise above.

**Tom Whitfield gets paged.** He is the Data Plane (DP) primary on-call for the week starting Tuesday, November 17.

**Why Data Plane and not Platform**
- Hydrant pages the **Data Plane primary on-call** when a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes. The launch notes explain that hitting the ceiling usually means a gateway problem rather than real traffic [1].
- Platform (PLAT) owns Hydrant, but DP owns the gateways [1].
- Platform's primary is paged only if the Hydrant controller itself is down [1].

**Who is on call the week of November 17** [7]

| Role | Person |
|---|---|
| Data Plane primary | **Tom Whitfield** |
| Data Plane secondary | Ines Duarte |
| Platform primary (not paged for this alert) | Jonas Feld |
| Platform secondary (not paged for this alert) | Sanjay Iyer |
| Incident commander | Oluwaseun Adeyemi |

**Escalation and swaps**
- The secondary, Ines Duarte, is paged if Tom doesn't acknowledge within 10 minutes [6][7].
- The rota lists swaps agreed after the October 20 publication. They cover the November 10 Data Plane week and the December 8 and 15 incident commander weeks. None touches November 17 [7].
- The rota was last edited October 28. PagerDuty is the record, so check it for any later swap before relying on this [7].
- Shifts start Tuesday at 10:00 local time. The outgoing primary posts a handover note in `#oncall-handover` by then, and it should mention any active Hydrant holds [6][7].

**Useful if you are the one paged**
- Don't scale by hand with `nwctl scale ingest`. Hydrant reverts manual changes within 2 minutes [1].
- To pin the replica count, use `nwctl hydrant hold --cell <cell> --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. A hold lasts at most 4 hours [1].
- Check the affected cell and the gateway TLS handshake errors first [1].
- Raising a cell's ceiling is a normal change. It needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver, Oluwaseun Adeyemi, whose delegate is Kofi Mensah [1][10].

**You owe them a first response within 2 hours.** Growth is the plan that includes 100 million events a month [6]. A customer on that plan reporting that production pipelines are down has a P1 (Critical) ticket. Under the support SLA effective August 1, 2026, Growth P1 first response is 2 hours [2].

**Why this is P1**
- P1 means production pipelines are down, or events aren't being ingested, for the customer's workspace [2]. That matches what the customer reported.
- The customer picks the priority when opening the ticket. Support may change it after triage but must tell the customer why [3]. That rule is from the 2025 edition, and I didn't find it restated in the August 2026 one.

**Which version applies**
- The August 2026 SLA cut Growth P1 first response from 4 hours to 2 hours [2]. The 2025 edition's 4-hour figure is out of date [3].

**Coverage and cadence**
- Growth P1 is covered 24/7, so the 2 hours are clock hours, not business hours [2].
- You owe updates every 4 hours until it's resolved [2].
- Business hours (08:00–18:00, Monday to Friday, in the customer's support region) only matter for lower Growth priorities [2].

**When the clock starts**
- The sources describe tickets coming in through the Hollowpine help center or by email to support@northwind.example [2].
- Slack Connect messages do not start an SLA clock [2].
- Phone paging for P1 is an Enterprise feature, so a Growth customer should use the help center or email [2].
- I didn't find an exact definition of the start time, such as ticket creation versus receipt.

**Escalation**
- If the P1 affects more than one workspace, declare an incident with `/incident declare` rather than waiting for engineering to notice [2]. Severity comes from the incident process, not the ticket priority [2].
- A SEV-1 is a full outage of ingest or pipelines for a cell, or data loss. It pages on-call immediately, assigns an incident commander within 15 minutes, and posts the first status page update within 20 minutes [1].
- Those engineering targets are internal. They don't replace the customer's 2-hour first-response target.

**Credits**
- Service credits for missed first-response targets apply only to Enterprise P1 tickets [2]. I found no equivalent credit for Growth.
- Growth has no phone line or Premium Support add-on. Both are Enterprise only [2].

Six incidents from July through October 2026 were SEV-1 or SEV-2: one SEV-1 and five SEV-2. They hit services owned by five teams: Data Plane, Platform, Identity & Billing, Observability, and (indirectly) Platform again for the Kafka layer under the SEV-1.

The incident log doesn't track owning teams and points to the service catalog for ownership [3]. I used the catalog's owner codes and the team directory to name the teams [1][11].

| Incident | Date | Sev | Service hit | Owning team (catalog) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| INC-2278: archive writes backed up, us-west hot buffer within 6 hours of retention limit | Jul 28 | SEV-2 | Driftwood | Platform (PLAT) [1][3] |
| INC-2291: us-east ingest outage, broker cert bundle missing intermediate CA | Aug 14 | SEV-1 | `ingest-gateway` | Data Plane (DP) [1][3] |
| INC-2302: SAML SSO logins failing for 61 workspaces | Aug 27 | SEV-2 | Keystone | Identity & Billing (IDB) [1][3] |
| INC-2327: hourly usage double-counted, 418 workspaces got false quota warnings | Sep 29 | SEV-2 | Beacon | Observability (OBS) [1][3] |
| INC-2340: duplicate September invoices, 201 card charges refunded | Oct 6 | SEV-2 | Ledger | Identity & Billing (IDB) [1][3] |
| INC-2351: Snowflake destinations failing to load for 63 workspaces | Oct 14 | SEV-2 | Conduit | Data Plane (DP) [1][3] |

## Teams involved
- **Data Plane (DP)** owned two services: `ingest-gateway` (the SEV-1) and Conduit (INC-2351). The manager is Priya Raman [11].
- **Identity & Billing (IDB)** owned two services: Keystone and Ledger. The manager is Harriet Vance [11].
- **Platform (PLAT)** owned Driftwood. The manager is Oluwaseun Adeyemi [11].
- **Observability (OBS)** owned Beacon. The manager is Ravi Subramanian [11].
- **Workspace Experience (WX)** and **Security (SEC)** owned no service hit by a SEV-1 or SEV-2. The only WX service in the log, Atlas, appears in a SEV-3 [3].

## Where reports and the catalog don't line up exactly
- **INC-2291 (SEV-1):** The postmortem's root cause was a routine certificate rotation on the internal Kafka brokers. The gateways then failed their TLS handshakes with those brokers [2]. The catalog lists Kafka clusters as PLAT-owned, while the gateway service is DP-owned [1]. So the failing service belonged to DP, but the change that triggered it was in PLAT's layer. The postmortem was written by Priya Raman (DP) "with the ingest team", and PLAT's Oluwaseun Adeyemi was incident commander [2][3]. The postmortem excerpts I found don't formally assign fault to either team.
- **INC-2340 (Ledger):** The Slack export shows IDB handling it. Arjun Mehta (IDB) declared it and owned the postmortem, and Harriet Vance (IDB) approved the billing change. The fix was an idempotency key on invoice creation, shipped October 8 [4][7]. Kofi Mensah (PLAT) was incident commander, but that's the incident-commander rotation, not ownership [4][11].
- **INC-2327 (Beacon):** The catalog lists Beacon under OBS. The incident commander was Priya Raman (DP) [3]. I found no cause or write-up text for this incident beyond the log, so I can't say which team's change caused it.
- **INC-2351 (Conduit):** The postmortem is still in review, due at the November 5 reliability meeting, and the log says not to speculate about the cause [3]. Harriet Vance (IDB) was incident commander, though Conduit is a DP service [3][1].

## Gaps
I found full write-ups for INC-2291 and INC-2340 only. For INC-2278, INC-2302 and INC-2327, the log says postmortems were published, but I couldn't retrieve their text [3]. If any of them names a different responsible team, I couldn't confirm that.

The vendor register lists four vendors, and together they cost **$198,500 a year**. Each entry states an annual cost directly, so I didn't need to convert any monthly or usage-based prices.

| Vendor (Register ID) | Service | Annual cost | Term | Renewal date |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cobaltline, Inc. (VEN-014) | Hosted log search and retention | **$96,000** [1] | 2 years [1] | March 31, 2027 [1] |
| Hollowpine Software Co. (VEN-031) | Support ticketing and help center | **$44,000** [4] | 1 year [4] | January 31, 2027 [4] |
| Parcelwise Ltd. (VEN-022) | Transactional email delivery | **$31,500** [2] | 1 year, auto-renews [2] | December 15, 2026 [2] |
| Saltmarsh Analytics GmbH (VEN-027) | Product analytics for the web app | **$27,000** [3] | 2 years [3] | June 30, 2027 [3] |

## Things to watch
- **Parcelwise:** It auto-renews on December 15, 2026, and the notice period is 30 days [2]. By my calculation, that puts the cancellation deadline around November 15, 2026, which is about two weeks away.
- **Hollowpine:** It renews on January 31, 2027, and its Data Processing Agreement (DPA) is still unsigned. It is running under security exception SEC-EX-117 [4]. The register gives no notice period for it. Hollowpine replaced our previous helpdesk in July 2026 [4]. The register doesn't give that old vendor's cost, so I can't say whether it still shows up in spend.
- **Cobaltline:** The register calls the current plan a flat fee. The Observability team will renegotiate in February 2027 and is comparing ingest-based pricing [1]. Notice is 60 days before the March 31, 2027 renewal [1], so the deadline is around January 30, 2027.
- **Saltmarsh:** Notice is 90 days before June 30, 2027 [3]. Product is considering replacing it with events routed through our own pipelines [3].

## Gaps
- I found only these four entries. The register IDs run from VEN-014 to VEN-031, so other vendors may exist that I didn't find. The Hollowpine entry mentions Hollowell, an office cleaning vendor with no system access [4]. I found no register entry or cost for Hollowell.
- The register gives no cost for other vendors the documents mention, such as Lookout, which holds pipeline run logs [1].
- The total covers only vendors with a register entry. It isn't the company's full vendor spend.

Starter workspaces can't use four endpoints at all. They get HTTP 403 on each of them, not 429 [1].

| Endpoint | What it does | Lowest plan with access |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /v2/events/batch` | Bulk backfill and replays | Growth (50 req/s) [1] |
| `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh` | Force an Enrich snapshot rebuild | Growth (1 per 10 minutes) [1] |
| `GET /v2/audit-log/export` | Audit log CSV export | Growth (1 per hour) [1] |
| `/v2/scim/*` | SCIM user provisioning | Enterprise only (20 req/s) [1] |

Endpoints marked "Not available" in the rate-limit table return 403 on that plan. Rate-limited endpoints return 429 with a `Retry-After` header [1]. SCIM is also unavailable on Growth [1].

**Endpoints Starter can use, with limits [1]:**
- `POST /v2/events`: 100 req/s.
- `POST /v1/track` (legacy): 50 req/s. It stops accepting events on April 30, 2027.
- `GET /v2/pipelines`: 10 req/s.
- `POST /v2/pipelines/{id}/runs`: 1 req/s.
- `GET /v2/usage`: 2 req/s.

Rate limits apply per workspace, not per API key [1].

Temporary raises for a one-off backfill apply only to plans that already have the endpoint. They don't unlock blocked endpoints for Starter [1].

I found no Support or Leadership document that adds Starter API restrictions beyond this rate-limit table (updated 2026-10-21).

Five production services are classed as Restricted in the service catalog, which is the source of truth for production services and their data classes [1].

| Service | What it does | Restricted data it holds | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ingest-gateway` | Accepts events from customer SDKs and the HTTP API, authenticates them and writes them to Kafka | In-flight event payloads only. Nothing is persisted beyond the Kafka hot buffer. | DP |
| `runner` | Executes customer pipelines: transforms, Enrich steps, destinations | Partition state in local RocksDB and reference-table snapshots | DP |
| Conduit | Source and destination connectors (Postgres, MySQL, Snowflake, warehouses) | Encrypted connector credentials and sync cursors | DP |
| Driftwood | Long-term object archive behind the hot buffer | Archived event payloads, partitioned by workspace and day | PLAT |
| Keystone | Authentication and authorization for the app and API | Hashed API keys, SSO/SAML configuration and session tokens | IDB |

[1] Driftwood was previously called the "cold store" in older runbooks [1].

## What "Restricted" means
The information security policy gives these examples of Restricted data: customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys. Restricted data never leaves production and never goes in tickets or Slack [2]. The service catalog says its "Restricted" and "Confidential" labels follow this policy table [1].

## Not Restricted
- **Confidential:** Ledger (billing; it stores only an opaque payment-provider token, never card numbers) and Atlas (workspace and account metadata, including customer names and emails) [1].
- **Internal:** Beacon (usage metering) and Lookout (dashboards and alerts) [1].
- **Supporting infrastructure:** Kafka, Kubernetes, managed Postgres and Teleport are listed as components without a data class [1]. Kafka holds the hot buffer of event payloads, and managed Postgres backs Keystone, so both sit close to Restricted data. The catalog doesn't classify them, so I haven't counted them.

## Why it matters
- Normal changes to a Restricted service need sign-off from the Head of Security or the security on-call delegate, on top of the owning team's change approver [3].
- Such PRs must also request `@northwind/security` as a reviewer [3].

## Vendor-hosted services
None of the vendors I found is classed as Restricted. Their highest data class is Confidential:
- Hollowpine Helpdesk [5]
- Saltmarsh Analytics [6]
- Cobaltline [7]
- Parcelwise [8]

The vendor registers say Restricted data must never reach these vendors: logs are scrubbed of payloads and credentials, and support tickets must not contain them [5][7].

## Gaps
I found no risk register or audit report in the Support or Leadership collections that names Restricted services. The Vendors collection holds four documents, and I reviewed those four registers.

Four incidents were declared in October 2026. The Engineering incident log, exported October 30, lists them [1].

| Incident | Date | Severity | Service | Cell | What happened |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| INC-2340 | Oct 6 | SEV-2 | **Ledger** | All cells | Duplicate September invoices; 201 card charges refunded [1] |
| INC-2351 | Oct 14 | SEV-2 | **Conduit** | us-east, us-west | Snowflake destinations failing to load for 63 workspaces [1] |
| INC-2358 | Oct 22 | SEV-3 | **Hydrant** | eu-central | Gateway replica count oscillating on Hydrant launch day, with no customer impact [1] |
| INC-2366 | Oct 27 | SEV-3 | **Atlas** | — | Invite and password-reset emails delayed about 2 hours behind a webhook backlog [1] |

The log says it covers every incident declared with `/incident declare` through October 30 [1]. I found nothing that adds an October incident after that date.

## Details on each incident
- **INC-2340 (Ledger):** Arjun Mehta declared it at 09:16 UTC, and Kofi Mensah was the incident commander [2].
  - The payment provider's webhook for the first batch timed out. Ledger's retry logic then re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [2].
  - It produced 312 duplicate invoices across 287 workspaces, and 201 were auto-charged. The refunds totalled $184,300 [2].
  - The postmortem was published October 13 [1].
  - The idempotency-key fix shipped October 8 [13].
- **INC-2351 (Conduit):** Harriet Vance was the incident commander, and it lasted 1h 50m [1].
  - The postmortem draft was circulated October 21. It is due for review on November 5 [1].
  - No root cause is recorded yet, and the log asks people not to speculate about it with customers [1].
- **INC-2358 (Hydrant):** Hydrant is the new ingest-gateway autoscaler, and it shipped October 22 [14].
  - The launch notes say the scale-down cool-off was raised in eu-central while the team investigates [12].
  - It lasted 25 minutes and needed no postmortem [1].
- **INC-2366 (Atlas):** It lasted 2h 10m and needed no postmortem [1].
  - The Parcelwise vendor register says Atlas sends transactional emails such as password resets and invites through Parcelwise. Bounce and complaint webhooks come back to Atlas [7].
  - The log does not say Parcelwise caused the backlog.

## Other sources
- **Support:** The two Support documents are SLA tier documents. They list no individual incidents, so I found no October incidents that exist only in Support records [6][8]. They do say that a P1 affecting more than one workspace should trigger an incident declaration [6].
- **Vendors:** The only vendor link I found is for INC-2340. A payment-provider webhook timeout set off the retry that caused the duplicate invoices, but the root cause was Northwind's non-idempotent invoice creation [2]. The vendor register entries don't mention any October incident.
- **Leadership:** The October offsite notes cover strategy and action items, not incidents [5].

## Not in October
INC-2327 (Beacon, Sep 29) was declared in September. Its postmortem was published October 6, so it can look like an October incident [1].

**You have 30 minutes.** A standard Enterprise customer (no Premium Support) gets a first response within 30 minutes on a P1 ticket. This is the current policy for tickets opened on or after August 1, 2026 [1].

## Enterprise vs. Enterprise + Premium Support (P1)

| Plan | First response | Updates | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Enterprise | 30 minutes | Every hour | 24/7 |
| Enterprise + Premium Support | 15 minutes | Every 30 minutes | 24/7, and the TAM joins the call |

Source: [1]

## Clock and coverage
- P1 coverage is 24/7, so the 30 minutes runs around the clock. Business hours don't pause it [1].
- Business hours are 08:00–18:00, Monday to Friday, in the customer's support region (US Pacific, US Eastern or UK). They apply to Enterprise P3 and P4, not P1 [1].
- Slack Connect messages do not start an SLA clock. The customer has to use the Hollowpine help center or email support@northwind.example. Enterprise customers can also page Support by phone for P1 [1].
- The documents I found don't say exactly when the clock starts. I'm assuming it starts when the ticket is opened or the page is made, but that isn't stated.

## What counts as P1
A P1 (Critical) is when production pipelines are down, or events are not being ingested, for the customer's workspace [1]. The customer picks the priority when opening the ticket. Support may change it after triage, but it must tell the customer why [2].

## Consequences of a miss
Each missed Enterprise P1 first-response target earns the customer a credit of 5% of that month's fee. Credits are capped at 25% per month. The account team requests them and Support Operations approves them [1].

## Outdated figure
The 2025 edition said 1 hour for Enterprise P1 and had no service credits for missed targets [2]. The August 1, 2026 edition replaces it [1].

If a P1 affects more than one workspace, declare an incident with `/incident declare`. Incident severity comes from the incident process, not from the ticket priority [1].

**A Regional sales director approves a 22% discount on an Enterprise deal, but the deal desk has to review it first.** This applies to quotes issued on or after October 1, 2026.

## Which rule applies
Two documents set approval limits, and they conflict:
- **Current rule:** The September 24, 2026 sales desk memo from Marcus Bell (CRO) and Renata Kowal (CFO) replaces the "Discount authority" table in the Pricing and discount policy [1]. For Enterprise deals, a discount over 15% and up to 25% goes to the Regional sales director [1].
- **Old rule:** The older policy table would send 20–30% to the VP of Sales [2]. The memo replaces that table, so ignore it [1].

## Approval path for 22%
1. **Build the quote in the CRM.** Put the discount on the first-year line [1].
2. **Deal desk review.** Any discount over 15% is routed to the deal desk automatically. The deal desk is run by Priscilla Okoye in sales operations. It checks margin, payment terms and any non-standard clauses, then forwards the quote to the approver [1].
3. **Regional sales director decision.** The director records the decision in the CRM. Email and Slack approvals don't count [1].

The target turnaround is 1 business day [1].

## Things to check
- **How the 22% is measured.** Discounts are measured against the first-year contract value at list price [1].
- **Multi-year deals.** A multi-year deal can add an extra 5% per committed year, capped at 10%. That extra doesn't count toward the approval thresholds, so it wouldn't push the deal into a higher tier [1].
- **Approval validity.** Approvals last 30 days. If the quote changes by more than 2 percentage points, it needs fresh approval [1]. A move from 22% to above 24% would need re-approval. A move above 25% would also change the approver to the VP of Sales [1].
- **Custom data retention.** If the deal includes retention beyond the standard period, the security team must approve it whatever the discount [1].
- **Questions.** Ask in `#deal-desk` or contact Priscilla directly [1].

The documents I found have no separate rule for first-year or new-customer discounts. They also don't name the individual Regional sales directors.

**The bake time is 45 minutes.** Since October 12, 2026, a deploy sits in the canary cell for 45 minutes before it can be promoted automatically [1]. This applies to deploys started on or after that date [1].

The engineering handbook still says 20 minutes [2]. That figure is out of date. The October 2026 pipeline note says it overrides the handbook where they differ, and that the handbook will be edited to match [1]. The change came from INC-2291, where some failures only appeared after caches or sessions expired [1].

## What has to pass for auto-promotion
- Error rate and p95 latency must stay within 10% of the baseline. This check is unchanged [1].
- There must be zero sustained TLS handshake errors between gateways and brokers in canary. This check is new [1].
- Runner consumer lag must not grow by more than 2 minutes during the bake. This check is also new [1].

Canary is a real-traffic cell that receives 5% of traffic and receives every deploy first [2][5].

## What happens after canary
- **Most services:** the deploy goes to all remaining cells at once [1].
- **Data-plane changes under `ingest/` or `runner/`:** these roll out in waves, in this order: `us-central`, `us-west`, `us-east`, then `eu-central`. There are 30 minutes between waves [1].

## Holding, blocking and rollback
- **Hold:** anyone can run `/deploy hold <deploy-id>` in Slack to stop a promotion. The deploy stays in canary until someone runs `/deploy release` or rolls it back [1].
- **Status:** `nwctl deploy status` shows where each in-flight deploy is, which checks it has passed, and how long until the next wave [1].
- **Rollback:** this is allowed at any time without approval, including during freezes [1][2].

## Timing constraints
- The deploy window is Monday to Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific [1].
- Friday deploys need approval from the on-call engineering manager [1].
- Changes to billing, authentication and the data plane need two approvals [1].

## Not found
I found no exceptions to the 45-minute bake, such as a shorter bake for hotfixes or different bake times by service tier. I also found no documentation of what happens when a promotion check fails, beyond the hold and rollback options above. The 45 minutes appears to apply to every deploy. If you need a documented exception, ask PLAT or OBS, who wrote the change note [1].

rows.answer:
**No. Don't run `nwctl scale ingest` by hand. The runbook step is out of date.**

## Why not
- The runbook still says to scale with `nwctl scale ingest --cell <cell> --replicas +4` if CPU is above 80% [1].
- The Hydrant launch notes (Oct 22) say Hydrant replaces that step. Hydrant is the new automatic gateway scaler [2].
- Hydrant treats the replica count as its own and reverts a manual change within 2 minutes [2].
- Hydrant has been enabled in us-west since October 15 [2].
- The change policy still lists `nwctl scale` as a standard-change example [14]. That text predates Hydrant, so ignore it for gateways.

## What 80% CPU tells you
Hydrant scales up when average gateway CPU stays above 65% for 3 minutes. It also scales up when Kafka produce latency p95 stays above 250 ms for 3 minutes. Each step adds 25% of current replicas, with a minimum of 2 [2]. If us-west is above 80% and 5xx is firing, Hydrant should already be scaling. Check why it isn't, or why scaling isn't helping:

1. **Is it at its ceiling?** The us-west floor/ceiling is 10 / 48 replicas [5]. If a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call. The launch notes say this usually means a gateway problem rather than real traffic [2].
2. **Was there a gateway deploy in the last 10 minutes?** Hydrant doesn't scale during that window [2]. Data-plane deploys now go canary → us-central → us-west → us-east → eu-central, with 30 minutes between waves [11]. Run `nwctl deploy status` to see whether a deploy is in flight [11].
3. **Is the Hydrant controller down?** That pages the Platform primary, and gateways keep their last replica count [2].

## Runbook steps that still apply
- Check the ingest dashboard to see which cell is affected [1][2].
- If the brokers are healthy, look at gateway TLS handshake errors. INC-2291 was a cert-chain problem that made every gateway in a cell fail handshakes at once, and broker logs showed nothing [1][4].
- The dashboard now has a TLS handshake errors panel [4]. Session tickets now last 30 minutes instead of 4 hours, so cert problems surface faster [8].

## What you can do
- **Pin the count while debugging** (for example, a bad gateway build): `nwctl hydrant hold --cell us-west --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`.
  - A hold lasts at most 4 hours and needs no approval.
  - Release it early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell us-west` [2].
- **If a recent deploy looks bad:** `/deploy hold <deploy-id>` stops promotion to later waves [11]. Rollbacks are allowed at any time without approval [11].
- **If you need more than 48 replicas:** raising a ceiling is a normal change. It needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver, Oluwaseun Adeyemi, or his delegate Kofi Mensah [2][16]. During a declared incident, the incident commander can approve it as an emergency change, with review within two business days [14][3].

## Incident handling
- Declare with `/incident declare` in Slack. This opens a channel, starts the timeline and pages the IC rotation [1].
- **SEV-2** is partial outage or degraded performance affecting many customers. Acknowledge within 15 minutes [1].
- **SEV-1** is a full ingest outage for a cell. The IC must be assigned within 15 minutes, and the first status page update goes out within 20 minutes. Updates then follow at least every 30 minutes [1][3].
- If unsure, declare higher. The IC can downgrade later [3].
- Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 gets a blameless postmortem within five business days [1].

## Gaps
I found no document on how to tell a traffic spike from a downstream failure beyond the TLS check and the ceiling signal. I also found no AWS quota information for us-west-2. The on-call rota I found covers only November–December, so I can't name today's Data Plane primary. Check PagerDuty.

Sandbar runs in **eu-central-1 (Frankfurt)**.

- **What Sandbar is:** It's the internal codename for EU data residency, which means building and running the `eu-central` cell. The Platform team (PLAT) owns it, Oluwaseun Adeyemi leads it, and its status is "Limited availability" [1].
- **The region:** The production cell inventory maps the `eu-central` cell to AWS region `eu-central-1` in Frankfurt. The cell opened on September 21, 2026, and its data residency is EU [2].
- **Data stays in the region:** A workspace lives in exactly one cell, and its event data doesn't leave that cell's region [2]. Application logs from `eu-central` stay in Lookout in-region. They aren't shipped to Cobaltline, which is US-only [2].

**Multi-region or failover:** Sandbar isn't multi-region today, and I found no failover or disaster-recovery region for it. A second EU cell, `eu-west` in `eu-west-1` (Ireland), is planned for Q2 2027. It's described as a second EU cell, with broker counts and gateway limits to be set during capacity planning. I found no source that calls it a failover for `eu-central` [2].

**Vendor and support docs:** My searches returned no vendor or support documents that mention Sandbar's region. The two sources above are the evidence.

**Naming caution:** Don't confuse Sandbar with Saltmarsh, which is a vendor [1]. Codenames like Sandbar are internal only and must not appear in customer-facing material [1].

rows.answer:
**Full cutover to the new payment provider is scheduled for January 19, 2027.** That date comes from the Identity & Billing weekly status posted October 26, 2026. It falls after the holiday freeze and after the January invoices have gone out. Arjun Mehta owns the cutover plan [1].

The migration is codenamed **Undertow**. It moves card collection and Ledger's customer tokens to the new provider. The Identity & Billing team (IDB) owns it, and its status is "In progress" [2]. I couldn't find the new or old provider's name in the knowledge base.

## Where things stand
- **Dual-running:** This started October 19. 5% of Growth workspaces now have card payments collected through the new provider, and Ledger writes to both providers. Reconciliation has shown no mismatches so far [1].
- **Token migration rehearsal #2:** It moved from October 30 to **November 12**. October 30 is the last business day of the month, which puts it in the month-end billing freeze. Arjun runs it, and Noor Haddad will check what customers would see on the billing emails [1].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** It runs from Friday, October 30 until invoices are sent, expected November 2. No normal changes to Ledger are allowed in that window [1].
- **Thanksgiving week:** Harriet Vance and Arjun are both out November 24–27, so normal Ledger or Keystone changes need planning around that [1].

## Open risk
The new provider's webhook retries are faster than the old provider's. Arjun is making sure the webhook handler is idempotent before cutover. This is the same class of bug as INC-2340, where a webhook timeout caused a retry that re-ran invoicing. That incident produced duplicate invoices and 201 card charges that were refunded [1][5].

## Changes to the timeline
- The October leadership offsite said the migration "will not finish until mid-January". That matches the January 19 date [4].
- The migration affects other projects. The Lantern billing portal's GA slipped from January to March 2027, and its beta moved from December to February. Plan changes in the portal are blocked until Undertow finishes [1][4].
- I found no sign that the January 19 date itself has slipped. It is the first firm date I found, since the status note says "Undertow has a date" [1].

## Not found
I found nothing on when the contract with the current payment provider ends or when it will be decommissioned. The vendor register has no entry for either provider. The Vendors collection holds Hollowpine, Parcelwise, Saltmarsh and Cobaltline, but no payment processor. I also found no detailed phase plan beyond dual-running at 5%, the token rehearsals and the final cutover. Arjun Mehta (cutover plan) or Harriet Vance (IDB manager) would be the people to ask.

The firehose handles **Restricted** data, and the **Data Plane (DP)** team owns it.

"The firehose" is the informal Slack name for the production service `ingest-gateway` [1]. The service catalog describes it as accepting events from customer SDKs and the HTTP API, authenticating them, and writing them to Kafka [4].

- **Data class:** The catalog marks `ingest-gateway` as Restricted. It stores only in-flight event payloads. Nothing is persisted beyond the Kafka hot buffer [4]. "Restricted" follows the data classification table in the information security policy [4]. I didn't open that policy, so I haven't checked the definition of Restricted.
- **Owner:** The catalog lists DP as the owner [4]. The Engineering directory shows Data Plane's engineering manager and change approver is Priya Raman, with Lin Zhou as delegate. Its Slack channel is `#team-dataplane` [3].
- **On-call:** The Data Plane rotation covers ingest gateways, pipeline runners and connectors [2].

**Related ownership detail:** Hydrant, the gateway autoscaler, is owned by Platform (PLAT). The gateways themselves stay with DP [5]. The Kafka clusters the gateway writes to are also PLAT's [4]. Hydrant stores no customer data and isn't a Restricted service [5].

rows.answer:
**Archived events stay in the attic for 365 days by default.** "The attic" is the informal name for Driftwood, the long-term event archive. Older documents call it the cold store [5]. The 365-day figure comes from retention standard v2, effective September 15, 2026 [2].

**Recent change.** Version 1 of the standard, approved February 2, 2026, set the default at 400 days [1]. Version 2 cut it to 365 days and says that where the two versions differ, v2 applies [2]. Some other documents still use the old number. For example, the pricing policy says sales can't offer retention beyond 400 days without security approval [3]. I didn't find any updated wording there.

**Overrides.**
- Enterprise customers can contract for a different archive period. Under v1 they could only go shorter [1]. Under v2 they can also go longer, up to 730 days, with security team approval [2].
- Per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags [2].
- Shortening retention requires a 30-day customer notice from the account team for Enterprise contracts that reference a retention period. It also needs an ADR [4].

**How deletion happens.** Object-storage lifecycle rules on the Driftwood buckets delete objects once they pass the retention period for their workspace [2]. Platform (PLAT) owns Driftwood [6]. Changing the lifecycle rules is a normal change under the production change approval policy [2].

**Early deletion.**
- Verified deletion requests, such as GDPR erasure, are completed in all live systems within 14 days. The limit was 30 days under v1 [2].
- When a workspace is closed, its archived event data is deleted within 14 days [2].

**Not covered by the 365 days.** Reference-table snapshots that are stored in Driftwood are deleted 7 days after they are replaced [2]. RFC-031 proposes keeping them in a separate bucket from the event archive [7].

**For an Enterprise customer with Premium Support, a P2 ticket gets a first response within 1 hour. After that, we update the customer every 2 hours. Coverage is 24/7.** [1]

These targets come from the SLA tiers that took effect August 1, 2026. They apply to tickets opened on or after that date [1].

**How P2 is defined.** A P2 (High) is a production pipeline that is degraded, meaning late or partially failing, with no reasonable workaround [1].

**How this compares with other plans**

| Plan | P2 first response | P2 update cadence | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Growth | 8 business hours | Daily | Business hours |
| Enterprise | 2 hours | Every 4 hours | 24/7 |
| **Enterprise + Premium Support** | **1 hour** | **Every 2 hours** | **24/7** |

All rows are from [1].

**Other points**
- Because P2 coverage is 24/7, the "business hours" definition (08:00–18:00, Monday to Friday, in the customer's support region, excluding public holidays) doesn't apply to it [1].
- The Premium Support P2 row does not mention a TAM on the call. A TAM joins the call only for P1 [1].
- Premium Support is sold only with Enterprise. It can't be added to Growth [1].
- The 2025 edition set Enterprise P2 at 4 hours for first response and every 8 hours for updates. It is superseded for tickets opened on or after August 1, 2026 [1][2].
- Support may change a ticket's priority after triage, and it must tell the customer why [2]. That rule appears in the 2025 edition. The 2026 page doesn't restate it, but doesn't say it changed.
- Service credits for missed targets apply only to Enterprise P1 first responses. A missed P2 target gets no credit [1].

rows.answer:
Hydrant will run at most **40** ingest gateway replicas in the cell in AWS region us-east-2.

**Which cell:** The cell in us-east-2 (Ohio) is named `us-central`. The name comes from the network latency zone it serves, not the AWS region. Don't confuse it with the `us-east` cell, which runs in us-east-1 [3].

**The limit:** The production cell inventory lists `us-central` with Hydrant gateway replicas of 8 at the floor and 40 at the ceiling [3]. Hydrant adjusts the replica count between those two numbers [1].

**What happens at the ceiling:**
- Each scale-up step adds 25% of the current replicas, with a minimum of 2. Steps are triggered by average CPU above 65% or Kafka produce p95 latency above 250 ms, either one sustained for 3 minutes [1].
- If a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call. The reasoning is that hitting the ceiling usually means a gateway problem rather than real traffic [1].
- Manual scaling with `nwctl scale ingest` is no longer allowed, because Hydrant reverts manual changes within 2 minutes [1].
- You can pin the count with `nwctl hydrant hold`, but a hold lasts at most 4 hours [1]. The hold command's own `--replicas` limit isn't documented in what I found.

**What I didn't find:** The knowledge base has nothing on AWS service quotas or instance capacity limits for this cell. It also has no exceptions or recent changes to the 40 ceiling. The inventory was last updated October 23, 2026, and Hydrant was enabled in `us-central` on October 19 [1][3].

rows.answer:
A Growth workspace can send **500 requests per second** to the legacy `POST /v1/track` endpoint [1].

**Details for Growth**
- **Burst:** short bursts of up to 2x the limit (so up to 1,000 req/s) are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- **Scope:** the limit applies per workspace, not per API key. All keys in a workspace share one budget [1].
- **Request size:** each request can carry at most 100 events [1].
- **Over the limit:** the API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota. Northwind's SDKs honor `Retry-After` automatically and back off exponentially [1].

**Comparison with other plans** [1]

| Plan | `/v1/track` limit |
|---|---|
| Starter | 50 req/s |
| Growth | 500 req/s |
| Enterprise (default) | 1,000 req/s |

**Exceptions and deprecation**
- **No raises:** `/v1/track` keeps its lower limits until it is switched off, and Northwind won't raise them for anyone [1].
- **Growth contracts:** Growth limits are fixed by contract. The only exception is a temporary raise of up to 72 hours for a one-off backfill, which the Data Plane on-call primary can grant. That exception is stated for any plan that has the endpoint, but the source says `/v1/track` limits won't be raised for anyone, so the two statements conflict for this endpoint [1].
- **Shutdown:** `/v1/track` stops accepting events on April 30, 2027 [1][2].
- **Migration:** customers should move to `POST /v2/events`, which allows 2,000 req/s on Growth. Every SDK released after March 2025 already uses it [1][2].

**Ravi Subramanian** was incident commander when SAML logins broke in August. The incident lasted **1 hour 35 minutes**.

The incident log lists this as INC-2302, dated August 27 [2]:
- **Severity:** SEV-2.
- **What happened:** SAML SSO logins failed for 61 workspaces after an identity-provider metadata refresh.
- **Service and scope:** Keystone, across all cells.
- **Postmortem:** published September 3.

The log measures durations from declaration to resolution [2]. The 1h 35m therefore runs from when the incident was declared, not from when customers first felt the impact. The only exception in the log is INC-2291, which is timed from first customer impact. The log gives no start or end clock times for INC-2302.

The INC-2302 postmortem itself didn't turn up in my searches. The commander and duration come only from the incident log. A later Keystone status note confirms the follow-up fix: the SAML metadata refresh now validates new metadata before swapping it in. It shipped October 15, and there has been no repeat since [1].

A **Growth account executive** can approve 12% off. They don't need deal desk review or anyone else's sign-off.

**Why**
- Under the sales desk memo of September 24, 2026, a Growth deal with a discount over 10% and up to 15% is approved by the account executive. Target turnaround is 1 business day [1].
- The memo applies to quotes issued on or after October 1, 2026. It replaces the "Discount authority" table in the older Pricing and discount policy [1].
- The old table is out of date for this case. It sent 10–20% discounts to the regional sales director [2]. That is now the rule only for Enterprise deals in the 10–15% band [1].

**Process**
- Build the quote in the CRM with the discount on the first-year line [1].
- Deal desk review is only triggered above 15%, so it doesn't apply here [1].
- The account executive must record the decision in the CRM. Email and Slack approvals don't count [1].
- The approval is valid for 30 days. If the quote changes by more than 2 percentage points, it needs fresh approval [1].

**Things to check**
- **Discount base:** the percentage is measured against first-year contract value at list price [1].
- **Annual prepayment:** Growth already gets a 15% discount for annual prepayment [1][2]. If the customer is asking for 12% in addition to that, the total is higher than 15%. That would put it over the deal desk threshold and require the regional sales director (over 15% up to 25%) [1]. The documents don't say whether the prepayment discount counts toward these thresholds, so confirm with the deal desk (Priscilla Okoye, sales operations) [1].
- **Multi-year deals:** an extra 5% per committed year, capped at 10%, can be added. It doesn't count toward the approval thresholds [1].
- **Non-profit or education customers:** they get 50% off Growth automatically, with no approval needed [1].
- **Custom data retention:** this still needs the security team, whatever the discount [1].

**Send a Growth customer an update on a P3 ticket every 3 business days.** This comes from the current SLA, effective August 1, 2026, and it applies to tickets opened on or after that date [1].

## Details for Growth P3

- **P3 definition:** a bug or question that has a workaround available [1].
- **First response:** 2 business days [1].
- **Update cadence:** every 3 business days [1].
- **Coverage:** business hours only [1].
- **Business hours:** 08:00–18:00, Monday to Friday, in the customer's support region (US Pacific, US Eastern or UK). The region's public holidays are excluded [1]. Weekends and holidays don't count toward the 3 days.

## Tickets opened before August 1, 2026

The 2025 edition set Growth P3 and P4 together at "as needed", with no fixed cadence [2]. The August 2026 edition replaces it and splits P3 and P4 into separate rows [1]. It says tickets opened on or after August 1, 2026 use the new targets [1]. The documents don't say which edition governs a ticket opened before that date and still open. Check with Support Operations if you have one.

## Related points

- Priority is the customer's choice when they open the ticket. Support can change it after triage but must tell the customer why [2]. The 2026 edition doesn't repeat this rule. If a P3 is re-triaged to P2, the cadence becomes daily [1].
- Only the helpdesk (the help center or email to support@northwind.example) starts an SLA clock. Slack Connect messages don't [1].
- I found nothing on whether the cadence pauses while a ticket waits on the customer, or on any special rules for escalated P3s. Treat the 3-business-day cadence as the baseline, and confirm with Support Operations (owner: Gwen Talbot) if you need an exception [1].

rows.answer:
An Enterprise workspace can force a reference-table snapshot rebuild **once every 2 minutes** by default. The endpoint is `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh`, which the rate-limit page describes as "Force an Enrich snapshot rebuild" [3].

**How the limit applies**
- The limit is per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in a workspace share one budget [3].
- A request over the limit gets HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header giving the seconds to wait [3].
- The page says short bursts of up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds. It doesn't say whether that applies to this endpoint's "1 per 2 minutes" cap [3].

**Comparison with other plans** [3]
| Plan | Forced rebuild limit |
|---|---|
| Starter | Not available (HTTP 403) |
| Growth | 1 per 10 minutes |
| Enterprise (default) | 1 per 2 minutes |

**Raises and exceptions**
- The contractual raise of up to 3x applies only to the ingest endpoints `/v2/events` and `/v2/events/batch`. The page lists no contractual raise for the refresh endpoint [3].
- The DP on-call primary can grant temporary raises of up to 72 hours for a one-off backfill, on any plan that has the endpoint. The page doesn't say whether that covers refresh [3].
- I found nothing on exceptions for concurrent rebuilds or table size.

**Why the limit is tight**
A forced refresh throws away the runner's snapshot and rebuilds it from a full table scan. That is expensive for large tables. Most customers never need it, because snapshots are kept current with change data capture [3]. The engineering docs say an automatic rebuild already happens if CDC lag exceeds 10 minutes [2]. For a 50M-row table, an RFC puts a rebuild at about 25 minutes, during which Enrich steps on that partition stall [1].

The rate-limit page was last updated October 21, 2026 [3].
