The knowledge base has no rate limit for `/v2/destinations`. The internal rate-limits page (updated October 21, 2026) lists nine endpoints, and `/v2/destinations` isn't one of them [1]. I also searched the Engineering, Support, Vendors, Company and Leadership collections and found no other mention of it. That includes the changelog and the service catalog. I'm not going to guess a number.

## What the documentation does say

**Limits apply per workspace.**
- Limits are per workspace, not per API key, so ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- Bursts of up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- Going over the limit returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header giving the seconds to wait. The SDKs honour it automatically and back off exponentially [1].
- Endpoints marked "Not available" on a plan return HTTP 403, not 429 [1].

**Growth limits on the documented management endpoints** are the closest comparison, though none of them is `/v2/destinations`:

| Endpoint | Growth limit |
|---|---|
| `GET /v2/pipelines` | 50 req/s [1] |
| `POST /v2/pipelines/{id}/runs` | 10 req/s [1] |
| `GET /v2/usage` | 10 req/s [1] |
| `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh` | 1 per 10 minutes [1] |
| `GET /v2/audit-log/export` | 1 per hour [1] |

Don't assume `/v2/destinations` matches any of these. The limits vary a lot by endpoint.

**Overrides on Growth:**
- Growth limits are fixed by contract. Customers who need more are told to talk to sales about Enterprise [1].
- The one exception is a temporary raise for a one-off backfill, up to 72 hours. The Data Plane on-call primary can grant it on any plan that has the endpoint [1].

## Next step
The page says Workspace Experience (WX) owns the management API limits [1]. Ask WX, or check the public API docs, to confirm whether `/v2/destinations` has its own limit. It may be missing from the table, or it may fall under a limit I couldn't find.

**What the incident log says [1]**

- Snowflake destinations failed to load for 63 workspaces. The affected service was Conduit, in the us-east and us-west cells.
- The incident lasted 1h 50m, and Harriet Vance was incident commander.

- No postmortem draft, Slack export, or incident channel log for INC-2351.
- No action items, owners, due dates or statuses.
- No sign that a vendor or support escalation was involved. I searched the Support and Vendors collections and found nothing.
- Conduit is owned by the DP team, according to the service catalog [8].

**Don't infer a cause from other incidents.** These look similar but are unrelated to INC-2351:
- INC-2264 (July, Snowflake auth failure) was a single workspace whose customer had rotated credentials [1].
- The changelog notes Snowflake key-pair auth in Conduit, with password auth to be removed in 2027 [4].
- Nothing links either of these to INC-2351.

**Next step:** check the postmortem draft that was circulated on October 21, or ask the author or Harriet Vance. After the November 5 reliability meeting, the incident log should list the accepted root cause and action items.

I can't tell you who it is, because the Data Plane on-call schedule for the week starting Tuesday, January 5, 2027 hasn't been published.

- **Published rota ends December 22.** The Engineering rota covers shifts starting November 3 through December 22, 2026 [1].
- **Later weeks aren't out yet.** The rota for shifts starting December 29 onward "will be published by December 15" [1]. That means January 5 isn't in any document I can see.
- **No swaps or overrides.** The only swaps on record are for November 10 (Data Plane) and December 8/15 (incident commander). Nothing touches January 5 [1].
- **No rotation formula.** The rota is a published table, not a rule. The Data Plane names don't repeat in a fixed order, so I can't work out the January primary from the pattern. I'd be guessing.

**What I did find that applies to that week**
- Shifts run one week, starting Tuesday at 10:00 local time. January 5, 2027 is a Tuesday, so it's a handoff day [4].
- The outgoing primary posts a handover note in `#oncall-handover` by Tuesday 10:00, and the incoming primary acknowledges it [1].
- The holiday change freeze runs December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, so it ends the day before this shift starts. During the freeze only standard and emergency changes ship [3].
- Swaps are arranged in `#oncall-swaps`. PagerDuty is the record for paging and pay, so a swap has to be reflected there before the shift starts [1][4].

**Data Plane people who appear in the November–December rota:** Ines Duarte, Yusuf Demir, Carla Benitez, Tom Whitfield and Lin Zhou [1]. Priya Raman is the Data Plane manager [7]. Being in the Nov–Dec rota doesn't mean any of them is on for January 5.

**Where to look:** check back after December 15 for the next rota, or look at the Data Plane schedule in PagerDuty. You can also ask in `#team-dataplane` or `#oncall-swaps` [7].

**Yes. Coriander Media keeps connection logs from video visits, and it keeps them for 30 days.** The log fields are IP address, room ID and timestamps. Coriander keeps them for troubleshooting [7].

**What Coriander does and doesn't hold**
- Coriander provides the real-time video/audio SDK and hosted media servers behind Juniper, Halcyon's new telehealth platform. Juniper is built in-house on the Coriander SDK [4][7].
- The PHI involved is live encrypted audio and video streams, participant display names, and room metadata [7].
- Coriander keeps no recordings. Recording is disabled at the account level, and Coriander cannot turn it on [7]. The Juniper steering committee also decided that recordings stay off, with no exceptions, including for training [1].
- Media is encrypted in transit between participants and Coriander's media servers [7].
- Data residency is US only [7].
- The BAA was executed on August 18, 2026. Coriander must notify the Privacy Officer within 72 hours of discovering a breach [7].

**Timing**
- Coriander is not live yet. The Juniper pilot starts January 12, 2027, and the network-wide rollout is March 2, 2027 [1]. Until then, visits run on Larkspur.
- Larkspur has a different exit arrangement. It returns visit metadata exports by April 15, 2027, and certifies destruction of the remaining data by April 30, 2027 [2].

**What I couldn't find**
- The knowledge base only has the vendor record summary for Coriander, not the contract or BAA text. I found nothing on what happens to Coriander-held data at contract end, such as return or deletion terms.
- I also found no Halcyon policy on retention of vendor-held telehealth logs. The 30-day figure comes only from the vendor record [7].
- Nothing says whether the 30-day period is a fixed deletion window or whether Coriander can keep logs longer, for example during an incident.
- If you need those answers, ask Dana Okafor, the internal owner in Virtual Care, or the Privacy Officer to check the BAA itself [7].

**Quillon Ambient deletes visit audio within 7 days after the clinician signs the note.** Quillon is Halcyon's AI scribe, currently in pilot. Its business associate record lists the audio retention as "Deleted within 7 days after the note is signed" [3].

The records I found don't answer the other questions in your plan:

- **Automatic or manual deletion:** The record gives a "within 7 days" deadline. It doesn't say whether Quillon deletes the audio automatically on signature or on a schedule. It also doesn't say whether anyone at Halcyon has to trigger deletion. It sets a maximum window, not an exact deletion time [3].
- **Contract and BAA wording:** The BAA was executed July 30, 2026. The knowledge base has only the summary record, not the agreement itself. The BAA prohibits model training on Halcyon data [3]. I found no clause-level text on audio storage or deletion.
- **Exceptions:** I found no mention of legal holds, patient requests or quality review changing the 7-day audio window. The pilot's note accuracy audit is a review of 30 notes per clinician by Clinical Informatics. The records don't say whether it uses audio [3].

Other points from the records:
- The data Quillon handles is visit audio, transcripts, draft notes, and patient name and date of birth. The systems inventory lists Quillon as holding visit audio and draft notes [3][6]. The 7-day retention figure covers audio only. I found no retention period for transcripts or draft notes.
- Patients can decline recording at any time. The clinician then turns off recording in the Quillon app and documents manually [3].

To confirm the exact deletion mechanism or any exceptions, ask Clinical Informatics (Grace Oyelaran), who own the Quillon vendor record. You could also ask the Privacy Officer to check the executed BAA [3].

**You get a 14-day grace period after the deadline, and then your access is suspended automatically.** The policy says all workforce members complete HIPAA training "annually by January 31," and that "access to clinical systems is suspended automatically if training is overdue by more than 14 days" [1].

**What that means for you**
- The cutoff is January 31 plus 14 days, so suspension begins after February 14.
- Today is October 31, 2026. If your training is already past due, the policy doesn't say how the clock works for you. It could be counted from the January 31 deadline or from a date set by your own training cycle.
- Because suspension is automatic, treat any overdue status as urgent. Don't count on a human making an exception. Confirm your status and due date with the compliance team or the Privacy Officer, Margaret Holloway [3].

**What I couldn't find**
- **Warnings or reminders:** The knowledge base doesn't describe reminder emails or escalation steps before suspension.
- **Getting access back:** There is no documented process or timeline for restoring access after a training-related suspension. The IT Service Desk (extension 4357) is the general entry point for problems [7], but I found nothing saying it handles reinstatement.
- **Vendor systems:** Nothing says vendor-run systems enforce training differently. Meridian EHR, the main clinical system, is run by Meridian Clinical Systems [5]. The policy refers to "clinical systems" generally and makes no exception for vendor-managed ones [1].

**Related points**
- Break-the-glass is not a workaround. It only lets users with active EHR access open charts outside their normal limits. It is also logged and reviewed [3].
- At onboarding, HIPAA training is required before you get EHR access [2]. This suggests training status and EHR access are linked, but the documents don't say so for renewals.

The safest step is to finish the training now. If you're already locked out or close to it, contact the Privacy Officer at privacy@halcyon.example [1] or the Service Desk.

rows.answer:
**Hand the patient off to the medical assistant within 10 minutes of check-in.** This is step 4 of the front-desk check-in sequence in the Patient intake procedure [3].

## Where the handoff fits
The front desk completes these steps before the handoff [3]:
1. Verify identity with a government photo ID. For minors, verify the guardian's ID and confirm guardianship on file.
2. Confirm insurance eligibility. If it fails, offer the self-pay estimate before the visit, not after.
3. Collect the copay. Patients with an outstanding balance over $250 are referred to billing but are never turned away.
4. Hand the patient off to the medical assistant within 10 minutes of check-in.

After the handoff, the medical assistant records vitals (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, weight, SpO2) and reconciles the medication list. The assistant also does the PHQ-2 depression screen for every adult at least once a year. A score of 3 or higher triggers the full PHQ-9 before the clinician enters the room [3].

## Related target
The 10-minute handoff sits inside a larger clinic target. Door-to-room time should be under 15 minutes for 90% of visits [3].

## Related timing rules
- **New patients:** They should complete digital intake in the app at least 24 hours before their first visit. The front desk calls anyone whose intake is incomplete at that point [3]. The goal is at least 80% of new patients finishing intake before arrival [3].
- **Late arrivals:** Under the October 2026 policy, a patient who arrives more than 10 minutes after their appointment time is offered the next open slot that day or is rescheduled. The clinician may still see them if the schedule allows. The policy says the shorter threshold protects the door-to-room target for the patients who follow [2]. This replaced the 2025 threshold of 15 minutes [4].
- **Interpreter or accessibility delays on our side:** These patients are never rescheduled for being late [2].
- **Interpreter access:** Video interpreters are available in more than 200 languages, within 2 minutes [3]. The Q3 2026 language access report gives Polyglen's targets as 2 minutes for the top 20 languages and ASL, and 5 minutes for all other languages [6].
- **Urgent or red-flag symptoms:** The escalation protocol covers these, for example chest pain with shortness of breath, stroke signs, SpO2 below 90%, or active suicidal ideation with a plan. Staff call 911 and notify the on-site clinician immediately [1]. It does not tie this to the 10-minute handoff window.

## What the knowledge base doesn't say
I found no documented process for monitoring the 10-minute handoff or for escalating when it is missed. The documents don't say who tracks it or what happens after a breach.

Related material I did find:
- A Q2 2026 operations review found medium and large clinics missing the door-to-room target on most afternoons. The September 1, 2026 staffing standard responded with more medical assistants per clinician in those clinics, an RN at every clinic, and a charge nurse on every shift in large clinics [5].
- Clinic managers review no-show rates monthly, but I found no equivalent review of handoff times [2].

**Don't throw the vaccines out yet.** A reading of 10 °C is outside the required 2–8 °C range. Halcyon's cold-chain procedure says "Do not discard anything" and sets out the steps below [1].

## What to do now [1]

1. **Protect the stock.**
   - Label the affected vaccines "Do not use".
   - Keep them refrigerated in a working unit. Move them if the current fridge can't hold temperature.
   - Record the reading, the time and how long the fridge was out of range.
2. **Call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour.** The pharmacist checks with the manufacturers on whether the stock can still be used.
3. **File a SafeReport.**
   - File it as a Level 4 near miss if no vaccine was given from the affected stock.
   - File it at a higher level if a patient received affected vaccine.
4. **Give no vaccine from that stock** until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing.

## Other points

- **Who decides:** The clinical pharmacist, working with the manufacturers, decides whether stock is usable or must be discarded. Clinic staff don't make that call. The knowledge base doesn't give manufacturer-specific stability limits.
- **Data to have ready:** The fridge logs readings automatically every 15 minutes, and the opening MA checks them [1]. Those logs should show when the excursion began and how long it lasted.
- **Frozen products:** Frozen vaccines are never refrozen or reused once thawed [1].
- **If a patient already received vaccine from this stock:** Report at a higher level than Level 4 [1]. When unsure, report at the higher level, and Quality & Patient Safety will reclassify if needed [6]. Also tell the charge nurse, or the clinic manager if no charge nurse is on shift [6].
- **Replacement stock:** Tier 1 vaccines are ordered weekly by the clinic manager. Tier 2 transfers from the nearest hub clinic arrive within 2 business days, and Tier 3 named-patient orders take about 5 business days. Transfers and Tier 3 orders go through the clinical pharmacist [1].
- **Fridge repair:** I found no vendor or repair contact for vaccine refrigerators. The vendor matrix says to open a ticket with the IT Service Desk (ext. 4357) for system problems, and not to call vendors directly unless the Service Desk asks [3]. That matrix covers IT systems, so it may not cover refrigerator repair. Ask your clinic manager who handles it.
- **Other documentation:** I found no requirement to notify the health department, and no named manufacturer contacts. The pharmacist handles manufacturer contact.

Today is Saturday, so confirm how to reach the clinical pharmacist out of hours. The documents I found don't give a contact number or an after-hours route.

Shifts run from Monday 08:00 Eastern to the next Monday 08:00 Eastern [1]. Tonight falls in week 44 (Oct 26 to Nov 2) [1]:

The on-call medical director is the senior physician for the whole network. Typical reasons to call [1][2][3]:

Record the time, who was notified, and the outcome in the encounter note or chart [2].

The knowledge base doesn't say whether anyone must be contacted before the answering service, such as a house supervisor. It also doesn't describe what happens if the backup doesn't respond either. **Short answer:** Halcyon's standard is **10 business days** from the request. HIPAA allows up to 30 calendar days, but Halcyon's own standard is tighter and applies to every patient request that isn't instantly available in the portal [1].

**Details for a patient's own chart copy**
- **Format and fee:** An electronic copy (secure email or encrypted USB) or a paper copy costs a **$6.50 flat fee**, and the turnaround is 10 business days [1]. The portal download is free and immediate, but this patient can't get what they need there [1].
- **Sliding-fee patients:** Fees are waived for patients in the sliding-fee program [1].
- **Unpaid balances:** Never refuse or delay a patient's request because of an unpaid balance [1].
- **Personal representatives:** A patient's personal representative falls under the same row and timeline as the patient [1].
- **Sensitive records:** Records with extra legal protection, such as substance use treatment records, are released only after the Privacy Officer has reviewed the request [1]. Margaret Holloway is the Privacy Officer, at privacy@halcyon.example [5]. This review may affect your timing, but I found no separate deadline for it.
- **Law enforcement and subpoenas:** These go to the Privacy Officer, not to HIM staff [1].
- **Questions:** Contact HIM through the intranet or at him@halcyon.example [1].

**Shorter or longer deadlines for other requests**
- Records sent to another treating provider are free, with a 3-business-day turnaround [1].
- Records for an attorney or insurer need a signed authorization. They cost $25 plus $0.25 per page and take 15 business days [1].

**What I didn't find**
- **Identity verification:** The knowledge base has no step-by-step procedure for verifying a patient's identity or taking a written request for a chart copy. The HIPAA privacy policy only says patients can request their own records through the portal [7]. Check with HIM or the Privacy Officer on how to confirm identity.
- **Extensions:** I found no documented process for extending past 10 business days. The only outer limit is HIPAA's 30 calendar days [1].
- **Outside vendors:** No release-of-information vendor appears in the vendor documents. The records are in the Meridian EHR [4], and the fee schedule puts requests with HIM [1].

**In practice:** Log the request date, tell the patient to expect the copy within 10 business days, and send it by secure email or encrypted USB, or on paper. Don't put PHI in email subject lines, and use `[secure]` encrypted email for any PHI in the body [4][7].

rows.answer:
The RCA team has to be chartered **within 72 hours**. Halcyon Health's Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy sets that deadline [1].

**Why it applies:** The policy classifies a "medication error requiring treatment" as a Level 2 event, an adverse event with harm [1]. Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets a root cause analysis, and QPS (Quality & Patient Safety) charters the RCA team within 72 hours [1]. If you're unsure of the level, report at the higher level. QPS will reclassify the event if needed [1].

**Who convenes it:** QPS charters the team [1]. The person reporting the event doesn't do this.

**Related deadlines:**
- **Immediately:** Make the patient safe and tell the charge nurse. If there is no charge nurse on shift, tell the clinic manager [1].
- **Within 1 hour:** For a sentinel event (Level 1) only, the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director [1]. A medication error requiring treatment is Level 2, so this step doesn't apply unless the event is upgraded.
- **Within 24 hours:** Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files a report in SafeReport. The attending clinician also discloses the event to the patient or family [1].
- **Within 45 calendar days:** The RCA must be completed, counted from the event becoming known [1]. The Patient Safety Committee, chaired by Dr. Kenji Watanabe, then reviews the RCA and its action plan [1].

**What the policy doesn't say:** It doesn't state whether the 72 hours runs from the event, its discovery, or the SafeReport filing. The 45-day completion deadline is tied to the event "becoming known", but the 72-hour wording has no stated start point [1]. The safest reading is that the clock starts when the event becomes known. I'd confirm that with QPS.

**No, not as a same-day start, unless Elmhurst already has a kit on hand.** The usual route is a transfer from a hub clinic, which takes up to 2 business days.

**Why**
- The shingles vaccine on the formulary is recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV), a 2-dose vial kit. It is Tier 2, which means it is stocked at hub clinics only [2].
- Elmhurst (ELH) is not a hub clinic [6].
- Non-hub clinics request a transfer from the nearest hub. Transfers arrive within 2 business days [2][6].
- Only Tier 1 items are marked "Give same day" [2]. RZV is not Tier 1.

**Options for this patient**
1. **Request a transfer to Elmhurst and book the dose for when it arrives.** Today is Saturday, and Elmhurst is open 09:00–12:00 [6]. The kit would arrive within 2 business days. The knowledge base doesn't say whether Saturday counts as a business day, so the earliest realistic date is about Tuesday, November 3. Ask clinic manager Patrick Oduya to confirm [6].
2. **Send the patient to a hub clinic today.** The hubs are Riverside, Northgate and Harbor Point. Their Saturday hours are 08:00–12:00, 08:00–14:00 and 08:00–16:00 [6]. I found no live inventory data, so call ahead to confirm they have a kit.

I did find a stock rule but no inventory count. Elmhurst could still have a kit on hand, so check the clinic's refrigerator before you rule out a same-day dose.

**Checks before giving the dose**
- **Age:** RZV is for ages 50 and over [2].
- **Who can give it:** only an RN or clinician. An MA cannot [2].
- **Series:** the second dose is due 2–6 months after the first [2]. Plan that visit when you book the first.
- **Cost:** the self-pay price is $205 per dose. It covers administration, and the 20% prompt-pay discount does not apply. Sliding-fee patients get the program discount [2]. Insured patients are billed to their plan [2]. At check-in, confirm eligibility in the practice management system. If eligibility fails, give the self-pay estimate before the visit [7]. The knowledge base doesn't say whether a given plan covers RZV, so verify that.
- **Cold chain:** if a fridge has read outside 2–8 °C, don't give vaccine from that stock until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing [2].

**What I couldn't find:** the contraindications, prior-vaccination screening and consent steps for RZV. None of these appear in the documents I found, so follow the clinician's standard assessment. I also found nothing on walk-in vaccine policy.

**Riverbend should schedule 1.5 medical assistants (MAs) per clinician, rounded up to the next whole person.**

**How I got there**
- The current standard took effect September 1, 2026. It replaced the 2025 standard [1].
- Riverbend (RVB) averaged 46 in-person visits per day in Q3 2026, according to the October 2026 clinic directory [3].
- The standard places each clinic in a band every quarter using that directory column [1][3].
- At 46 visits a day, Riverbend falls in the **Medium** band, which covers 40 to 80 visits. That band calls for 1.5 MAs per clinician [1].

**What the standard defines**
- "MAs per clinician" means the MAs scheduled for each physician or nurse practitioner who is seeing patients. You round up to the next whole person [1].
- Medium-band clinics need at least 2 physicians or NPs on site [1].
- At the minimum of 2 clinicians, 1.5 × 2 = 3 MAs.
- With more clinicians on, scale it the same way and round up. For example, 3 clinicians would need 4.5, so 5 MAs. This is my arithmetic from the rule. The standard doesn't give the example.
- The same Medium band also requires at least 1 RN on site and at least 3 front desk staff [1].
- Riverbend is closed Saturday and Sunday, so the Saturday session ratio of 1.0 doesn't apply [3].

**What changed from the 2025 standard**
- Under the 2025 standard, Riverbend's 46 visits would also have been Medium (45 to 90), but at 1.25 MAs per clinician [2].
- The September 2026 revision raised the Medium ratio to 1.5. It also lowered the band thresholds [1].
- If you're still scheduling at 1.25, update to 1.5.

**Caveats**
- I found no Riverbend-specific exceptions to the ratio.
- Riverbend is only 6 visits above the 40-visit Medium threshold. If its volume fell below 40 in a later quarter, it would move to the Small band at 1.0 MA per clinician [1][3].

**How fast Bayline must respond**
- A lab feed that stops arriving is a P1. The matrix defines P1 as a system down, or any problem that creates a patient-safety risk, and gives "results not arriving" as its example [1].
- Bayline's P1 response time for the HL7 results feed into Switchyard is **30 minutes**. Bayline staffs a 24/7 interface desk for it [1].
- This is a contractual first response from a qualified engineer. It is not a time to resolve the problem [1].
- For comparison, Bayline's P2 response is 2 hours and its P3 response is the next business day [1].

**Who gets paged**
- Clinic staff open a ticket with the Halcyon IT Service Desk (ext. 4357, or the intranet tile). They should not call Bayline directly unless the Service Desk asks them to [1].
- The Service Desk contacts Bayline and tracks its response against the matrix. For any P1 it also pages the owning team's system steward [1].
- INT owns the Bayline feed [1], and its system steward is **Owen Mbeki** [6].
- I found no separate on-call rota for the Integration Services team. The steward is the named person in the documents I found.

**If Bayline misses the 30 minutes**
- The Service Desk escalates to Bayline's account manager and tells the owning team's steward [1].
- Two missed P1 responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in Bayline's annual review [1].

**Related points**
- The on-call medical director (answering service 555-0144, option 2) is a separate route. That role receives critical lab results when the ordering clinician can't be reached [10]. It can also approve emergency changes to clinical systems [6][10]. The documents don't say it is paged for a feed outage.
- After RCA-26-07, the Interface team added an alert for when more than 1% of a lab's results in an hour use a fallback match. Unmatched results now go to a manual work queue [2].
- The Bayline agreement had no change-notice obligation when the July incident happened. An amendment requiring 30 days' notice of feed changes is still in progress [2].

**Escalate to Meridian Clinical Systems.** Wren is the Meridian EHR upgrade to release 2027.1 [5]. Meridian must respond to a P1 within **15 minutes** [1].

**Which vendor**
- Meridian supports the Meridian EHR 24/7. The owning team is Clinical Informatics (CI) [1].
- For any scheduled Meridian EHR upgrade, Meridian staffs a live bridge line with its own engineers for the whole cutover window. This is in addition to its 24/7 support [1]. Use the bridge line first during the Wren cutover.
- The cutover is scheduled for Saturday, February 6, 2027, starting at 22:00 Eastern. It has 6 hours of planned downtime and must finish by 04:00 Sunday [2]. CSCAB set the date and will make the final go/no-go decision on January 27, 2027 [2].

**What counts as a P1**
A P1 is any of these [1]:
- A system that is down or unusable at one or more clinics.
- Any problem that creates a patient-safety risk, for example results not arriving.

A P2, a major function that is degraded but has a workaround, gets a 2-hour response from Meridian. A P3 gets a next-business-day response [1].

**If Meridian misses the 15 minutes**
- The Service Desk escalates to Meridian's account manager and tells the owning team's steward [1]. For CI, the steward is Grace Oyelaran [4].
- Two missed P1 responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer. They are also recorded in the vendor's annual review [1].

**A related vendor: Bayline**
Wren includes retesting the Switchyard interfaces to all reference labs, to be done by January 15, 2027 [2][5]. If the lab results feed breaks during the cutover, that may be a Bayline Reference Laboratories issue rather than a Meridian one. Bayline has a 24/7 interface desk with a 30-minute P1 response [1]. Switchyard is built in-house, so the Service Desk pages the owning team directly, Integration Services, using the same P1–P3 priorities [1].

**Clinical escalation**
If an emergency change to a clinical system is needed to stop ongoing patient harm, the on-call medical director may approve it, and CSCAB reviews it at its next meeting [4]. Reach them through the answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [3].

**Gaps in what I found**
- The knowledge base has no Wren-specific contact numbers or bridge line details. It also has no Meridian contract or business associate record.
- The 15-minute P1 figure comes from the vendor escalation matrix, not from the contract itself.

Four languages missed their connect-time target in Q3 2026 (July 1 – September 30), based on average connect times. Two missed the 2-minute target and two missed the 5-minute target [1].

| Language | Tier and target | Avg connect | Over target by | Sessions | Dropped calls |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Karen | 5-minute | 6:18 | 1:18 | 141 | 4.6% |
| Somali | 5-minute | 5:40 | 0:40 | 226 | 3.8% |
| Vietnamese | 2-minute | 2:26 | 0:26 | 1,031 | 2.2% |
| Arabic | 2-minute | 2:12 | 0:12 | 703 | 2.9% |

All figures in the table come from the Q3 language access report [1].

**Targets.** Polyglen's service levels set a 2-minute target for the top 20 languages and American Sign Language. All other languages have a 5-minute target. Connect time runs from the clinician pressing "Request interpreter" to the interpreter joining [1][2].

**Languages that met target:**
- **2-minute tier:** Spanish (0:48), Mandarin (1:22), Cantonese (1:51), Korean (1:37), French (1:12) and ASL video (1:58). ASL and Cantonese were close to the limit [1].
- **5-minute tier:** Haitian Creole (3:54) and the 61 "all other" languages combined (3:31) [1].

**Caveats**
- The report gives averages only. It doesn't show the share of individual calls that met the target, so some calls in the "met" languages were probably slower than target.
- The 61 "other" languages are reported as one group. Individual languages inside it could have missed the target without showing up here [1].
- This is the first quarterly report in this format. Earlier quarters were reported monthly by Polyglen and aren't restated, so there is no prior-quarter comparison [1].
- The patient intake procedure says interpreters are available "within 2 minutes" for 200+ languages [5]. The Polyglen contract only guarantees 2 minutes for the top 20 languages and ASL, and 5 minutes for the rest [2].
- The vendor escalation matrix says a Polyglen P1 covers an interpreter not connecting at all. Slow connections within target are tracked in the quarterly report instead, not escalated [3].

**Follow-up.** Renewal discussions with Polyglen start in November 2026, and the contract renews February 28, 2027. Clinical Operations wants to add Haitian Creole and Karen to the 2-minute tier [2]. Haitian Creole met its current 5-minute target, but at 3:54 it would miss a 2-minute target. Karen missed its current target.

I found no documented exclusions, such as outages or low-volume languages, for this quarter.

- Cedar Hollow (CDH) [1]

## Recent changes and exceptions
- Northgate extended its Saturday hours to 14:00 from September 5, 2026 [1].

## Saturday staffing
Under the staffing standard, every Saturday session needs at least 1 physician or NP, 1 MA per clinician, 1 RN and 2 front desk staff. This applies to every clinic band [3].

## Telehealth
The telehealth front desk is not an in-person clinic. It is open Saturdays 08:00–16:00 [1].

## Vendor contracts
I found no vendor contract that sets Saturday hours or staffing at a specific clinic. The vendor documents cover only software support hours.

Four items on the formulary are Tier 3, meaning they aren't stocked at any clinic and are ordered for a named patient. The formulary was effective September 15, 2026 [1]. The four items are:

| Item | Presentation | Self-pay price | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Td | 0.5 mL prefilled syringe | $46 | Tdap is preferred. Td is given only on request [1]. |
| Pneumococcal conjugate, PCV21 | 0.5 mL prefilled syringe | $280 | Given only when the clinician specifies PCV21. PCV20 is the stocked default [1]. |
| HPV vaccine, 9-valent | 0.5 mL prefilled syringe | $295 per dose | Ages 9–45 [1]. |
| Meningococcal B vaccine | 0.5 mL prefilled syringe | $190 per dose | Ages 16–23, or on specialist advice [1]. |

All four are given by an RN or clinician, not by an MA [1].

**How Tier 3 ordering works**
- Tier 3 items are ordered from the wholesaler for a named patient, and the formulary says to allow 5 business days [1].
- Tier 3 named-patient orders go to the clinical pharmacist. The formulary lists Dr. Farah Qureshi, PharmD, as the clinical pharmacist lead [1].
- Clinic managers do not handle these through the weekly order. That weekly order form is for Tier 1 stock only [1].

**Items that look similar but are stocked**
- Tier 2 items are stocked only at hub clinics. They are recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV), adult hepatitis B vaccine and ceftriaxone 500 mg [1].
- The hub clinics are Riverside, Northgate and Harbor Point [2].
- Non-hub clinics request a transfer from the nearest hub, and transfers arrive within 2 business days [1].
- Everything else on the formulary is Tier 1, stocked at every clinic and given the same day [1].

**Other points**
- The formulary has no clinic-specific exceptions to Tier 3 status. I found no later change to the tiers.
- The documents I found don't name the wholesaler.
- Anything not on the formulary can't be given in clinic without approval from the Pharmacy and Therapeutics subcommittee [1].

Four clinics count as large under the current standard: Harbor Point, Northgate, Riverside and Elm Park. A clinic is large if it averages more than 80 in-person visits per day. The standard took effect September 1, 2026, and replaced the 2025 standard [1]. Each clinic's band is reset every quarter using the "Avg visits per day" column in the clinic directory [1][3].

The directory's figures are Q3 2026 averages (July–September), last updated October 12, 2026 [3].

| Clinic | Code | Avg visits/day | Band |
|---|---|---|---|
| Harbor Point | HBP | 118 | Large |
| Northgate | NGT | 102 | Large |
| Riverside | RVS | 94 | Large |
| Elm Park | ELP | 85 | Large |
| Northbridge | NBR | 52 | Medium |
| Riverbend | RVB | 46 | Medium |
| Elmhurst | ELH | 38 | Small |
| Cedar Hollow | CDH | 31 | Small |

The telehealth front desk has no band. It is staffed separately [3].

**Why the list changed:** The old 2025 standard set "large" at more than 90 visits per day [2]. Under that threshold only Harbor Point, Northgate and Riverside would qualify. Elm Park at 85 visits is large only because the new threshold is lower. The 2025 standard also set medium at 45–90 and small at under 45 [2]. Under the new standard, Riverbend (46) and Northbridge (52) are medium, and Elmhurst (38) and Cedar Hollow (31) are small [1][3].

**What large clinics must have:**
- At least 3 physicians or NPs on site [1].
- 2.0 MAs per clinician [1].
- At least 2 RNs on site, one of them a designated charge nurse on every shift [1].
- At least 4 front desk staff [1].

I found no exceptions, overrides or reclassifications in the documents I searched. Elm Park is only 5 visits above the cutoff, so a small drop in volume could move it to medium at the next quarterly review [1][3].

Five vendors give round-the-clock P1 support. A sixth, ClearPath, covers P1 around the clock but nothing else. Two vendors offer no round-the-clock P1 support. Everything below comes from the vendor support and escalation matrix, updated October 15, 2026 [1].

## Vendors with 24/7 P1 support

| Vendor | Service | Support hours | P1 first response |
|---|---|---|---|
| Polyglen Interpreting | Interpreter operations desk | 24/7 | 10 minutes |
| Meridian Clinical Systems | Meridian EHR | 24/7 | 15 minutes |
| Coriander Media | Video SDK and hosted media servers | 24/7 | 20 minutes |
| Bayline Reference Laboratories | HL7 results feed into Switchyard | 24/7 interface desk | 30 minutes |
| ClearPath Software | ClearPath PM | 24/7 for P1 only. Otherwise 07:00–19:00 Eastern, Mon–Fri | 30 minutes |

[1]

- **Response times:** these are contractual first responses from a qualified engineer, not resolution times [1].
- **Meridian upgrades:** for any scheduled EHR upgrade, Meridian also staffs a live bridge line with its own engineers for the whole cutover window [1].
- **Polyglen:** its P1 covers an interpreter not connecting at all. Slow connections within target are tracked in the quarterly language access report instead [1].
- **Coriander:** it supports the video layer under the new Juniper platform. Juniper's pilot isn't scheduled until January 12, 2027 [5], but the matrix already lists Coriander's terms [1].

## Vendors without 24/7 P1 support

- **Larkspur Telehealth** (current telehealth platform): support runs 07:00–21:00 Eastern, 7 days a week, with a 1-hour P1 response [1]. Support continues through the month-to-month extension and ends when the extension ends [1]. That extension runs through March 31, 2027 [5].
- **Quillon Ambient** (AI scribe pilot): support runs 06:00–22:00 Eastern, Mon–Sat, with a 2-hour P1 response. There is no out-of-hours P1 line. Outside support hours, clinicians stop using the scribe and document manually [1].
- **RotaLeaf** (HR and leave system): support runs 08:00–18:00 Eastern, Mon–Fri, with a 4-hour P1 response [1].

## In-house systems

Switchyard, Pillbox, the Halcyon app, the Juniper application layer and SafeReport have no outside vendor. The Service Desk pages the owning team directly, using the same P1–P3 priorities [1].

## What counts as P1, and how to raise one

- **Definition:** P1 means the system is down or unusable at one or more clinics, or the problem creates a patient-safety risk, such as results not arriving [1].
- **Who to call:** open a ticket with the IT Service Desk on extension 4357 or through the intranet tile. Clinic staff shouldn't call vendors directly unless the Service Desk asks them to [1].
- **What the Service Desk does:** it contacts the vendor and tracks the vendor's response. For any P1 it also pages the owning team's system steward [1].
- **If a vendor misses its P1 response time:** the Service Desk escalates to the vendor's account manager and tells the steward [1].
- **Repeat misses:** two missed P1 responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in the vendor's annual review [1].

Vendors that don't yet support a live Halcyon system aren't in the matrix. Their support terms are agreed when the contract is signed [1].

The vendor business associate records I found don't list support hours. I found no separate SLA documents, so the matrix is the only source for these terms.

**We don't charge anything.** Halcyon eliminated the no-show fee, effective October 5, 2026 [2]. The policy was approved on September 23, 2026 and replaces the 2025 policy in full [2].

**What changed**
- The old policy charged a $25 fee for each no-show after a patient's second one in 12 months. Medicaid and sliding-fee patients were exempt [1]. That policy no longer applies.
- Unpaid no-show fees billed before October 5, 2026 are waived. Revenue Cycle Management will reverse them on patient statements, and front desk staff should not try to collect them [2].
- The Q2 2026 review behind the change found that the fees were rarely collected and fell hardest on patients just above the sliding-fee threshold. It also found they had no measurable effect on no-show rates [2].

**What counts as a no-show now**
- A missed appointment is a no-show only if the patient did not cancel at least 2 hours ahead. The old window was 24 hours [1][2].
- For in-person visits, a patient who arrives more than 10 minutes late is offered the next open slot that day with any clinician, or is rescheduled. The clinician may still see them if the schedule allows [2].
- For telehealth visits, the clinician waits 15 minutes, and the telehealth front desk calls the patient twice in that time. If the patient still doesn't join, the visit is marked a no-show [2].
- Patients who are late because of an interpreter or accessibility issue on our side are never rescheduled for being late [2].
- No patient is discharged for no-shows [2]. The old policy allowed a discharge review after the fifth no-show [1].

**Your questions about exceptions, waivers and billing**
- Because there is no fee, the old waiver step no longer applies. Previously, front desk staff could waive the fee for documented emergencies with the clinic manager's approval [1].
- The October 2026 policy text I found doesn't list any fee that varies by appointment type, provider or location.
- I found nothing in the billing FAQ or the vendor material about a payer rule that affects no-show charges.

**The limit is 10 minutes.** Under the current policy (revised October 2026), a patient who arrives more than 10 minutes after their appointment time must be offered the next open slot that day with any clinician, or be rescheduled [1]. The policy says the shorter threshold protects the door-to-room target for the patients who follow [1].

**Older threshold:** The 2025 policy used 15 minutes [2]. The October 2026 revision, updated October 5, 2026, replaces it [1]. If a clinic still works from the 15-minute rule, that guidance is out of date.

**What the front desk does after the threshold**
- Offer the next open slot that day with any clinician, or reschedule [1].
- The clinician may still see the patient if the schedule allows [1]. The 2025 version added that the front desk should not promise this [2]. The 2026 text doesn't repeat that line, but it's safest not to promise it.

**Exceptions**
- A patient who is late because of an interpreter or accessibility issue on Halcyon's side is never rescheduled for being late [1].

**Related points that affect late patients**
- A visit counts as a no-show only if the patient doesn't arrive (or join) and didn't cancel at least 2 hours beforehand. Cancelling by replying to a reminder counts [1].
- On a patient's third no-show in 12 months, a care coordinator calls to ask about barriers. They can offer ride vouchers, a telehealth visit, a different time of day, or an interpreter booked in advance [1].
- The no-show fee has been eliminated, and unpaid fees billed before October 5, 2026 are waived. Staff should not try to collect them [1].
- No patient is discharged for no-shows [1].
- For telehealth, the clinician now waits 15 minutes, and the front desk calls the patient twice. The patient is marked a no-show only if they still don't join [1].

**Gaps in the documents:** I found no variation by appointment type, provider, or visit length. That covers new patients, procedures, and specialty visits. I also found no separate rule for clinical urgency or a step for documenting late arrivals. The 10-minute rule appears to apply to all in-person visits. If you need a rule for a specific visit type, ask Clinical Operations, which co-owns the policy.

**A large clinic needs 2.0 medical assistants (MAs) scheduled for each physician or NP seeing patients.** This comes from the clinic staffing standard effective September 1, 2026, which replaced the 2025 standard [1]. The ratio is the number of MAs scheduled per physician or NP seeing patients, rounded up to the next whole person [1].

## What counts as "large"
- A clinic is large if it averages **over 80 in-person visits a day**. The 2025 standard set the line at over 90 [1][2].
- Clinics are re-banded every quarter using the "Avg visits per day" column in the clinic directory [1].
- A large clinic must have at least 3 physicians or NPs on site, so it needs at least **6 MAs** on the schedule when the minimum clinician count is working [1]. That is my arithmetic from 3 clinicians × 2.0. More clinicians on the schedule means proportionally more MAs.

## Current ratios by band (effective September 1, 2026) [1]
| Band | Visits/day | MAs per clinician | Min. clinicians | Min. RNs | Min. front desk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small | Under 40 | 1.0 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| Medium | 40–80 | 1.5 | 2 | 1 | 3 |
| Large | Over 80 | 2.0 | 3 | 2, one designated charge nurse | 4 |
| Saturday session (any band) | — | 1.0 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| Sunday session (Harbor Point) | — | 1.0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

The ratio went up because the Q2 2026 operations review found that medium and large clinics were missing the door-to-room target on most afternoons [1]. The 2025 standard required only 1.5 MAs per clinician for large clinics and 1.25 for medium [2].

## Which clinics are large now
Based on Q3 2026 volumes in the October directory [4]:
- **Large (over 80):** Harbor Point (118), Northgate (102), Riverside (94) and Elm Park (85).
- **Medium (40–80):** Riverbend (46) and Northbridge (52).
- **Small (under 40):** Elmhurst (38) and Cedar Hollow (31).

The directory says the band is set from this column each quarter [4]. Elm Park would have been medium under the 2025 thresholds, but it is large under the current ones. I derived the band assignments from the thresholds myself. The directory doesn't list them.

## Coverage and scheduling rules
- **Saturdays and Sundays:** These sessions use the 1.0 ratio whatever the clinic's band [1].
- **Clinician shortfall:** Every clinic needs at least one physician or NP on site during open hours. If coverage drops below that, the clinic manager calls the float pool first. If the float pool can't cover, the manager asks the regional medical director whether to reduce the schedule. Where clinically appropriate, in-person visits are converted to telehealth [1][2][3].
- **Float pool:** The network keeps 2 physicians/NPs, 2 RNs and 1 front desk person on call daily [1]. The standard lists no on-call MAs. I found no MA-specific backup rule in the sources.
- **Time off:** Clinicians must request PTO at least 60 days ahead. Non-clinical staff give at least 2 weeks' notice [3]. Approvals follow submission order, except Thanksgiving week and December 20–January 2, which rotate year to year [3]. Sick time is 48 hours a year [3].
- **Why MAs matter for flow:** Front desk staff hand patients to the MA within 10 minutes of check-in [5]. The door-to-room target is under 15 minutes for 90% of visits [5].

## Gaps in the knowledge base
- I found no vendor or staffing-agency contract that supplies temporary MAs. The vendor records cover interpreting, billing, AI scribe and survey services only [6][7][8][9].
- I found no document setting MA shift lengths or break rules.
- The 2026 standard doesn't say how to handle a quarter in which a clinic moves bands. It only says bands are reset quarterly [1].

**Short answer:** Not as a planned practice. Since September 1, 2026, every Halcyon clinic, including small ones, must have at least one RN on site during open hours [1]. A day without an RN is a below-minimum session. It is allowed only as a last resort, after you have tried the float pool, and it must be reported.

## Current rule
- The 2026 staffing standard replaced the 2025 one. The 2025 standard said an RN was "not required" in small clinics. The 2026 standard requires one RN in small clinics and on Saturday sessions [1][2].
- The change followed a Q2 2026 review. It found small clinics without an RN were sending too many triage calls to the physician [1].
- The standard was approved by Rosa Delgado (Director of Clinical Operations) and Marisol Vance (Chief Nursing Officer). Clinics had until October 1, 2026 to comply [1].
- Small means under 40 average visits a day. Under the Q3 2026 directory, Elmhurst (38) and Cedar Hollow (31) are small [1][4].
- Some older-looking guidance no longer applies. The 2025 line "in small clinics without an RN, the physician or NP handles triage calls" is superseded [2].

## If your RN is out
1. **Call the float pool.** The network has 2 RNs on call daily, and the pool was increased by two RNs to cover the gap [1].
2. **If the float pool can't cover,** ask the regional medical director whether to reduce the schedule [1].
3. **If the session runs without an RN,** report it in SafeReport as a near miss so QPS can track it [1]. Under the 2025 standard this was only a staffing-log entry [2].

I found no written waiver or exception process for small clinics, and no named approver for running without an RN. The regional medical director's role is limited to deciding whether to reduce the schedule [1].

## What an RN-less day affects
- **Physician/NP:** You still need at least one on site. If that drops, call the float pool, then convert visits to telehealth where clinically appropriate [1][3].
- **Vaccines and injectables:** MAs can give only the Tier 1 items marked for MAs, under standing orders [1][6]. Those are:
  - standard-dose and high-dose flu vaccine
  - Tdap
  - B12
- **RN-only items:** Several Tier 1 items are RN or clinician only. These are the COVID-19 vaccine, PCV20 and medroxyprogesterone [6]. Without an RN, a clinician has to give them.
- **Charge nurse:** In small clinics, the clinic manager fills the charge-nurse role unless two or more RNs are on shift [1]. The manager is also the escalation point when no charge nurse is on shift [4].
- **Closing instead:** If a site has to close unexpectedly, including for staffing, tell the telehealth front desk supervisor and post the closure on the Halcyon app [4]. Hub clinics act as the backup site for patients [4].

## Gaps in the knowledge base
- I found no state licensing or scope-of-practice rules on RN presence.
- I found no agency-vendor or telehealth-RN backfill option for clinics. The only RN backfill described is the float pool.
- Sick-time policy says nothing specific about RN absences. It repeats the physician/NP coverage rule [3].

If this is a real scheduling decision, check with your regional medical director and Clinical Operations.

**The Meridian EHR upgrade cutover is set for Saturday, February 6, 2027, starting at 22:00 Eastern. Planned downtime is 6 hours.** [1]

The Meridian upgrade is tracked under the codename "Wren" (Meridian EHR upgrade to release 2027.1) [7]. The Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) approved the cutover plan, CHG-2026-118, on October 28, 2026 [1].

## Timing and downtime
- **Start:** Saturday, February 6, 2027, 22:00 Eastern [1].
- **Planned downtime:** 6 hours [1].
- **Hard finish:** The cutover must be finished by 04:00 Sunday. Harbor Point's Sunday clinic opens at 10:00, and the time after the cutover is for verification [1].
- **Final go/no-go:** CSCAB will decide on January 27, 2027 [1]. The date is approved but not final until then.

## Has it changed?
I found no sign of a reschedule. The October 28 CSCAB minutes are the most recent source on the cutover. The projects register lists Wren's target only as "Q1 2027" and says CSCAB sets cutover dates, not the register [7]. Wren was in integrated testing as of October 19 [7].

## Downtime procedures and support
- **Clinics:** All clinics will use paper downtime procedures during the cutover [1]. I didn't find a detailed downtime procedure document, only this statement in the minutes.
- **Lab interfaces:** Integration Services will retest the Switchyard interfaces to all reference labs by January 15, 2027 [1]. The register says these interfaces must be retested after the upgrade [7].
- **Vendor support:** For any scheduled Meridian upgrade, Meridian Clinical Systems staffs a live bridge line with its own engineers for the whole cutover window. This is in addition to its 24/7 support [2].
- **Reporting problems:** Staff should open a ticket with the IT Service Desk (extension 4357) and should not call vendors directly unless the Service Desk asks. A system down at one or more clinics is a P1, and Meridian's P1 response time is 15 minutes [2].

## Gaps
The knowledge base has no Meridian vendor document with the vendor's own cutover timeline or outage estimate. The 6-hour figure comes only from the internal CSCAB minutes.

The check goes live on **Wednesday, November 18, 2026**. The CSCAB approved that release date on October 28, 2026 [3].

**What the check is**
- It is a positive patient identification check that runs before lab results are released to the patient portal. Its project codename is **Heron** [2].
- It is action 4 from the root cause analysis of lab results filed to the wrong patient's chart (RCA-26-07) [2][4].

**Timeline and approvals**
- Heron is change request CHG-2026-121, a significant change. The steward approved it. Dr. Rao (AR) gave clinical safety sign-off after reviewing test results: in 400 test releases, every mismatched identifier was held for manual review [3].

Karen interpreters took an average of **6 minutes 18 seconds (6:18)** to connect in Q3 2026 (July–September) [1]. Q3 is the last full quarter before today, October 31, 2026.

**Details**
- **Volume:** There were 141 Karen sessions, totaling 2,690 interpreted minutes [1].
- **Dropped calls:** 4.6% of Karen calls dropped. That is the highest rate of any language in the report [1].
- **How it's measured:** Connect time runs from the clinician pressing "Request interpreter" to the interpreter joining [1].

**Against the target**
- Polyglen Interpreting supplies the interpreters. Karen is in its 5-minute tier, which covers all languages outside the top 20 and American Sign Language [1][2].
- Karen averaged 1 minute 18 seconds over that 5-minute target [1].
- Somali also missed the target, at 5:40. Haitian Creole, at 3:54, and the 61 other languages combined, at 3:31, were within it [1].
- The report says dropped calls are highest for the smaller 5-minute-tier languages. A dropped call often means waiting for the same interpreter to become free again [1].

**What happens next**
- Clinical Operations will raise every language that missed its target at the Polyglen renewal discussion in November 2026 [1].
- Clinical Operations also wants Karen, along with Haitian Creole, moved to the 2-minute tier [2].
- Polyglen's P1 escalation covers an interpreter not connecting at all. Slow connections within target are tracked only in the quarterly language access report [6].

**Caveats**
- The report gives only an average. It has no median, no spread, and no breakdown by month or by clinic, so I can't say how many Karen calls were much slower or faster than 6:18.
- The patient intake procedure says interpreters are available "within 2 minutes" in more than 200 languages. That doesn't match the 5-minute tier that applies to Karen [3][2].

A self-pay patient pays **$72** for the 2026–27 high-dose flu shot. That price includes the administration fee [1].

**Price details**
- The shot is a 0.7 mL prefilled syringe for patients 65 and over [1].
- The $72 self-pay price applies to uninsured and self-pay patients. Insured patients are billed to their plan instead [1].
- It is a Tier 1 item, so every clinic stocks it and gives it the same day [1].
- An MA, RN or clinician may give it [1].
- For comparison, the standard-dose flu shot is $35 for ages 6 months to 64 years [1].

**Discounts**
- **Prompt-pay discount:** The usual 20% discount for paying in full on the day does not apply to vaccines. The formulary says vaccine prices are already set at cost plus administration, so a patient who pays on the day still pays $72 [1][6].
- **Sliding-fee program:** Patients in the program receive the program discount on vaccines [1]. The billing FAQ says the program applies to households under 250% of the federal poverty level and reduces visit costs by 40–100% [6]. It doesn't say whether vaccine prices get that same 40–100% range, only that the "program discount" applies [1].

**Other fees**
I found no separate office-visit charge for a vaccine-only visit. The formulary says the $72 includes administration [1]. The self-pay visit rates in the billing FAQ are $120 for an established patient and $165 for a new patient [6]. Those rates apply to visits, and no document says they are added to a vaccine given alone. If the flu shot is given during a regular visit, such as an annual physical ($195), the visit fee would presumably be billed separately. That is my inference, not something the documents state [6].

**Vendor contract pricing**
The knowledge base has no vendor or wholesaler contract pricing for the high-dose flu vaccine. The only current-season price I found is the formulary's $72, effective September 15, 2026 [1].

**ClearPath must respond to a P2 ticket within 4 hours.** The vendor support and escalation matrix (updated October 15, 2026) sets this as ClearPath Software's P2 response time for ClearPath PM [1].

## What the 4 hours covers
- **It is a first response, not a fix.** The matrix says response times are contractual first responses from a qualified engineer, not resolution times [1].
- **Support hours limit when it applies.** ClearPath's support is 24/7 for P1 only. Otherwise it runs 07:00–19:00 Eastern, Monday to Friday [1].
- **P2 falls under the limited hours.** I'd read it that way because only P1 is listed as 24/7. The matrix doesn't say outright whether the 4 hours counts only inside the support window. It also doesn't say when the clock starts.
- **Example:** a P2 raised on a Saturday, like today, would most likely not be answered until the next support window opens on Monday. Check this with the Service Desk if timing matters.

## How P2 is defined
A P2 is "a major function is degraded but a workaround exists" [1]. For comparison:
- **P1** means the system is down or unusable at one or more clinics, or there is a patient-safety risk. ClearPath's P1 response is 30 minutes [1].
- **P3** covers minor problems, single-user issues and questions. ClearPath's P3 response is 2 business days [1].

## How Halcyon handles it
- Open a ticket with the Halcyon IT Service Desk (extension 4357, or the Service Desk tile on the intranet) for every problem. Clinic staff shouldn't call ClearPath directly unless the Service Desk asks them to [1].
- The Service Desk contacts the vendor and tracks its response against the matrix [1].
- The owning team for ClearPath PM is RCM [1].

## Gap in the documents
The only documented escalation step for a missed response covers P1. The Service Desk escalates to the vendor's account manager and tells the owning team's steward, and two missed P1 responses in a quarter go to the HIPAA Security Officer [1]. I found no stated procedure or penalty for a missed P2 response. I also couldn't find the ClearPath contract itself, so this answer rests on the internal matrix.

## Answer

Halcyon charges patients **$25** to complete an FMLA certification form. The standard turnaround is **7 business days** [1]. The fee schedule lists the form as "Form completion by clinician" [1].

## Details that affect the fee and timing

- **Payment timing:** The fee is paid before the form is released, not before it is started [1].
- **Sliding-fee program:** Fees are waived for patients in the sliding-fee program [1]. Patients with household income under 250% of the federal poverty level qualify for that program, and front desk staff can start the application at check-in [6].
- **Unpaid balances:** Staff should never refuse or delay a patient's records request because of an unpaid balance [1]. That sentence appears in the section on copies of records, so I can't confirm it also covers form requests.
- **Where the rule applies:** The schedule covers every clinic and requests made through the telehealth front desk. All requests are logged in the HIM request queue in Meridian EHR [1]. HIM is Health Information Management. It owns the schedule, and you can reach it through the intranet or at him@halcyon.example [1].
- **Effective date:** The schedule took effect July 1, 2026 [1].

For comparison, the short-term disability form costs $40 and also takes 7 business days [1].

## What I couldn't find

- **Urgent or rush requests:** The knowledge base has no expedited option or rush fee for FMLA forms.
- **Recertifications and multiple forms:** It has no separate pricing or timing for these.
- **Visit requirement:** It doesn't say whether a patient needs an appointment before the clinician completes the form. It also doesn't say what authorization is required.
- **Vendors:** No vendor in the vendor records handles FMLA paperwork for patients. RotaLeaf is the HR and leave system for staff, not a patient forms service [3].

rows.answer:
Halcyon Health's documents don't give a self-pay price for the RSV vaccine. The 2026–27 in-clinic vaccine and injectable formulary has no RSV entry, so I can't give you a number.

**What the formulary says**
- The formulary lists every vaccine and injectable Halcyon clinics give on site. It says anything not on the list "cannot be given in clinic without approval from the Pharmacy and Therapeutics subcommittee" [1].
- The vaccines listed are influenza (standard and high-dose), COVID-19, Tdap, Td, PCV20, PCV21, recombinant zoster, hepatitis B, HPV and meningococcal B. B12, ceftriaxone and medroxyprogesterone injections are also listed [1].
- RSV doesn't appear among them. That suggests Halcyon doesn't currently stock or give it in clinic, though the documents don't say this outright.
- I also searched the Vendors collection, which covers business associates and support contracts. It has no vaccine wholesaler or acquisition-cost information, so I found nothing on RSV costs.

**How self-pay vaccine pricing works**
These rules would apply if RSV were added:
- The self-pay price covers uninsured and self-pay patients, and it includes the administration fee [1].
- Prices are "cost plus administration." The 20% prompt-pay discount for paying in full on the day doesn't apply to vaccines [1].
- Patients in the sliding-fee program get the program discount instead [1]. That program is for households under 250% of the federal poverty level, and it cuts visit costs by 40–100% [2].
- Self-pay patients get a good-faith estimate before a scheduled service [2].
- Balances over $200 can go on an interest-free payment plan of up to 12 months [2].
- The closest priced items are pneumococcal PCV20 at $265, recombinant zoster at $205 per dose, and high-dose flu at $72 [1]. These are not RSV prices, so don't quote them as estimates.

**Next step**
Ask the clinical pharmacist lead, Dr. Farah Qureshi, or the Pharmacy and Therapeutics subcommittee whether RSV vaccine can be given in clinic [1]. Tier 3 items not on the shelf can be ordered for a named patient from the wholesaler, with about 5 business days' lead time [1]. Because RSV isn't on the formulary, that route would need approval first.

**I can't tell you who is on call for the week of December 14, because that rota hasn't been published.** The December rota will be published by November 20, 2026 [1]. Today is October 31.

**What the knowledge base has**
- The only rota on file is the November 2026 one, published October 19 by the Office of the CMO. It covers weeks 44–49, from October 26 to the 08:00 Monday handover on December 7 [1].
- The week you're asking about, December 14 to 21 (week 51 by the rota's numbering), isn't in that rota. The December 7 week isn't either, because the table ends at 08:00 on December 7.
- I found no swaps or substitutions for that week. The only logged swap is Dr. Ingrid Solberg covering Thanksgiving Day for Dr. Helen Mwangi [1].
- I found no outside vendor or agency that supplies on-call medical directors. The vendor matrix lists none [6].

I'd also advise against guessing from the rotation pattern. The order isn't a fixed cycle: the primary and backup pairings vary, and the Thanksgiving week has an exception [1].

**How the rota works**
- Shifts run from Monday 08:00 Eastern to the following Monday 08:00 Eastern [1].
- Swaps need both physicians' agreement and must be logged with the Office of the CMO at least 72 hours ahead, so the answering service can update its schedule [1].

**What to do**
- Check back after November 20 for the December rota.
- Send rota questions to the Office of the CMO [1].
- For a live clinical need, call the answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2. It pages whoever is on call, and the backup if there's no callback within 10 minutes [1].

I couldn't find the Q2 2026 average connect time for Karen interpreters. The knowledge base has no Q2 figure for any language.

**Why the Q2 number is missing**
- The Q3 2026 language access report (July 1 – September 30) is "the first quarterly report in this format." It says earlier quarters "were reported monthly by Polyglen and are not restated here" [1].
- Polyglen sends Clinical Operations a monthly quality report covering connect times, dropped calls and patient complaints [2]. Those monthly reports for April–June 2026 aren't in the knowledge base. I also found no monthly breakdown for Karen.

**Closest figure: Q3 2026 (July–September), not Q2**

| Measure | Karen, Q3 2026 |
|---|---|
| Sessions | 141 [1] |
| Interpreted minutes | 2,690 [1] |
| Average connect time | 6:18 (m:ss) [1] |
| Dropped calls | 4.6% [1] |
| Tier and target | 5-minute tier, connected within 5 minutes [1] |

Karen missed its target in Q3. It was the slowest of the listed languages and had the highest dropped-call rate [1]. Please don't treat 6:18 as the Q2 figure.

**Context**
- **Vendor and owner:** Karen interpreting is delivered through Polyglen Interpreting (BA-007). Clinical Operations owns the relationship, and the named owner is Rosa Delgado [2].
- **Measurement:** Connect time runs from the clinician pressing "Request interpreter" to the interpreter joining [1].
- **Escalation:** Polyglen's P1 response covers an interpreter not connecting at all. Slow connections within target are tracked in the quarterly language access report instead [5].
- **Renewal:** Clinical Operations wants Haitian Creole and Karen added to the 2-minute tier. It will raise every language that missed its target at the November 2026 renewal discussion [1][2].

To get the Q2 number, ask Clinical Operations (Rosa Delgado) for Polyglen's April, May and June 2026 monthly quality reports. You would need to combine the three months weighted by session count, since a simple average of the monthly averages could be misleading.

**There is no response-time SLA for Tallgrass Survey yet.** The knowledge base doesn't contain one, and none can exist until the contract is signed.

**Why there's no SLA**
- Tallgrass is only a proposed business associate (record BA-021). Its signed order form is on hold until the business associate agreement (BAA) is executed [1].
- The BAA is still open. Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable responses for 5 years, and Halcyon will accept 18 months [1].
- Halcyon's vendor support and escalation matrix lists only vendors that support live Halcyon systems. It says vendors that don't yet support a live system are not listed, and that "their support terms are agreed when the contract is signed" [3].
- Tallgrass isn't live. Until the BAA is signed, the post-visit satisfaction score is collected with the in-app survey in the Halcyon app [1][2]. The Juniper steering committee notes say Tallgrass will send the survey only after its BAA is signed [2].

**What would probably apply**
The matrix shows how Halcyon handles vendor support today. Tallgrass's contract could follow a similar structure, but nothing says it will.
- Response times are contractual first responses from a qualified engineer, not resolution times [3].
- They're set by priority: P1 is system down or a patient-safety risk, P2 is a major function degraded with a workaround, and P3 is minor issues [3].
- Existing vendors' P1 targets range from 10 minutes (Polyglen) to 4 hours (RotaLeaf). That range shows what's typical, not what Tallgrass will agree to [3].
- Staff open tickets with the IT Service Desk (extension 4357) instead of calling vendors. The Service Desk tracks the vendor's response [3].
- If a vendor misses a P1 response, the Service Desk escalates to the vendor's account manager and tells the owning team's steward. Two missed P1 responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in the vendor's annual review [3].
- The matrix describes no financial penalties or service credits. Any for Tallgrass would have to come from its contract.

**Next steps and timing**
- Privacy Officer Margaret Holloway is due to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026 [1].
- If the BAA isn't signed by January 31, 2027, Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) will look at other survey vendors [1].
- Lorraine Pike (QPS), the internal owner, should ask Tallgrass for its support hours and response times by priority before the order form is signed. After signing, Tallgrass should be added to the matrix [1][3].

The knowledge base doesn't say how much a physician is paid for a week on the on-call medical director rota. I searched the Clinical Operations, People And Policy and Vendors collections. None of them has a stipend, rate or other compensation figure for this role.

**What the knowledge base does say about the rota**
- Each on-call shift runs from Monday 08:00 Eastern to the following Monday 08:00 Eastern, so it is a full week [1].
- The Office of the Chief Medical Officer owns the rota. The current version was published October 19, 2026 [1].
- The rota names an on-call medical director and a backup for each week [1].
- Swaps need both physicians' agreement and must be logged with the Office of the CMO at least 72 hours ahead [1].
- Duties include:
  - receiving critical lab results when the ordering clinician can't be reached;
  - being notified of sentinel events;
  - approving emergency clinical-system changes;
  - advising on transfers and unexpected clinic closures [1].

**What I found on pay, and why it doesn't answer your question**
- Staff who work on a paid holiday get 1.5× pay plus a floating holiday [2][3]. Nothing says this applies to on-call medical director shifts. One example is the Thanksgiving swap on November 26–27, which the rota doesn't tie to any pay rule [1].
- The two policies disagree on the number of paid holidays. The PTO and clinic scheduling policy says 8 [2]. The annual leave policy effective October 1, 2026 says 9 [3]. The newer annual leave policy is likely the current one.
- Onboarding benefits cover things like the HSA contribution and CME allowance. They don't cover call pay [8].
- The vendor records cover business associates and support matrices. None of them covers physician compensation [9][12].

I found nothing on whether pay differs for weekends, holidays or seniority. I also found no governing compensation policy or update date. This kind of figure is usually in a physician employment contract or a compensation schedule. You could ask the Office of the CMO, which owns the rota, or the People team at people@halcyon.example. That address appears in the leave policy [3].

For an answer, ask the People team, which owns the annual leave policy [1]. Halcyon may have a separate bereavement policy that isn't in this knowledge base, or bereavement may be handled informally through annual leave.

Yes. Halcyon pairs every new clinical hire with a **preceptor** for **90 days**. A preceptor is closer to a mentor than a buddy [6].

## Halcyon's preceptor program
- **Who gets one:** every new clinical hire [6].
- **Length:** 90 days [6].
- **Check-ins:** weekly for the first month, then every other week [6].
- **Sign-offs:** the preceptor signs off on your competency checklist at 30, 60 and 90 days [6].
- **First week:** days 4–5 are spent shadowing at your home clinic with your preceptor [6].

## How it compares with Northwind's buddy
Northwind's onboarding guide mentions a buddy, but it gives no length and no formal structure.
- The buddy works alongside your manager to walk you through the first two weeks [1].
- In week two, the buddy suggests people for you to book 1:1s with. You're expected to meet at least five people outside your team [1].

The guide covers your first two weeks, but it doesn't say how long the buddy assignment lasts. I found no Northwind document that states a duration.

| | Northwind buddy | Halcyon preceptor |
|---|---|---|
| Duration | Not stated (the guide covers the first two weeks) [1] | 90 days [6] |
| Cadence | Not stated | Weekly for month one, then every other week [6] |
| Formal sign-off | None mentioned | Competency checklist at 30, 60 and 90 days [6] |

## What the knowledge base doesn't say
Halcyon's onboarding page doesn't say how preceptors are chosen or matched. It also doesn't give any eligibility requirements or preceptor duties beyond the check-ins and sign-offs above. I found no separate preceptor policy.

Yes. Northwind's closest equivalent is the **service catalog**, which the **Platform team (PLAT)** maintains. It differs from your PHI inventory in two ways. It classifies data by a general sensitivity scale, not by PHI. I also found no documented review schedule for it.

## What Northwind keeps

**Service catalog (Engineering)**
- It is described as "the source of truth for which production service does what, what data it keeps, and which team owns it." It was last updated October 2, 2026 [1].
- For each production service it records what the service does, the data it stores, a data class and an owning team [1].
- It covers nine services, including `ingest-gateway`, `runner`, Conduit, Driftwood, Keystone, Ledger, Atlas, Beacon and Lookout [1].
- It also lists shared infrastructure with owners: Kafka and Kubernetes clusters and Managed Postgres (all PLAT), and Teleport (SEC) [1].
- The cell inventory is a companion page, also maintained by PLAT. It lists cells, regions and data residency. It leaves service ownership to the service catalog [4].

**Vendor registers (Vendors collection)**
- Each third party gets its own register entry with an ID, such as VEN-014 for Cobaltline [8].
- Entries record the data processed, the highest data class, whether customer data is involved, DPA status, security review, SOC 2 status and data residency [6][8][10][11].

## Data classification, with no PHI category

Northwind's classes are Restricted, Confidential, Internal and Public, defined in the information security policy [7]. The catalog uses these classes [1]. Examples:
- Restricted: customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys [7].
- Confidential: financials, contracts and employee data [7].

I found nothing in Northwind's documents that classifies data as PHI. Leadership also recently passed on acquiring a healthcare analytics startup because of "HIPAA obligations we are not set up for" [17]. So Northwind's inventory can't tell you which systems hold PHI. A customer's event payloads could in principle contain regulated data, and those payloads are Restricted.

## Who owns each system

The catalog gives each service a team code [1]:
- **DP (Data Plane):** `ingest-gateway`, `runner`, Conduit.
- **PLAT (Platform):** Driftwood, plus the Kafka, Kubernetes and Postgres infrastructure.
- **IDB (Identity & Billing):** Keystone, Ledger.
- **WX (Workspace Experience):** Atlas.
- **OBS (Observability):** Beacon, Lookout.
- **SEC (Security):** Teleport.

The engineering team directory maps each code to a manager, a change approver and a delegate. It is owned by VP Engineering Dmitri Sokolov [2]. Ownership has practical weight. A team's change approver signs off on normal production changes to its services. Changes to services storing Restricted data also need the Head of Security or the security on-call delegate [3].

Vendor register entries usually name a business owner:
- Cobaltline: the Observability team (OBS) [8].
- Saltmarsh: Product (Mateo Alvarez) [10].
- Hollowpine: Support Operations (Gwen Talbot) [11].
- Parcelwise: no business owner field. It says to direct questions to the team that owns the source system, which is Atlas [6].

## Who maintains it and how often

- **Maintainer:** The Platform team maintains the service catalog [1]. To change an owner, you open a PR against the page and tag the old and new engineering managers [1]. A new datastore needs an ADR before it appears in the catalog [1].
- **Review frequency:** I found no stated review cadence or audit process for the catalog. The only visible signal is the "last updated" date.
- **Other cadences I found:**
  - Team leads run quarterly access reviews [7].
  - The Security team reviews the data retention standard every six months [12].
  - Security owns the information security policy [7].

## Gaps compared with your PHI inventory

1. There is no PHI or regulated-data flag.
2. There is no stated review cycle.
3. The catalog covers production services only. Third-party systems sit in separate vendor registers.
4. Some vendor entries are incomplete. For example, the Hollowpine DPA is unsigned and operating under security exception SEC-EX-117 [11].
