At Halcyon, patient events are logged in **SafeReport**. Anyone involved in the event or who witnessed it must file the report, and it is due within 24 hours. I only searched Halcyon's side. I didn't look up Northwind's `/incident declare` process, so there's no comparison with it here.

## Where it's logged
- SafeReport is Halcyon's patient safety event reporting system. It's built on the intranet and owned by Quality & Patient Safety (QPS). It holds event descriptions and patient identifiers [3].
- Don't use Slack, even in DMs, for PHI [3].
- Privacy incidents are separate. Examples are a misdirected fax, a lost device, or a chart left open on an unattended screen. Report these to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours at privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [1][7].

## Who files
- Anyone involved in the event or who witnessed it files the SafeReport. The policy says reporting is "never optional and never punished" [1].
- The charge nurse coordinates the immediate response. That means assigning who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications or records. If no charge nurse is on shift, the clinic manager does this [1].
- The attending clinician tells the patient or family about the event. The charge nurse or medical director is present [1].
- Large clinics have a designated charge nurse. In small and medium clinics, one is designated when two or more RNs are on shift. Otherwise the clinic manager fills the role [6].

## How soon
| When | What |
|---|---|
| Immediately | Make the patient safe and follow the clinical escalation protocol, calling 911 if needed. Then tell the charge nurse, or the clinic manager if there is no charge nurse [1]. |
| Within 1 hour | For a sentinel event (Level 1), the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director [1]. |
| Within 24 hours | File the SafeReport. The attending clinician also discloses the event to the patient or family [1]. |
| Within 72 hours | QPS charters the root cause analysis (RCA) team for Level 1 and 2 events [1]. |
| Within 45 calendar days | The RCA is completed, counted from when the event became known [1]. |

The 24-hour SafeReport deadline is the same for every severity level. The policy gives no separate filing deadline for Levels 3 and 4 [1].

## Severity levels
- **Level 1, sentinel event:** death or permanent harm, severe temporary harm, a wrong-patient or wrong-site procedure, or suicide within 72 hours of a visit.
- **Level 2, adverse event with harm:** for example, a medication error requiring treatment.
- **Level 3, no-harm event:** the error reached the patient but caused no harm.
- **Level 4, near miss:** the error was caught before it reached the patient [1].

If you're unsure which level applies, report at the higher one. QPS will reclassify if needed [1].

## After it's filed
- The Patient Safety Committee reviews completed RCAs and their action plans. Chief Medical Officer Dr. Kenji Watanabe chairs it. It meets monthly and tracks each action item to closure [1].
- QPS decides whether to report to a state health department or accrediting body, and makes those reports [1].
- Events caused by software or patient-facing automation follow the same policy. The fixes then go through clinical systems change control [1].
- A session run without an RN is logged in SafeReport as a near miss [6].
- To reach the on-call medical director, call the answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2. If there's no callback within 10 minutes, it pages the backup [11].

**Short answer:** Northwind reviews incidents on a blameless basis, which is close to your just-culture approach but not identical. The incident commander (IC) picks the author. In practice that is usually the responder who knew the failure best, not the IC.

## Is it blameless or just-culture?

Northwind's docs use the word "blameless" and never "just culture."

- Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 gets a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution [1][2][3].
- The FAQ says a postmortem doesn't mean someone is in trouble. It says reviews look "at the system and the process, not at individuals," and that names appear only in the timeline [3].
- The knowledge base doesn't say how Northwind handles individual accountability or reckless conduct. That distinction is usually what separates just culture from purely blameless review, so I can't say Northwind matches your approach on that point.

## Who writes the review?

- **Policy:** "The IC picks the author, usually the responder who knew the most about the failure" [3].
- **INC-2340 (duplicate invoices):** Kofi Mensah was IC. On resolving the incident he named Arjun Mehta as postmortem owner, due October 13 [5]. Arjun had declared the incident and diagnosed the root cause [5]. The log shows the postmortem was published October 13 [2].
- **INC-2291 (ingest outage):** The author was Priya Raman "with the ingest team" [4]. The IC was Oluwaseun Adeyemi [2], so the author was not the IC.
- **IC role:** The IC coordinates and doesn't debug [3]. ICs come from a separate rotation (Kofi Mensah, Priya Raman, Harriet Vance, Oluwaseun Adeyemi, Ravi Subramanian), and each serves one week at a time [7].

## How reviews are run and tracked

- **Timeline:** The five-business-day clock starts at resolution [3]. The incident log shows INC-2291 resolved August 14 and published August 21 [2][4].
- **Review forum:** Postmortems are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [1][3]. That meeting also maintains the incident log [2].
- **Content:** The INC-2291 postmortem has sections for impact, timeline, what went poorly and action items. Each action item has an owner and often a due date and status [4]. I found no formal template document.
- **Follow-ups:** Items are tracked with owners and status. Examples are the INC-2340 follow-ups in the Identity & Billing weekly status [6] and the action items in the INC-2291 postmortem [4].
- **Open review:** The INC-2351 draft was circulated October 21 and is due at the November 5 reliability meeting. Root cause and action items will be added once it is accepted [2]. The sources don't name its author. The IC was Harriet Vance [2].
- **Exemptions:** SEV-3 incidents are marked "Not required" for a postmortem [2].

## Customer-impacting incidents

I found no separate review process for customer-impacting incidents. The customer-facing steps run alongside the postmortem:

- For SEV-1 incidents affecting Enterprise workspaces, the account team checks whether SLA credits are owed under the 99.95% commitment. It contacts the customer within one business day [3].
- The communications lead handles status page updates and customer messages [3].
- The INC-2291 postmortem records the customer impact: 96 support tickets and SLA credits issued to 41 Enterprise customers [4].

I didn't find any Support or Leadership documents on postmortems.

rows.answer:
**Yes. Northwind runs quarterly access reviews, and access that isn't re-confirmed is revoked automatically.** The only source that covers this is the information security policy. It gives the rule in one line and doesn't describe the process behind it.

## What the policy says
- **Frequency and owner:** "Quarterly access reviews are run by each team lead." [1]
- **If nobody signs off:** "Access that is not re-confirmed is revoked automatically." [1] Silence therefore removes access. Nobody has to act to revoke it.
- **Leavers:** All access is revoked within one hour of someone's final working time [1]. This is separate from the quarterly cycle.
- **Policy owner:** The Security team owns the policy, which was last reviewed in July 2026 [1].

## Other controls that limit standing access
- Production access goes through Teleport and expires after 8 hours. Nobody has standing access to production databases [1].
- Access to customer data needs a ticket linked to a support case or incident, and all sessions are recorded [1].
- Emergency access to a customer workspace expires after 2 hours. A second engineer must approve it, and that engineer can't be on the same case [2].
- Emergency sessions are recorded and kept for one year. Security reviews a sample of sessions every week, plus every session that used write access [2].
- Security exceptions to the policy need written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [1].

## What I couldn't find
- **Escalation and sign-off detail:** The documents don't say how a team lead confirms access, what evidence is kept, or whether Security checks that reviews were done. They also don't say what happens to a team lead who skips the review. The only stated consequence is automatic revocation.
- **Which tool does the revocation:** This isn't named.
- **EHR access:** Northwind doesn't appear to hold EHR data. Its leadership notes say it declined a healthcare analytics acquisition because of "HIPAA obligations we are not set up for" [3]. Its most sensitive data class is "Restricted" customer event data, in services such as `runner`, Driftwood and Keystone [4]. The quarterly review isn't tied to any monthly access-log review, as your compliance team does for EHR logs. The nearest equivalent is the weekly sample review of emergency-access sessions [2].
- **Vendor access reviews:** The vendor register entries for Cobaltline and Hollowpine don't mention periodic access reviews. They cover DPA status, security review, SOC 2 and renewal dates [5][6]. Hollowpine currently operates under security exception SEC-EX-117 because its DPA isn't signed [6].

If you need this to satisfy a HIPAA-style audit, ask Security (`#security-help`) for the underlying review procedure and evidence. The policy line alone probably won't be enough.

Sources: [1] Information security policy; [2] Emergency access to customer workspaces; [3] Leadership offsite notes (Oct 2026); [4] Service catalog; [5] Vendor register: Cobaltline; [6] Vendor register: Hollowpine Helpdesk.

rows.answer:
Before staff can use a new AI tool with patient data, it needs a security risk assessment, a signed business associate agreement (BAA), and an entry in the systems inventory. Clinical use also needs a CMIO safety review. The usual turnaround is **6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA** [2]. I didn't search Northwind's #vendor-review process, so I haven't compared the two.

## What Halcyon requires

To request a tool, email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui). Any tool that will handle PHI needs [2]:

1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed BAA with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO.

- **Inventory entry:** The inventory is maintained by the HIPAA Security Officer. A new system that will hold PHI needs its risk assessment, its BAA (if a vendor is involved) and its inventory entry **before go-live** [1]. The CSCAB minutes of Oct 28, 2026 repeated this: before go-live, not after [11].
- **BAA:** A vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI is a business associate. A signed BAA must be in place before any PHI is disclosed, including test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [3].
- **CMIO review:** The CMIO is Dr. Anjali Rao. Her delegate is Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [14].

## Who signs off

- The Privacy Officer and HIPAA Security Officer own the approved-AI-tools list and receive requests [2].
- The CMIO gives the clinical safety review for clinical use [2].
- For Quillon Ambient, expanding beyond the pilot clinics needs a Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) decision plus a clinical safety review based on pilot data [8]. CSCAB meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern and reviews "significant changes", which include patient-facing automation [14]. The AI-tools page doesn't say whether every new AI tool goes to CSCAB.

## How long it takes

- **Typical:** 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [2].
- **Quillon Ambient:** the risk assessment was completed in July 2026 and the BAA was executed July 30, 2026 [8]. The pilot started August 17, 2026 [8].
- **Tallgrass Survey Co. (not an AI tool, but a useful example):**
  - The BAA draft arrived in August 2026 and is still unsigned [3].
  - The open issue is data retention. Tallgrass wants 5 years and Halcyon will accept 18 months [3].
  - The risk assessment passed with conditions in September [3].
  - The Privacy Officer is due to send revised language by Nov 6, 2026 [3].
  - If the BAA isn't signed by Jan 31, 2027, QPS will look at other vendors [3].

## While review is pending

There is no interim-use route. PHI must never go into AI tools that aren't on the approved list [2][6]. That rules out:

- Public chatbots and general-purpose assistants, on any device including personal phones [2].
- Browser extensions that summarize pages [2].
- Meeting transcription apps [2].
- Translation apps for clinical conversations. Staff should use the interpreter service instead [2].

"De-identified" is not a loophole. Removing a name isn't enough, so any patient details count as PHI [2]. Other AI scribes are not approved, even for trials [8].

## Currently approved tools [2]

| Tool | PHI allowed? | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Quillon Ambient | Yes | Pilot clinics only (Riverside and Elm Park). Patient verbal consent at the start of every visit. Clinician reviews and signs every note. |
| Meridian draft replies | Yes | Clinician edits or approves before sending. Never auto-sent. |
| Halcyon Assist | No | Policy questions only. |

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** At Halcyon the equivalent is the **system steward** of the owning team. For the patient app that is **Felix Brandt** of Digital Health Engineering – Patient Engagement (DHE-PE). For a purely cosmetic change, his approval is enough on its own.

## Who owns the bill-pay screen
- The Halcyon app covers digital intake, messaging and bill pay. DHE-PE owns it, and it is built in-house [7].
- Each owning team has one system steward who approves changes to that team's systems. DHE-PE's steward is Felix Brandt [1].

## Is the steward's OK enough?
Yes, if the change really is cosmetic.
- The clinical systems change control policy lists "cosmetic changes" as a **minor change**, which needs **steward approval only** [1].
- Significant changes need the steward, a clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO (Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate Dr. Benedict Osei), and review at CSCAB [1]. Those apply to changes that affect:
  - patient-facing automation, including reminders, outreach messages and the patient app's clinical content;
  - medication information, or orders and results routing;
  - clinical decision support;
  - scheduler cutovers [1].
- A visual tweak to bill pay touches none of these. Minor changes are simply noted at CSCAB, with no vote or clinical review. For example, CHG-2026-126 was "Minor; steward approval only. Noted." [3]

I found no extra compliance, privacy or payment-screen review for minor changes. The only PHI-related rule I found is that a project adding a **new place where PHI is stored** needs a security risk assessment and an inventory entry before go-live [3]. A cosmetic tweak doesn't do that.

## Where it stops being "just cosmetic"
The change moves into significant territory if it:
- alters patient-facing messages or automated outreach, such as reminder or notification wording [1];
- changes clinical content in the app [1];
- changes what the screen does, rather than how it looks. The policy doesn't define "cosmetic" precisely, so confirm the classification with Felix if there's any doubt.

## Comparison with Northwind
| | Northwind | Halcyon |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Team's **change approver**, with a named delegate [13] | Team's **system steward** [1] |
| Backup when absent | Yes, each approver has a delegate [13] | I found no delegate listed for stewards [1] |
| Cosmetic change | Not a "normal" change. A change that is already pre-approved needs only normal PR review [12] | Minor change, steward approval required [1] |
| Extra approvers | Restricted-data services also need the Head of Security [12] | Only for significant changes: CMIO sign-off and CSCAB [1] |

Your Northwind habit doesn't transfer exactly, in two ways:
- At Northwind, a purely cosmetic change wouldn't normally need the approver at all. Only changes to "authentication, authorization or billing logic" are normal changes [12], and the handbook requires two PR approvals, one from a code owner, for code touching billing [15].
- At Halcyon, even a cosmetic change needs the steward's sign-off.

rows.answer:
Both clients fixed the problem the same way. Each added an idempotency key, so a repeat send is recognised and blocked. The keys differ, and so does the process each client added around them.

## Northwind Labs: duplicate September invoices (INC-2340, October 6)

**What went wrong:** The month-end invoicing job ran twice for some workspaces. The payment provider's webhook for the first batch timed out at 06:05. Northwind's retry logic then re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [6]. The result was 312 duplicate invoices across 287 workspaces. 201 of them were auto-charged, and all 201 were refunded, totalling $184,300 [6].

**The fix:**
- **Idempotency key:** invoice creation now uses a key per workspace and billing period [6]. It was merged and deployed the same day, and a dry run of the job produced zero duplicates [6]. The changelog lists it as shipped in release 2026.10.2 on October 8 [8][9].
- **Daily reconciliation report:** a report now compares invoices against charges. It is marked done [9].
- **Webhook-timeout alert:** an alert for provider webhook timeouts during a billing batch is still open, due November 6 [9]. That timeout started this incident, so this protection is not yet in place.
- **Portal change:** the Lantern invoice history now hides voided duplicates [9].

## Halcyon Health: duplicate medication reminders (IR-0412, September 3)

**What went wrong:** On September 2, the reminder scheduler was moved to a new job runner. During the cutover the old and new runners were both active, and neither checked whether a reminder had already been sent [1]. On September 3, 2,318 patients received each reminder two to four times between 06:00 and 09:40 Eastern. Twelve patients took an extra dose of a once-daily medication, and none needed treatment [1].

**The fixes:**
1. **Idempotency key:** reminders now carry a key made of patient, medication and scheduled time. A reminder whose key already exists is never sent again [1].
2. **Cutover runbook and sign-off:** scheduler cutovers need a written runbook and a clinical safety sign-off [1]. Under the change-control policy, the runbook must state how double-running is prevented [2].
3. **Message wording:** reminders now say "If you already took this dose, you don't need to take it again." [1]

Halcyon has also applied the idempotency-key rule to new patient-facing automation. The Marigold project's acknowledgement message follows the rules adopted after IR-0412, including the idempotency key on every message [5].

## Comparison

| | Northwind (Ledger invoicing) | Halcyon (reminder scheduler) |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Webhook timeout, then a batch retry | Old and new runners both active during a cutover |
| Technical fix | Key per (workspace, billing period) | Key per (patient, medication, scheduled time) |
| Process or other safeguards | Reconciliation report; timeout alert still open | Cutover runbook, clinical sign-off, wording change |

rows.answer:
**Northwind Labs covers you from day one. Halcyon Health covers you from the first of the month after you start, so you may wait up to about a month.**

| | Northwind Labs | Halcyon Health |
|---|---|---|
| Medical, dental and vision start | Your first day [1] | The first of the month after your start date [2] |
| Typical gap with no coverage | None | Anywhere from a few days to about a month |

**Examples for Halcyon**
- If you start on November 16, coverage would begin December 1.
- If you start on November 2, coverage would still begin December 1, which is almost a month later.

I'm reading "the first of the month after your start date" literally, as the first day of the next calendar month. The policy doesn't say what happens if you start on the 1st itself. Confirm that with Halcyon's People team (people@halcyon.example appears in their leave policy [6]).

**Clinical hires at Halcyon**
Halcyon sets a clinician's start date after credentialing, which takes 30 to 60 days [2]. The insurance rule is written for new hires generally, so benefits would still follow your start date, not your offer date. If you're a clinician, expect a longer lead time before you start and before coverage begins.

**What I couldn't find**
- Enrollment deadlines or paperwork windows at either company.
- Whether contractors, part-time staff or other employment types are treated differently. Both documents describe benefits for new employees in general.
- Any waiting period at Northwind beyond the "starts on your first day" statement.

If you need continuous coverage, ask either company about enrollment deadlines. At Halcyon, also ask about a bridge option such as COBRA or a marketplace plan for the gap.

**Short answer:** Northwind Labs has a holiday change freeze. Halcyon Health, as far as the knowledge base shows, does not.

## Northwind Labs: freeze from December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027

- **Dates and scope:** The holiday freeze runs December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027. During it, only standard and emergency changes ship [1]. The policy doesn't say whether January 4 is included. Confirm that before scheduling anything on that day.
- **What still ships:**
  - Standard changes are pre-approved and need only a normal PR review. Examples are `nwctl scale`, flipping a flag already rolled out in canary, automated credential rotation, and restarting a runner pod [1].
  - Emergency changes can be approved by the incident commander during a declared incident. The owning team's change approver must review them within two business days [1].
  - Rollbacks are allowed at any time, without approval, including during freezes [1][4].
- **What is blocked:** Normal changes. These include schema migrations, infrastructure configuration, retention settings, and auth or billing logic changes [1]. Get them out before December 18.
- **Exceptions:** If a team's change approver and delegate are both unavailable, the VP Engineering may approve. Exceptions are logged in `#eng-changes` [1]. During an incident, the incident commander can approve skipping the canary bake with `/deploy expedite` [4].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** This is a separate, recurring freeze. It blocks normal changes to Ledger from the last business day of the month until invoices go out, usually the 2nd [1]. For December, plan around December 31 to about January 2. That date is my inference from the rule, not a stated date.
- **Deploy window:** Deploys are Monday to Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific. Friday deploys need on-call engineering manager approval [4].
- **Pipeline timing:** A canary bake of 45 minutes applies. A typical change takes about 50 minutes to reach all cells, and a data-plane change takes about 2.5 hours [4].
- **On-call:** The December 22 week is staffed as "holiday freeze" [2]. The rota for shifts starting December 29 onward will be published by December 15 [2].
- **Related dates:**
  - The Thanksgiving-week approvers for Identity & Billing (Harriet Vance and Arjun Mehta) are both out November 24–27 [3].
  - The Undertow billing-provider cutover is scheduled for January 19, 2027, after the freeze [3].

## Halcyon Health: no IT freeze, but change control still applies

- **Freeze status:** The October 2026 Juniper steering committee notes say: "No IT freeze at Halcyon." Clinic managers did ask that pilot training not land in the week of December 21 [6]. I found no other holiday freeze policy.
- **Normal change control still applies:**
  - Minor changes need only the system steward's approval [10].
  - Significant changes need the steward's approval, CMIO clinical safety sign-off (Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate Dr. Benedict Osei), and review at CSCAB. CSCAB meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [10]. Significant changes include patient-facing automation, medication, orders or results routing, decision support rules, and scheduler or job-runner cutovers [10].
  - Emergency changes, to stop ongoing patient harm, can be approved by the on-call medical director, with CSCAB reviewing at its next meeting [10].
  - Cutovers need a written runbook explaining how double-running is prevented [10].
- **CSCAB holiday schedule:** I found nothing on whether CSCAB skips meetings over the holidays. Ask the Office of the CMIO, because that decides whether a significant change can get approved in late December.
- **Dates already set:**
  - The Juniper pilot is January 12, 2027, with go/no-go at the December 16 steering meeting [6].
  - A cutover is scheduled for Saturday, February 6, 2027 at 22:00 Eastern, with final go/no-go at CSCAB on January 27 [12].
  - Heron, Kestrel and Marigold are targeted for Q4 2026 [15]. Cutover and go-live dates are set by CSCAB, not the register [15].

## Vendor and support coverage

- **Halcyon:** No vendor blackout dates are listed. Most vendors offer 24/7 support, or 24/7 for P1. Some have limited hours [7]:
  - Larkspur runs 07:00–21:00 Eastern, 7 days.
  - Quillon runs 06:00–22:00 Eastern, Monday to Saturday, with no out-of-hours P1 line.
  - RotaLeaf runs 08:00–18:00 Eastern, Monday to Friday.
  - ClearPath's non-P1 support runs 07:00–19:00 Eastern, Monday to Friday.
  - Meridian staffs a live bridge line for any scheduled EHR upgrade [7].
  - The matrix doesn't say whether holiday hours differ.
- **Northwind:** Customer support "business hours" are 08:00–18:00 Monday to Friday in the customer's region, excluding that region's public holidays. P1 for Growth and Enterprise is 24/7 [9]. Non-P1 response on Growth and Enterprise tiers will therefore slow around public holidays.

## Gaps

- I found no documented holiday blackout dates for any vendor.
- I found no holiday CSCAB schedule for Halcyon.
- I found nothing confirming whether Northwind's end date of January 4 is inclusive.

**Err high at both companies. At Northwind the incident commander can change the rating. At Halcyon, Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) can.**

## Northwind Labs (incident severity)

**Which way to err:** Declare the higher severity. The Incident roles FAQ says: "When unsure, declare higher; downgrading is cheap" [3].

**Who can change it later:**
- Whoever declares the incident picks the initial severity [3].
- The incident commander (IC) "can raise or lower it at any time" [3].
- The IC is paged from a dedicated rotation when someone runs `/incident declare` [3]. The rotation currently includes Kofi Mensah, Priya Raman, Harriet Vance, Oluwaseun Adeyemi and Ravi Subramanian [13].
- Support tickets don't set severity. A P1 ticket priority doesn't decide it, because "severity is set by the incident process, not by the ticket priority" [4].

**Why it matters:** The level determines the response [2].
- SEV-1 means data loss or a full outage of ingest or pipelines for a cell. It means a page immediately, and an IC assigned within 15 minutes.
- SEV-2 means a partial outage or degraded performance affecting many customers. It means a page, with acknowledgement within 15 minutes.
- SEV-3 means a single-customer issue or a degraded non-critical feature. It means a ticket, handled the next business day.

Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 also needs a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution [3]. The Thursday reliability meeting reviews postmortems [3].

## Halcyon Health (patient safety events)

**Which way to err:** Report at the higher level. The Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy says: "When unsure, report at the higher level. QPS will reclassify if needed" [5]. The levels are [5]:
1. Sentinel event
2. Adverse event with harm
3. No-harm event
4. Near miss

**Who can change it later:** QPS (Quality & Patient Safety) reclassifies [5]. The policy names no individual or approval step for this. It doesn't say who inside QPS makes the call or how a reclassification is recorded. The QPS system steward is Lorraine Pike [12], but that is her change-control role, not a stated reclassification authority.

**Related steps in the policy:**
- Reporting is "never optional and never punished" [5].
- The charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour of a sentinel event [5].
- Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets a root cause analysis (RCA). QPS charters the team within 72 hours, and the RCA is due within 45 calendar days [5].
- The Patient Safety Committee, chaired by CMO Dr. Kenji Watanabe, reviews completed RCAs [5].
- Halcyon's escalation protocol takes the same stance: "When in doubt, escalate" [11].

## Summary

| | Northwind | Halcyon |
|---|---|---|
| If unsure | Declare higher [3] | Report at the higher level [5] |
| Who can change it | The IC, up or down, at any time [3] | QPS [5] |
| Documented review | Postmortem for SEV-1 and SEV-2, reviewed Thursdays [3] | RCA for Level 1 and 2, reviewed by the Patient Safety Committee [5] |

Neither knowledge base documents a formal approval process for changing a rating. Northwind's rule is the IC's authority. Halcyon's is a one-line statement that QPS will reclassify.

Both agreements are stuck on one disputed term about how the vendor may use the data. Neither has a signed agreement yet.

## Northwind Labs: Hollowpine Software Co. (helpdesk, VEN-031)

**What's holding it up:** Hollowpine wants the right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model. That is the main open point in the data processing agreement (DPA) [8]. Hollowpine's draft arrived in July 2026, and the redlines have been with Northwind's legal team since August [8].

**How Northwind is operating in the meantime:**
- Hollowpine runs under security exception SEC-EX-117, approved by the Head of Security on August 24, 2026 [8].
- The security review (VR-102) was a conditional pass. AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until the DPA is signed [8].
- Hollowpine handles ticket content, customer names and emails, and uploaded attachments [8].

**Deadlines and next steps:**
- The information security policy says exceptions expire after 90 days [14]. Counting from August 24, that would be about November 22, 2026. That date is my calculation, not one the register states.
- If the DPA is still unsigned when the exception lapses, Support Operations (Gwen Talbot) must either get it renewed or move ticket intake back to email [8].
- The contract renews January 31, 2027, at $44,000 a year [8].
- I found no named legal owner or target signing date for the redlines.

## Halcyon Health: Tallgrass Survey Co. (patient surveys, BA-021 proposed)

**What's holding it up:** The business associate agreement (BAA) is not executed, and the two sides disagree on retention. Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable survey responses for 5 years for benchmarking. Halcyon will accept 18 months [1]. Tallgrass sent its draft in August 2026 [1].

**Consequences and workarounds:**
- The signed order form is on hold until the BAA is executed [1].
- No PHI may go to Tallgrass before then, including test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [1].
- The security risk assessment was completed in September 2026 and passed with conditions [1].
- Until the BAA is signed, post-visit satisfaction scores for Juniper and in-person visits come from the in-app survey in the Halcyon app [1][2]. The October 2026 Juniper steering committee notes confirm this [2].

**Owners and deadlines:**
- The Privacy Officer, Margaret Holloway, is to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026 [1].
- The internal owner is Quality & Patient Safety (Lorraine Pike) [1].
- If the BAA isn't signed by January 31, 2027, Quality & Patient Safety will look at other survey vendors [1].
- Halcyon's tool-approval guidance says turnaround is typically 6–10 weeks, mostly spent waiting on the BAA [4].

## Comparison

| | Hollowpine (Northwind) | Tallgrass (Halcyon) |
|---|---|---|
| Disputed term | Vendor's right to train its AI model on ticket content | Retention of identifiable responses: vendor wants 5 years, Halcyon offers 18 months |
| Interim cover | Security exception SEC-EX-117, with AI features off | No PHI shared, with the in-app survey used instead |
| Next step | Legal redlines continue; renew the exception or revert to email if it lapses | Halcyon's Privacy Officer sends revised retention language by Nov 6, 2026 |
| Backstop | Exception expiry, about Nov 22 (my calculation) | Jan 31, 2027, then look at other vendors |

**Halcyon's self-pay prompt-pay discount is bigger: 20%, against 15% for Northwind's annual Growth prepayment.**

**Northwind Labs (annual Growth prepayment)**
- Growth lists at $1,200 a month. Prepaying annually earns 15% off, which comes to $12,240 a year [6].
- The September 24, 2026 sales memo keeps the 15% prepay discount unchanged [7]. The memo applies to quotes issued on or after October 1, 2026 [7].
- Discounts are measured against the first-year contract value at list price [7].
- Multi-year deals can add 5% per committed year, capped at 10%. That extra doesn't count toward the approval thresholds [6][7].
- A 15% discount is within an account executive's authority on a Growth deal [7]. Anything above 15% goes to the deal desk [7].
- Registered non-profits and accredited educational institutions get 50% off Growth automatically. That is separate from the prepay discount [6].

**Halcyon Health (self-pay, paid in full on the day)**
- Self-pay patients pay at the time of service. They get a 20% prompt-pay discount if they pay in full that day [1].
- Self-pay rates are $165 for a new patient visit, $120 for an established patient visit, $79 for telehealth and $195 for an annual physical [1]. The 20% applies to these rates, so a new patient visit would come to $132. That figure is my calculation.
- The discount does not apply to vaccines and injectables. Those prices are already set at cost plus administration [2].
- Patients in the sliding-fee program get the program discount instead. It reduces visit costs by 40–100% for households under 250% of the federal poverty level [1][2].

**Caveats**
- The two discounts aren't like for like. Northwind's is 15% off a year of subscription. Halcyon's is 20% off a single visit.
- The 20% has exclusions. It doesn't cover vaccines and injectables, and sliding-fee patients get the program discount.
- Northwind's 15% can rise with a multi-year commitment, up to 25% in total (15% plus the 10% cap). Both policies say it is allowed, but I found no worked example. For a plain annual prepay, Halcyon's 20% is still higher.

**Tomás Herrera (Halcyon Health)** is the Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) lead and system steward.

- **System steward for RCM.** Each owning team has one steward who approves changes to its systems. Tomás is RCM's [3]. Significant changes also need a clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO and review by the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB). Those are changes to patient-facing automation, medication information, orders or results routing, clinical decision support rules or alerts, and scheduler or job-runner cutovers [3].
- **Project Kestrel lead.** Kestrel is the ClearPath scheduling rules that block patients located in states where the clinician isn't licensed. As of the October 19 register it was "Build complete; awaiting release," targeted for Q4 2026 [9].
- **Link to Juniper.** The Juniper steering committee notes say Juniper depends on those ClearPath rules. Tomás confirmed they are in RCM's November release [1].
- **Internal owner of a vendor.** He is the internal owner of the Brightwater Billing Services business associate record (BA-003). Brightwater handles claims scrubbing, patient statement printing and mailing, and payment plans [6]. The contract renews November 30, 2026, and pricing renegotiation is in progress. No non-renewal notice has been given [6].

**Tomasz Wierzbicki (Northwind Labs)** is the Head of Security.

- **Security team lead and change approver.** He leads the SEC team (`#security-help`) and is its named change approver for normal production changes. The delegate is "Security on-call" [5]. His initials in RFCs are "TW" [5].
- **Owner of the customer data retention standard (v2).** It took effect September 15, 2026. It cut default archive retention from 400 to 365 days and shortened deletion-request completion from 30 to 14 days. It also lets enterprise customers contract for retention up to 730 days with security team approval [12].
- **Security reviewer on RFC-031.** The RFC covers persisting Tributary snapshots. His review is pending. He wants a threat model for copying Restricted data across tiers, and nothing ships to private beta until he signs off [19].
- **Leadership action item.** VP Engineering Dmitri Sokolov is to unblock the RFC-031 security review with Tomasz by the end of October [8]. Today is October 31, so that deadline is now. The documents don't show whether it was met.

**Notes for your records**
- These are two different people at two different companies. The spellings (Tomás and Tomasz) and surnames differ.
- Neither appears as a vendor contact in the other company's records. Tomás is named only as an internal owner in Halcyon's Vendors collection [6]. I found no vendor entry for Tomasz.

rows.answer:
## Northwind Labs

**Who can approve on the spot:** The incident commander (IC) can approve emergency changes during a declared incident [7]. That includes changes that would normally need the owning team's change approver [9]. The IC is paged from a dedicated rotation when someone runs `/incident declare` [9].

- **Example:** In INC-2340, a billing-logic fix would normally need the Identity & Billing approver, Harriet Vance. She noted that the IC, Kofi Mensah, could also approve it because a declared incident was under way [8].
- **Skipping the canary bake:** During an incident, the IC can approve skipping the bake with `/deploy expedite`. The expedite is logged in `#eng-changes` [12].
- **Rollbacks:** These are allowed at any time without approval, including during freezes [12].
- **Fallback for normal changes:** If a team's approver and delegate are both unavailable, the VP Engineering may approve. These exceptions are logged in `#eng-changes` [7]. This fallback is written for normal changes, not emergencies.

**Review afterwards:**
- Emergency changes must be reviewed retroactively by the owning team's change approver within two business days [7].
- Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 also gets a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution. It is reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [9].

## Halcyon Health

**Who can approve on the spot:** The on-call medical director may approve an emergency change. The policy defines emergency changes as those made "to stop ongoing patient harm" [1]. The on-call medical director is the senior physician on duty for the whole network [2]. To reach them, call the answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2. The service pages the backup if there is no callback within 10 minutes [2].

Normal approvals do not apply to emergencies. Significant changes need the system steward, the CMIO's clinical safety sign-off, and review at the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) [1].

**Review afterwards:**
- CSCAB reviews the emergency change at its next meeting [1]. It meets weekly on Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1].
- CSCAB decisions are logged in the change register on the intranet [1].
- Changes made without the required approvals are reported to Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) as safety events [1].
- If software or patient-facing automation caused the event, the sentinel and adverse event reporting policy also applies. The fixes then go through clinical systems change control [6].

## Key differences

| | Northwind Labs | Halcyon Health |
|---|---|---|
| On-the-spot approver | Incident commander, in a declared incident [7] | On-call medical director [1] |
| Trigger | A declared incident [7] | Stopping ongoing patient harm [1] |
| Review body | Owning team's change approver [7] | CSCAB [1] |
| Review deadline | Within 2 business days [7] | Next CSCAB meeting [1] |

The sources don't give Halcyon a fixed review deadline in days. Its timing depends on the weekly CSCAB schedule.
